passages.label: Title
passages.text:
Council Directive 2000/78/EC
of 27 November 2000
establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,
Having regard to the Treaty establishing the European Community, and in particular Article 13 thereof,
Having regard to the proposal from the Commission(1),
Having regard to the Opinion of the European Parliament(2),
Having regard to the Opinion of the Economic and Social Committee(3),
Having regard to the Opinion of the Committee of the Regions(4),
Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) In accordance with Article 6 of the Treaty on European Union, the European Union is founded on the principles of liberty, democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the rule of law, principles which are common to all Member States and it respects fundamental rights, as guaranteed by the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and as they result from the constitutional traditions common to the Member States, as general principles of Community law.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) The principle of equal treatment between women and men is well established by an important body of Community law, in particular in Council Directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976 on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment for men and women as regards access to employment, vocational training and promotion, and working conditions(5).

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) In implementing the principle of equal treatment, the Community should, in accordance with Article 3(2) of the EC Treaty, aim to eliminate inequalities, and to promote equality between men and women, especially since women are often the victims of multiple discrimination.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) The right of all persons to equality before the law and protection against discrimination constitutes a universal right recognised by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the United Nations Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, United Nations Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and by the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, to which all Member States are signatories. Convention No 111 of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) prohibits discrimination in the field of employment and occupation.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) It is important to respect such fundamental rights and freedoms. This Directive does not prejudice freedom of association, including the right to establish unions with others and to join unions to defend one's interests.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) The Community Charter of the Fundamental Social Rights of Workers recognises the importance of combating every form of discrimination, including the need to take appropriate action for the social and economic integration of elderly and disabled people.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) The EC Treaty includes among its objectives the promotion of coordination between employment policies of the Member States. To this end, a new employment chapter was incorporated in the EC Treaty as a means of developing a coordinated European strategy for employment to promote a skilled, trained and adaptable workforce.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) The Employment Guidelines for 2000 agreed by the European Council at Helsinki on 10 and 11 December 1999 stress the need to foster a labour market favourable to social integration by formulating a coherent set of policies aimed at combating discrimination against groups such as persons with disability. They also emphasise the need to pay particular attention to supporting older workers, in order to increase their participation in the labour force.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) Employment and occupation are key elements in guaranteeing equal opportunities for all and contribute strongly to the full participation of citizens in economic, cultural and social life and to realising their potential.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) On 29 June 2000 the Council adopted Directive 2000/43/EC(6) implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin. That Directive already provides protection against such discrimination in the field of employment and occupation.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) Discrimination based on religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation may undermine the achievement of the objectives of the EC Treaty, in particular the attainment of a high level of employment and social protection, raising the standard of living and the quality of life, economic and social cohesion and solidarity, and the free movement of persons.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) To this end, any direct or indirect discrimination based on religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation as regards the areas covered by this Directive should be prohibited throughout the Community. This prohibition of discrimination should also apply to nationals of third countries but does not cover differences of treatment based on nationality and is without prejudice to provisions governing the entry and residence of third-country nationals and their access to employment and occupation.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) This Directive does not apply to social security and social protection schemes whose benefits are not treated as income within the meaning given to that term for the purpose of applying Article 141 of the EC Treaty, nor to any kind of payment by the State aimed at providing access to employment or maintaining employment.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) This Directive shall be without prejudice to national provisions laying down retirement ages.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) The appreciation of the facts from which it may be inferred that there has been direct or indirect discrimination is a matter for national judicial or other competent bodies, in accordance with rules of national law or practice. Such rules may provide, in particular, for indirect discrimination to be established by any means including on the basis of statistical evidence.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) The provision of measures to accommodate the needs of disabled people at the workplace plays an important role in combating discrimination on grounds of disability.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) This Directive does not require the recruitment, promotion, maintenance in employment or training of an individual who is not competent, capable and available to perform the essential functions of the post concerned or to undergo the relevant training, without prejudice to the obligation to provide reasonable accommodation for people with disabilities.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) This Directive does not require, in particular, the armed forces and the police, prison or emergency services to recruit or maintain in employment persons who do not have the required capacity to carry out the range of functions that they may be called upon to perform with regard to the legitimate objective of preserving the operational capacity of those services.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) Moreover, in order that the Member States may continue to safeguard the combat effectiveness of their armed forces, they may choose not to apply the provisions of this Directive concerning disability and age to all or part of their armed forces. The Member States which make that choice must define the scope of that derogation.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) Appropriate measures should be provided, i.e. effective and practical measures to adapt the workplace to the disability, for example adapting premises and equipment, patterns of working time, the distribution of tasks or the provision of training or integration resources.

passages.label: Recital 21
passages.text: (21) To determine whether the measures in question give rise to a disproportionate burden, account should be taken in particular of the financial and other costs entailed, the scale and financial resources of the organisation or undertaking and the possibility of obtaining public funding or any other assistance.

passages.label: Recital 22
passages.text: (22) This Directive is without prejudice to national laws on marital status and the benefits dependent thereon.

passages.label: Recital 23
passages.text: (23) In very limited circumstances, a difference of treatment may be justified where a characteristic related to religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation constitutes a genuine and determining occupational requirement, when the objective is legitimate and the requirement is proportionate. Such circumstances should be included in the information provided by the Member States to the Commission.

passages.label: Recital 24
passages.text: (24) The European Union in its Declaration No 11 on the status of churches and non-confessional organisations, annexed to the Final Act of the Amsterdam Treaty, has explicitly recognised that it respects and does not prejudice the status under national law of churches and religious associations or communities in the Member States and that it equally respects the status of philosophical and non-confessional organisations. With this in view, Member States may maintain or lay down specific provisions on genuine, legitimate and justified occupational requirements which might be required for carrying out an occupational activity.

passages.label: Recital 25
passages.text: (25) The prohibition of age discrimination is an essential part of meeting the aims set out in the Employment Guidelines and encouraging diversity in the workforce. However, differences in treatment in connection with age may be justified under certain circumstances and therefore require specific provisions which may vary in accordance with the situation in Member States. It is therefore essential to distinguish between differences in treatment which are justified, in particular by legitimate employment policy, labour market and vocational training objectives, and discrimination which must be prohibited.

passages.label: Recital 26
passages.text: (26) The prohibition of discrimination should be without prejudice to the maintenance or adoption of measures intended to prevent or compensate for disadvantages suffered by a group of persons of a particular religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation, and such measures may permit organisations of persons of a particular religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation where their main object is the promotion of the special needs of those persons.

passages.label: Recital 27
passages.text: (27) In its Recommendation 86/379/EEC of 24 July 1986 on the employment of disabled people in the Community(7), the Council established a guideline framework setting out examples of positive action to promote the employment and training of disabled people, and in its Resolution of 17 June 1999 on equal employment opportunities for people with disabilities(8), affirmed the importance of giving specific attention inter alia to recruitment, retention, training and lifelong learning with regard to disabled persons.

passages.label: Recital 28
passages.text: (28) This Directive lays down minimum requirements, thus giving the Member States the option of introducing or maintaining more favourable provisions. The implementation of this Directive should not serve to justify any regression in relation to the situation which already prevails in each Member State.

passages.label: Recital 29
passages.text: (29) Persons who have been subject to discrimination based on religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation should have adequate means of legal protection. To provide a more effective level of protection, associations or legal entities should also be empowered to engage in proceedings, as the Member States so determine, either on behalf or in support of any victim, without prejudice to national rules of procedure concerning representation and defence before the courts.

passages.label: Recital 30
passages.text: (30) The effective implementation of the principle of equality requires adequate judicial protection against victimisation.

passages.label: Recital 31
passages.text: (31) The rules on the burden of proof must be adapted when there is a prima facie case of discrimination and, for the principle of equal treatment to be applied effectively, the burden of proof must shift back to the respondent when evidence of such discrimination is brought. However, it is not for the respondent to prove that the plaintiff adheres to a particular religion or belief, has a particular disability, is of a particular age or has a particular sexual orientation.

passages.label: Recital 32
passages.text: (32) Member States need not apply the rules on the burden of proof to proceedings in which it is for the court or other competent body to investigate the facts of the case. The procedures thus referred to are those in which the plaintiff is not required to prove the facts, which it is for the court or competent body to investigate.

passages.label: Recital 33
passages.text: (33) Member States should promote dialogue between the social partners and, within the framework of national practice, with non-governmental organisations to address different forms of discrimination at the workplace and to combat them.

passages.label: Recital 34
passages.text: (34) The need to promote peace and reconciliation between the major communities in Northern Ireland necessitates the incorporation of particular provisions into this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 35
passages.text: (35) Member States should provide for effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions in case of breaches of the obligations under this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 36
passages.text: (36) Member States may entrust the social partners, at their joint request, with the implementation of this Directive, as regards the provisions concerning collective agreements, provided they take any necessary steps to ensure that they are at all times able to guarantee the results required by this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 37
passages.text: (37) In accordance with the principle of subsidiarity set out in Article 5 of the EC Treaty, the objective of this Directive, namely the creation within the Community of a level playing-field as regards equality in employment and occupation, cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States and can therefore, by reason of the scale and impact of the action, be better achieved at Community level. In accordance with the principle of proportionality, as set out in that Article, this Directive does not go beyond what is necessary in order to achieve that objective,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
HAS ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:
CHAPTER I
GENERAL PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Purpose
The purpose of this Directive is to lay down a general framework for combating discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation as regards employment and occupation, with a view to putting into effect in the Member States the principle of equal treatment.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Concept of discrimination
1. For the purposes of this Directive, the "principle of equal treatment" shall mean that there shall be no direct or indirect discrimination whatsoever on any of the grounds referred to in Article 1.
2. For the purposes of paragraph 1:
(a) direct discrimination shall be taken to occur where one person is treated less favourably than another is, has been or would be treated in a comparable situation, on any of the grounds referred to in Article 1;
(b) indirect discrimination shall be taken to occur where an apparently neutral provision, criterion or practice would put persons having a particular religion or belief, a particular disability, a particular age, or a particular sexual orientation at a particular disadvantage compared with other persons unless:
(i) that provision, criterion or practice is objectively justified by a legitimate aim and the means of achieving that aim are appropriate and necessary, or
(ii) as regards persons with a particular disability, the employer or any person or organisation to whom this Directive applies, is obliged, under national legislation, to take appropriate measures in line with the principles contained in Article 5 in order to eliminate disadvantages entailed by such provision, criterion or practice.
3. Harassment shall be deemed to be a form of discrimination within the meaning of paragraph 1, when unwanted conduct related to any of the grounds referred to in Article 1 takes place with the purpose or effect of violating the dignity of a person and of creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment. In this context, the concept of harassment may be defined in accordance with the national laws and practice of the Member States.
4. An instruction to discriminate against persons on any of the grounds referred to in Article 1 shall be deemed to be discrimination within the meaning of paragraph 1.
5. This Directive shall be without prejudice to measures laid down by national law which, in a democratic society, are necessary for public security, for the maintenance of public order and the prevention of criminal offences, for the protection of health and for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.

passages.label: Article 3
Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Occupational requirements
1. Notwithstanding Article 2(1) and (2), Member States may provide that a difference of treatment which is based on a characteristic related to any of the grounds referred to in Article 1 shall not constitute discrimination where, by reason of the nature of the particular occupational activities concerned or of the context in which they are carried out, such a characteristic constitutes a genuine and determining occupational requirement, provided that the objective is legitimate and the requirement is proportionate.
2. Member States may maintain national legislation in force at the date of adoption of this Directive or provide for future legislation incorporating national practices existing at the date of adoption of this Directive pursuant to which, in the case of occupational activities within churches and other public or private organisations the ethos of which is based on religion or belief, a difference of treatment based on a person's religion or belief shall not constitute discrimination where, by reason of the nature of these activities or of the context in which they are carried out, a person's religion or belief constitute a genuine, legitimate and justified occupational requirement, having regard to the organisation's ethos. This difference of treatment shall be implemented taking account of Member States' constitutional provisions and principles, as well as the general principles of Community law, and should not justify discrimination on another ground.
Provided that its provisions are otherwise complied with, this Directive shall thus not prejudice the right of churches and other public or private organisations, the ethos of which is based on religion or belief, acting in conformity with national constitutions and laws, to require individuals working for them to act in good faith and with loyalty to the organisation's ethos.

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Reasonable accommodation for disabled persons
In order to guarantee compliance with the principle of equal treatment in relation to persons with disabilities, reasonable accommodation shall be provided. This means that employers shall take appropriate measures, where needed in a particular case, to enable a person with a disability to have access to, participate in, or advance in employment, or to undergo training, unless such measures would impose a disproportionate burden on the employer. This burden shall not be disproportionate when it is sufficiently remedied by measures existing within the framework of the disability policy of the Member State concerned.

passages.label: Article 6
passages.text:
Article 6
Justification of differences of treatment on grounds of age
1. Notwithstanding Article 2(2), Member States may provide that differences of treatment on grounds of age shall not constitute discrimination, if, within the context of national law, they are objectively and reasonably justified by a legitimate aim, including legitimate employment policy, labour market and vocational training objectives, and if the means of achieving that aim are appropriate and necessary.
Such differences of treatment may include, among others:
(a) the setting of special conditions on access to employment and vocational training, employment and occupation, including dismissal and remuneration conditions, for young people, older workers and persons with caring responsibilities in order to promote their vocational integration or ensure their protection;
(b) the fixing of minimum conditions of age, professional experience or seniority in service for access to employment or to certain advantages linked to employment;
(c) the fixing of a maximum age for recruitment which is based on the training requirements of the post in question or the need for a reasonable period of employment before retirement.
2. Notwithstanding Article 2(2), Member States may provide that the fixing for occupational social security schemes of ages for admission or entitlement to retirement or invalidity benefits, including the fixing under those schemes of different ages for employees or groups or categories of employees, and the use, in the context of such schemes, of age criteria in actuarial calculations, does not constitute discrimination on the grounds of age, provided this does not result in discrimination on the grounds of sex.

passages.label: Article 7
passages.text:
Article 7
Positive action
1. With a view to ensuring full equality in practice, the principle of equal treatment shall not prevent any Member State from maintaining or adopting specific measures to prevent or compensate for disadvantages linked to any of the grounds referred to in Article 1.
2. With regard to disabled persons, the principle of equal treatment shall be without prejudice to the right of Member States to maintain or adopt provisions on the protection of health and safety at work or to measures aimed at creating or maintaining provisions or facilities for safeguarding or promoting their integration into the working environment.

passages.label: Article 8
passages.text:
Article 8
Minimum requirements
1. Member States may introduce or maintain provisions which are more favourable to the protection of the principle of equal treatment than those laid down in this Directive.
2. The implementation of this Directive shall under no circumstances constitute grounds for a reduction in the level of protection against discrimination already afforded by Member States in the fields covered by this Directive.
CHAPTER II
REMEDIES AND ENFORCEMENT

passages.label: Article 9
passages.text:
Article 9
Defence of rights
1. Member States shall ensure that judicial and/or administrative procedures, including where they deem it appropriate conciliation procedures, for the enforcement of obligations under this Directive are available to all persons who consider themselves wronged by failure to apply the principle of equal treatment to them, even after the relationship in which the discrimination is alleged to have occurred has ended.
2. Member States shall ensure that associations, organisations or other legal entities which have, in accordance with the criteria laid down by their national law, a legitimate interest in ensuring that the provisions of this Directive are complied with, may engage, either on behalf or in support of the complainant, with his or her approval, in any judicial and/or administrative procedure provided for the enforcement of obligations under this Directive.
3. Paragraphs 1 and 2 are without prejudice to national rules relating to time limits for bringing actions as regards the principle of equality of treatment.

passages.label: Article 10
passages.text:
Article 10
Burden of proof
1. Member States shall take such measures as are necessary, in accordance with their national judicial systems, to ensure that, when persons who consider themselves wronged because the principle of equal treatment has not been applied to them establish, before a court or other competent authority, facts from which it may be presumed that there has been direct or indirect discrimination, it shall be for the respondent to prove that there has been no breach of the principle of equal treatment.
2. Paragraph 1 shall not prevent Member States from introducing rules of evidence which are more favourable to plaintiffs.
3. Paragraph 1 shall not apply to criminal procedures.
4. Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall also apply to any legal proceedings commenced in accordance with Article 9(2).
5. Member States need not apply paragraph 1 to proceedings in which it is for the court or competent body to investigate the facts of the case.

passages.label: Article 11
passages.text:
Article 11
Victimisation
Member States shall introduce into their national legal systems such measures as are necessary to protect employees against dismissal or other adverse treatment by the employer as a reaction to a complaint within the undertaking or to any legal proceedings aimed at enforcing compliance with the principle of equal treatment.

passages.label: Article 12
passages.text:
Article 12
Dissemination of information
Member States shall take care that the provisions adopted pursuant to this Directive, together with the relevant provisions already in force in this field, are brought to the attention of the persons concerned by all appropriate means, for example at the workplace, throughout their territory.

passages.label: Article 13
passages.text:
Article 13
Social dialogue
1. Member States shall, in accordance with their national traditions and practice, take adequate measures to promote dialogue between the social partners with a view to fostering equal treatment, including through the monitoring of workplace practices, collective agreements, codes of conduct and through research or exchange of experiences and good practices.
2. Where consistent with their national traditions and practice, Member States shall encourage the social partners, without prejudice to their autonomy, to conclude at the appropriate level agreements laying down anti-discrimination rules in the fields referred to in Article 3 which fall within the scope of collective bargaining. These agreements shall respect the minimum requirements laid down by this Directive and by the relevant national implementing measures.

passages.label: Article 14
passages.text:
Article 14
Dialogue with non-governmental organisations
Member States shall encourage dialogue with appropriate non-governmental organisations which have, in accordance with their national law and practice, a legitimate interest in contributing to the fight against discrimination on any of the grounds referred to in Article 1 with a view to promoting the principle of equal treatment.
CHAPTER III
PARTICULAR PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 15
passages.text:
Article 15
Northern Ireland
1. In order to tackle the under-representation of one of the major religious communities in the police service of Northern Ireland, differences in treatment regarding recruitment into that service, including its support staff, shall not constitute discrimination insofar as those differences in treatment are expressly authorised by national legislation.
2. In order to maintain a balance of opportunity in employment for teachers in Northern Ireland while furthering the reconciliation of historical divisions between the major religious communities there, the provisions on religion or belief in this Directive shall not apply to the recruitment of teachers in schools in Northern Ireland in so far as this is expressly authorised by national legislation.
CHAPTER IV
FINAL PROVISIONS

passages.label: Article 16
passages.text:
Article 16
Compliance
Member States shall take the necessary measures to ensure that:
(a) any laws, regulations and administrative provisions contrary to the principle of equal treatment are abolished;
(b) any provisions contrary to the principle of equal treatment which are included in contracts or collective agreements, internal rules of undertakings or rules governing the independent occupations and professions and workers' and employers' organisations are, or may be, declared null and void or are amended.

passages.label: Article 17
passages.text:
Article 17
Sanctions
Member States shall lay down the rules on sanctions applicable to infringements of the national provisions adopted pursuant to this Directive and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are applied. The sanctions, which may comprise the payment of compensation to the victim, must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive. Member States shall notify those provisions to the Commission by 2 December 2003 at the latest and shall notify it without delay of any subsequent amendment affecting them.

passages.label: Article 18
passages.text:
Article 18
Implementation
Member States shall adopt the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive by 2 December 2003 at the latest or may entrust the social partners, at their joint request, with the implementation of this Directive as regards provisions concerning collective agreements. In such cases, Member States shall ensure that, no later than 2 December 2003, the social partners introduce the necessary measures by agreement, the Member States concerned being required to take any necessary measures to enable them at any time to be in a position to guarantee the results imposed by this Directive. They shall forthwith inform the Commission thereof.
In order to take account of particular conditions, Member States may, if necessary, have an additional period of 3 years from 2 December 2003, that is to say a total of 6 years, to implement the provisions of this Directive on age and disability discrimination. In that event they shall inform the Commission forthwith. Any Member State which chooses to use this additional period shall report annually to the Commission on the steps it is taking to tackle age and disability discrimination and on the progress it is making towards implementation. The Commission shall report annually to the Council.
When Member States adopt these measures, they shall contain a reference to this Directive or be accompanied by such reference on the occasion of their official publication. The methods of making such reference shall be laid down by Member States.

passages.label: Article 19
passages.text:
Article 19
Report
1. Member States shall communicate to the Commission, by 2 December 2005 at the latest and every five years thereafter, all the information necessary for the Commission to draw up a report to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of this Directive.
2. The Commission's report shall take into account, as appropriate, the viewpoints of the social partners and relevant non-governmental organisations. In accordance with the principle of gender mainstreaming, this report shall, inter alia, provide an assessment of the impact of the measures taken on women and men. In the light of the information received, this report shall include, if necessary, proposals to revise and update this Directive.

passages.label: Article 20
passages.text:
Article 20
Entry into force
This Directive shall enter into force on the day of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Communities.

passages.label: Article 21
passages.text:
Article 21
Addressees
This Directive is addressed to the Member States.
Done at Brussels, 27 November 2000.
For the Council
The President
É. Guigou

findings.title: Article 6(2) changes the stated scope of the occupational age exception
findings.explanation: English expressly refers to admission or entitlement to retirement or invalidity benefits. Danish refers generally to access to occupational social security schemes, potentially allowing the age exception for a wider range of schemes while leaving benefit-entitlement ages less explicitly covered. Interpreting access to include benefits could resolve the latter issue but would not supply the missing retirement-or-invalidity qualification.

findings.title: German potentially narrows the duty to remove discriminatory contractual terms
findings.explanation: Article 16(b) uses “contracts or collective agreements” in English and “Arbeits- und Tarifverträgen” in German. German could therefore narrow this specific duty to invalidate or amend discriminatory terms by excluding covered agreements that are not employment contracts, such as certain self-employment or vocational training agreements. The Directive's broader protections still apply.

impact_families.title: Personal care and maintenance duties
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), particularly Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: An age-related recruitment measure supports middle-aged applicants returning after providing personal care to an adult relative, without a legal maintenance obligation. The applicants do not independently fall within the examples of young people or older workers.
impact_families.rationale:
Even assuming that Swedish confines this category to maintenance obligors, exclusion from the example does not exclude personal carers from Article 6(1). The list is expressly illustrative. Listed and unlisted measures must satisfy the same legitimate-aim, appropriateness and necessity requirements. Neither express recognition nor its absence establishes a different exemption or discrimination decision.
Counterreading: Swedish and Danish maintenance terminology, German and Czech care terminology, and French responsibility for dependants can be reconciled around obligations toward dependent people. Their equal authority and the open list favour an inclusive interpretation; a strict maintenance-only interpretation is not established as the governing multilingual meaning.
impact_families.uncertainty: Swedish wording may exclude personal carers without a legal maintenance duty from this express example. Article 6(1)(a) is non-exhaustive and the general legitimate-aim and necessity test remains available. A distinct legal entitlement or changed justification outcome has not been established from the example's wording alone.

impact_families.title: Remuneration and recommendations
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), particularly Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: A national measure establishes age-related starting pay for young workers to promote vocational integration. Alternatively, a measure regulates employment recommendations according to age.
impact_families.rationale:
Even if recomendación retains its literal recommendation meaning, remuneration remains within the broader employment-conditions wording. Employment recommendations can likewise fall within access-to-employment conditions. Both measures remain subject to the same general justification test, and the examples are non-exhaustive. Neither removal of the express pay example nor addition of recommendations establishes a changed legal outcome.
Counterreading: The surrounding employment terms and the remuneration wording in French, German and Portuguese strongly support reading the provision consistently as addressing pay. That conclusion follows from textual coherence and the provision's function, rather than treating English as controlling. The literal recommendation reading is unlikely to govern multilingual interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Spanish noun may change which conditions are named in Article 6(1)(a), but that provision lists non-exhaustive examples subject to the general legitimate-aim and necessity test. An age-related pay rule or employment-recommendation rule can still be assessed under that test. No changed justification result follows from the example's wording alone.

impact_families.title: Completed correction of discriminatory provisions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 16(b)'s invalidation and amendment alternatives, read with Article 2.
impact_families.effect: An undertaking retains a recruitment rule established to constitute prohibited discrimination, with no applicable exception. An effective judicial invalidation procedure exists, but the rule has not been invalidated or amended and is not automatically void.
impact_families.rationale:
If completed invalidation or amendment is required, providing an effective invalidation procedure alone ceases to satisfy Article 16(b). Actual amendment remains an alternative, and Article 16(a) does not independently remove this private rule. The change is substantial because it alters the required corrective result across the provision's categories, without requiring a subsequent discriminatory act.
Counterreading: The authentic versions have equal authority. Polish can describe the result secured by an effective legal framework, including invalidation on application. French, German and Dutch expressly accommodate that possibility; Lithuanian, Croatian and Romanian use result-focused wording. Reading the provision as requiring an effective corrective framework could reconcile these formulations. A universal requirement for completed intervention is therefore not established.
impact_families.uncertainty:
This is a conditional difference in the Member State's compliance obligation. It establishes neither an actual national failure nor a particular entitlement to compensation. Effective automatic invalidity would remove the distinction; continued appearance of words in a document alone would not prove non-compliance.
Unresolved: No additional dependency prevents the stated conditional difference, provided the provision is within scope, established as discriminatory, and remains legally intact despite an effective invalidation route.

impact_families.title: Maintenance obligors as beneficiaries
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), particularly Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: An age-related employment protection covers middle-aged workers who owe financial maintenance to former spouses but provide no personal care. Assume they are outside the young-person and older-worker examples and that financial maintenance alone falls outside the disputed care category.
impact_families.rationale:
The wording can change express inclusion, but Article 6(1)(a) creates no automatic entitlement or exemption for named groups. The opening justification test applies equally to maintenance obligors and personal carers, and the non-exhaustive list permits measures for either. A changed legal outcome therefore remains unsupported even on the assumed categorical distinction.
Counterreading: Financial support may itself constitute a caring responsibility. Hungarian maintenance terminology, French dependants terminology and German care terminology support an interpretation encompassing different forms of responsibility for others. The authentic versions do not establish mutually exclusive beneficiary classes.
impact_families.uncertainty: Hungarian wording may expressly include financial maintenance obligors who provide no personal care. Article 6(1)(a) nevertheless gives non-exhaustive examples governed by the general legitimate-aim and necessity test. Express inclusion alone has not been shown to change the treatment of a particular measure or its legal justification.

impact_families.title: Slovenian participation criteria refer to the Directive instead of national law
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(2), particularly the criteria reference, legitimate interest and consent; Article 9(3).
impact_families.effect: An equality association excluded by an additional national eligibility criterion seeks participation with the claimant's consent, arguing that only Directive-defined criteria may govern.
impact_families.rationale:
The Slovenian text expressly refers to criteria defined in this Directive rather than national law. However, the supplied provisions establish no replacement organisational eligibility test. Even accepting that reference, neither admission of this association nor displacement of its particular national restriction follows. Legitimate interest remains required. The change in wording therefore does not yet support a concrete changed standing outcome or an awarded impact tier.
Counterreading: Directive-defined criteria can describe the standards whose compliance the organisation seeks to secure, without exhaustively regulating procedural eligibility or excluding national criteria. This reading harmonizes the provision's functions without silently treating English as superior.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Slovenian criteria phrase may describe the Directive's substantive compliance standards rather than replace national rules for an organisation's legitimate interest. The Directive identifies no alternative organisational eligibility test that would decide this association's standing. Consent and applicable time limits also remain conditions, so a changed standing outcome is unestablished.

impact_families.title: Training agreements outside employment contracts
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 2, 3(1)(b) and 16(b).
impact_families.effect: A private vocational-training admission agreement contains a term established to exclude applicants because of sexual orientation, with no applicable exception. It creates no employment relationship, and the term appears in no collective, undertaking or professional rule.
impact_families.rationale:
Article 3(1)(b) covers access to vocational training in the public and private sectors. If Finnish Article 16(b)'s contractual limb reaches only employment and collective agreements, this separate admission agreement loses that Article's express voiding-or-amendment duty; the Directive's substantive protection and other remedies still apply. The separate independent-professional-activity limb does not capture the stated agreement.
Counterreading: All authentic versions have equal authority. Czech, German and Italian also use employment-contract language; French and Dutch use broader terms. A common interpretation could broaden the occupational understanding of the contractual category or retain an employment-specific limb with protection elsewhere. Finnish's broad independent-activity wording strengthens the need to examine the whole list rather than infer exclusion from the contractual phrase alone.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The conditional effect depends on the agreement truly being outside employment and every other Article 16(b) category. The authentic versions may be reconciled by a broader reading of the contractual limb. No actual national failure or lawful discrimination follows.
Unresolved: The agreement’s precise classification and the reach of the contractual limb under a multilingual reading remain open; the conditional change to the express Article 16(b) duty is otherwise identifiable.

impact_families.title: Conditional additional malice requirement
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 11; Articles 1–10, 15 and 17; recital 30.
impact_families.effect: Following an internal equality complaint, an ordinary civilian employer withdraws a modest discretionary benefit to recoup complaint-handling costs. Objective disadvantage and employer counteraction are established, but distinct malicious intent is not proved. There is no dismissal, independent protected-ground discrimination or harassment, and no additional national protection.
impact_families.rationale:
The Estonian override retains pahatahtliku, suggesting malicious treatment where English requires adversity. The surrounding clause preserves employer causation; it does not expressly define malice. The internal complaint satisfies the alternative trigger regardless of court-only wording. No relevant exception applies, and Articles 9, 10 and 17 do not eliminate an assumed substantive malice requirement. Both reviewers identify this mechanism; their different benefit and shift examples do not establish different legal thresholds.
Counterreading: Read pahatahtliku as wrongful retaliatory disadvantage, consistently with the employer-response clause, recital 30 and other authentic adverse-treatment formulations. That interpretation removes the additional intent threshold.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Malice may add nothing beyond proven retaliatory counteraction. A protective-purpose shift change, as in reviewer B, also requires care to establish counteraction; the selected scenario expressly establishes that limb. No automatic Article 10 burden shift for every victimisation claim is assumed.
Unresolved: Whether malice is independently required and how it is established; whether national law supplies broader protection.

impact_families.title: Personal carers entering employment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), particularly Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: An age-related vocational-training measure benefits unemployed middle-aged applicants returning after providing unpaid personal care. They financially support nobody and do not fall within the young-person or older-person examples.
impact_families.rationale:
Assuming both restrictions prevail, these applicants fall outside the named category. They remain eligible for measures justified under the open Article 6(1) test, and inclusion in the example would not remove its legitimate-aim and proportionality requirements. The broader Greek reference to older people also changes an illustration without establishing a separate exemption. No concrete changed legal decision follows from either descriptive difference.
Counterreading: The express coverage of access to employment and vocational training resists limiting workers to people already employed. Supporting others can encompass practical care, while German care terminology and French and Italian dependants terminology support a shared concern for dependency responsibilities. A strict current-worker-and-financial-provider restriction is therefore less persuasive in the multilingual context.
impact_families.uncertainty: Greek wording may exclude unpaid personal carers who do not financially support another person from this express example. Article 6(1)(a) is non-exhaustive, however, and the same legitimate-aim and necessity test remains available. A different outcome for such a measure has not been established.

impact_families.title: Teaching appointments outside schools
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(2), read with Articles 2, 4(1)–(2) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: An adult-education institution in Northern Ireland, outside the narrower school category, recruits a teacher under an expressly authorised religious-community balancing arrangement. If 'εκπαιδευτικά ιδρύματα' includes that institution, the broader reading grants Article 15(2) non-application where a school-only reading does not.
impact_families.rationale:
The conditional change is the inclusion of additional teaching appointments within a statutory exclusion. Article 2's definitions do not narrow the institutional expression or supply an alternative school boundary. The effect is moderate for an identifiable additional group, without requiring a finding that its recruitment practices violate another rule.
Counterreading: An educational institution can itself be a school, so the Greek expression need not enlarge the exception. French, German and English expressly connect teacher recruitment with schools. Their wording, read with the common purpose and equal authority of all versions, favours a shared school-sector meaning, although the quoted text does not define the precise institutional boundary.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No particular institution or national authorisation is established. The example assumes an institution genuinely outside the narrower school category and a post qualifying as teacher recruitment; neither every educational institution nor every employee necessarily qualifies. A genuine and determining occupational requirement under Article 4, including an applicable religious-ethos rule under Article 4(2), or qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently affect lawfulness. Neither follows from Article 15 eligibility or legislative authorisation alone.
Unresolved: The hypothetical fixes the institutional boundary needed for the conditional comparison. Classification of an actual institution would require further facts and legal context. Article 2(5) may independently protect a necessary statutory measure, but does not determine eligibility under Article 15(2).

impact_families.title: Express protection after termination is limited to employment relationships
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(1), including its general-access guarantee; Article 9(3); Article 2.
impact_families.effect: A former vocational trainee brings a timely discrimination claim concerning a non-employment training relationship. The employment-specific survival clause is invoked to contest access.
impact_families.rationale:
Töösuhe specifies employment, whereas the English text refers to a relationship generally. Nevertheless, the Estonian paragraph independently guarantees procedures to everyone who considers themselves wronged through unequal treatment. Accepting the employment-specific meaning does not establish that former non-employees lose access. No concrete changed access outcome survives Article 9(1)'s independent guarantee, so no conditional impact tier is assigned.
Counterreading: Isegi juhul introduces an additional assurance for ended employment, not an exhaustive condition for access. The general guarantee continues to cover everyone otherwise within the Directive.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Estonian employment-specific survival phrase may give former employees an additional assurance without excluding others. Article 3(1)(b) covers vocational training, and Article 9(1) grants access to all persons who consider themselves wronged, subject to Article 9(3) deadlines. The hypothetical assumes a timely claim on a protected ground. No identified provision removes that general access solely because a non-employment training relationship ended. A changed access outcome remains unestablished even if the disputed phrase is read narrowly.

impact_families.title: Teacher recruitment exemption boundaries
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(2), read with Articles 2, 4(1)–(2) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: First, legislation genuinely permits by implication a community-balancing exclusion for teacher recruitment at a Northern Ireland school, without express authorisation. Second, legislation expressly authorises such an exclusion for recruiting a teacher at an educational institution genuinely outside the narrower school category. The broader Estonian reading grants Article 15(2) eligibility in each scenario through a different boundary change.
impact_families.rationale:
The first scenario isolates the authorisation threshold while keeping the institution a school. The second isolates institutional reach while satisfying express authorisation. Either supported broader reading changes the application of the religion-or-belief provisions for an identifiable group. Their combination does not establish a wider scale or consequence sufficient for a high assessment.
Counterreading: Finnish, French and English expressly retain both schools and express authorisation. The common purpose and those equally authoritative formulations support understanding the Estonian clause as subject to both boundaries. 'Õpetajate' may also carry a school-focused meaning in context. The multilingual reading therefore favours harmonisation, although the operative wording does not conclusively define the institutional boundary.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Neither an actual legislative permission nor an affected appointment is established. Implied permission must derive from legislation rather than silence. For the second scenario, the recruit must qualify as a teacher and the institution must genuinely lie outside the narrower school category. A genuine and determining occupational requirement under Article 4, including an applicable religious-ethos rule under Article 4(2), or qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently affect lawfulness. Neither follows from Article 15 eligibility or legislative authorisation alone.
Unresolved: Article 2's definitions do not supply either disputed boundary. Article 2(5) could separately protect necessary statutory measures, but permission alone does not establish necessity. Final liability under other provisions or national law remains open; neither conditional Article 15(2) eligibility comparison requires that liability to be established.

impact_families.title: Possible requirement for both judicial and administrative remedies
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(1), compared with Article 9(2) and subject to Article 9(3).
impact_families.effect: A hypothetical Member State provides judicial enforcement for timely, covered direct-discrimination complaints but no administrative enforcement route.
impact_families.rationale:
Romanian și is conjunctive, whereas the supplied English permits either category or both. If paragraph 1 requires both categories to be available, the hypothetical system must add administrative access. Paragraph 2's și/sau concerns organisational participation and is not an express exception to paragraph 1. This supports a moderate change in the required procedural provision, without establishing a right to duplicate litigation, cumulative remedies or a different discrimination decision.
Counterreading: Procedurile judiciare și administrative can name the relevant classes collectively rather than require every system to establish both. The provision's accessibility focus supports this harmonization.
impact_families.uncertainty: Romanian 'judicial and administrative' may name procedural categories collectively. Its Article 9(2) uses 'and/or', and Spanish and Czech Article 9(1) expressly allow alternatives, making a mandatory dual-route reading uncertain. Moderate addresses only the conditional duty to add an administrative route in the stated hypothetical; it does not imply duplicate remedies or an actual breach.

impact_families.title: Nationality and immigration safeguards
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(2), read with Articles 3(1) and 2(1)–(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: A third-country national challenges a residence-permit condition restricting access to employment and disadvantaging people of a particular religion.
impact_families.rationale:
The Latvian relative clause attaches the non-interference wording to nationality-based treatment rather than clearly stating an independent immigration safeguard. Nevertheless, Article 2 still requires discrimination on a protected ground; a conditional nationality exclusion does not itself establish protection against nationality discrimination. The final legal-status phrase can also be read as a separate exclusion. The proposed employment restriction therefore does not establish a changed scope outcome even if the immigration safeguard is narrowed.
Counterreading: The French and Czech texts distinguish nationality, immigration provisions and legal-status treatment. Their structure supports reading the Latvian sentence as expressing the same three boundaries. That harmonizing interpretation is stronger than treating the relative clause as an intentional change in coverage, although the wording alone cannot settle the ultimate interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The decisive uncertainty is whether a particular restriction would escape the remaining legal-status exclusion. For an indirect-discrimination claim, Article 2(2)(b) also requires examination of objective justification; Article 2(5) preserves qualifying necessary national measures.
Unresolved: What restriction would cease to be safeguarded while independently satisfying Article 3(1) and Article 2, without remaining excluded as treatment arising from legal status?

impact_families.title: Non-member organisational participation
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(1)(d), checked against Article 3(1)(a)–(c) and Article 2(2)(a), (5).
impact_families.effect: A workers' organisation invites non-members to contribute voluntarily to drafting its policy but excludes an otherwise comparable contributor solely because of sexual orientation. The contribution involves no recruitment, vocational training, membership decision or benefit provided to the contributor.
impact_families.rationale:
Estonian expressly covers belonging to an organisation and its benefits, without separately naming involvement. If that wording excludes independent non-member participation, the stated contribution loses the scope protection afforded by involvement. Article 3(1)(a)–(c) supplies no alternative coverage on these facts. The refusal engages Article 2's direct-discrimination concept under the broader scope reading; no necessary national measure under Article 2(5) is posited.
Counterreading: Belonging can encompass active participation, and organisational benefits may include opportunities to participate. French and Finnish expressly protect engagement or activity, strengthening that broader interpretation. The narrower reading is therefore less persuasive in multilingual context, particularly for members' activities.
impact_families.uncertainty:
This establishes a conditional difference in protection for the specified activity, not a finding about an actual organisation or a final violation. Participation that confers benefits or forms part of employment or training may remain covered independently.
Unresolved: For an actual activity, its relationship to membership, benefits, employment and training would require verification. Those alternative routes are excluded by the stated hypothetical facts.

impact_families.title: Individual vocational assessment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(1)(b), checked against Article 3(1)(a), (c)–(d) and Article 2(2)(a), (5).
impact_families.effect: A standalone careers service makes vocational information available to everyone but refuses an otherwise comparable applicant an individual aptitude assessment solely because of sexual orientation. The assessment provides vocational guidance and is independent of recruitment, education, training, employment and organisational benefits.
impact_families.rationale:
Latvian names vocational information where other authentic texts name guidance or counselling. If information excludes the stated individual assessment, access to that service falls outside the narrower category while remaining vocational guidance under the broader reading. The other Article 3(1) limbs do not restore coverage on the stated facts. The result is a conditional loss of protection for a defined service, sufficient to support a moderate impact.
Counterreading: Information of all types and levels can encompass personalised advice and assessment feedback. The Czech counselling wording and German Berufsberatung support that inclusive interpretation. In multilingual context, this broader reading is stronger than a restriction to impersonal information.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The ultimate interpretation of vocational information remains open. An actual service might combine information, counselling and education, or be a condition of access to employment, preserving coverage independently. No actual refusal or final violation is established.
Unresolved: An actual service's functions and links to recruitment, education or employment would need verification. For the stated standalone assessment, the conditional distinction follows once the narrower meaning of information is assumed.

impact_families.title: Scheme entry versus benefit eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 6(2), 6(1), including 6(1)(b), and 2(2)(a).
impact_families.effect: National law relies on Article 6(2) for an occupational retirement scheme that excludes employees under 25 from membership. Membership admission is legally distinct from eligibility for benefits; the restriction involves no actuarial calculation and neither originates in nor produces sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
If benefit eligibility excludes separate admission, the membership restriction loses that specific exemption. The provision concerning different ages for employee categories elaborates the covered thresholds; it does not independently exempt every age restriction. The actuarial limb does not cover a separate membership exclusion. Article 6(1), including employment advantages under paragraph (b), may provide another justification, but cannot restore eligibility under Article 6(2).
Counterreading: Swedish eligibility language can encompass entry as a preliminary condition of obtaining future benefits. German membership terminology, French adhesion terminology and Dutch entry-age terminology expressly distinguish admission from benefit entitlement. Read together with the scheme context, these support harmonization that includes admission; the benefit-only reading is less persuasive as the ultimate multilingual interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The scenario depends on an actual scheme treating membership separately from benefit eligibility. National law must exercise Article 6(2), and the age rule must satisfy its sex-discrimination condition. The multilingual interpretation may still include entry ages. Article 6(1) could provide an independent justification, so loss of this specific exemption does not establish unlawful discrimination.

impact_families.title: Training-capability limb omitted; refusal outcome unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, recital 17 and Article 2(1)–(2), including Article 2(2)(b)(i)–(ii); Articles 3 and 5 are material omitted dependencies.
impact_families.effect: Test case: an applicant whose disability engages the Directive can undertake vocational training but cannot yet perform the intended job. Admission is refused solely because the applicant lacks current job capability.
impact_families.rationale:
Italian expressly includes training among the actions but attaches only the essential-job-functions test; it lacks the separate capacity-to-undergo-training limb present in the supplied German, French and other versions. This supports the alleged textual difference. However, even accepting a current-job-capability reading leaves the expressly preserved accommodation duty intact. Article 2 requires a protected-ground discrimination analysis; a neutral admission prerequisite remains subject to legitimate-aim, appropriateness and necessity requirements. Neither the omission nor 'né prevede la formazione' independently establishes an operative permission to refuse otherwise protected training.
Counterreading: Read the recital's competence limitation in relation to the activity requested. Training ordinarily develops capabilities not yet possessed; requiring completed job competence before training would need contextual justification. The Italian accommodation safeguard and Article 2's Article 5 cross-reference reinforce that harmonization without treating another authentic language as controlling.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 3(1)(b) covers vocational training, and Article 5 requires employers to accommodate disabled persons for training unless the burden is disproportionate. The example still depends on whether the provider is the responsible employer and whether present job capability is an appropriate and necessary admission criterion under Article 2. The Italian recital alone does not establish lawful refusal.

impact_families.title: Membership before acquisition of benefit rights
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 6(2), 6(1), including 6(1)(b), and 2(2)(a).
impact_families.effect: National law invokes Article 6(2) for an occupational retirement scheme admitting employees only from age 25. Admission is legally separate from the granting or acquisition of benefit rights. The rule does not calculate benefits and neither originates in nor produces sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
Assuming that the Polish wording excludes separate scheme admission, the entry restriction falls outside Article 6(2). The reference to different ages for employees or categories remains linked to the covered age thresholds. The benefit-calculation limb does not independently cover an admission restriction. Article 6(1) may justify an employment advantage subject to a minimum age, but its legitimate-aim and proportionality requirements constitute a separate route.
Counterreading: Acquisition of benefit rights can begin with joining a scheme, allowing the Polish wording to encompass admission. German, French and Hungarian expressly distinguish entry from entitlement, supporting that harmonizing interpretation. A strict benefit-rights-only reading is therefore less persuasive in the multilingual context, although the authentic versions do not settle every scheme structure.
impact_families.uncertainty: Membership may itself create pension rights in an actual scheme, eliminating the stated separation from entitlement. National law must exercise the Article 6(2) option, and the rule must satisfy its sex-discrimination condition. The multilingual interpretation may encompass admission despite the narrower wording. A separate Article 6(1) justification may also remain available, so no overall discrimination outcome is determined.

impact_families.title: Initiating proceedings versus participating in proceedings
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(2), read with Article 9(1) and (3).
impact_families.effect: In a hypothetical national system, a qualifying organisation may initiate proceedings but cannot enter an existing case. With the claimant's approval, it seeks to support a timely, otherwise covered direct-discrimination claim already filed by an employee.
impact_families.rationale:
Iniciar expressly describes initiation. If an initiation-only minimum prevails, Article 9(2) would not require access for later supporting participation; a participation-inclusive construction would protect that role. This is a concrete change in the required procedural protection. Article 9(1) preserves the individual's access but does not independently confer the organisation's role. The supported consequence is moderate: a specific participation entitlement changes, without evidence that the claim or its merits necessarily change.
Counterreading: An organisation can initiate an intervention within existing proceedings, and en su apoyo can encompass assistance throughout a case. Thus iniciar need not confine protection to whoever commenced the principal action. The conditional rating assumes that stronger harmonization does not prevail.
impact_families.uncertainty: Spanish 'iniciar' may include starting an intervention in an existing case, and 'en su apoyo' may allow continuing support. German and Portuguese participation wording supports harmonization. Moderate assumes an initiation-only minimum with a qualified organisation, claimant consent and a timely claim; no actual national exclusion or different merits result is established.

impact_families.title: Scheme admission age limits
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), including its employee-category and calculation clauses; Articles 6(1), including (b), and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: National law exercises Article 6(2) for a covered occupational pension scheme. The scheme bars membership before age 25 through a standalone entry condition, distinct from benefit-entitlement ages and any actuarial calculation, without resulting sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
The Estonian expression ties the age limits to obtaining pension or invalidity benefits. If that benefit-only construction prevails, the standalone membership restriction loses Article 6(2) eligibility. The following 'including' clause is grammatically an elaboration of those limits, not an independent exemption for every age distinction within a scheme. A membership bar is not itself an insurance-statistical calculation. Article 6(1), including its employment-advantage example, remains subject to justification and proportionality. Its availability does not restore eligibility under Article 6(2). Neither Article 2(2)(b) nor the conditional national-measures reservation in Article 2(5) automatically supplies the missing exemption.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats entering a scheme as a stage in obtaining benefits. German and Dutch expressly distinguish membership from benefit entitlement, making that distinction a substantive contextual argument for admission coverage. Finnish benefit-focused wording supports the narrower textual possibility. These conflicting formulations leave the ultimate construction open without treating English or a numerical majority as decisive.
impact_families.uncertainty: In some schemes, joining may itself confer pension rights; the hypothetical separates admission from entitlement. Whether the authentic versions can be reconciled to include admission is open. Real membership effects, scheme coverage and national adoption need checking. Article 6(1) may provide an independent justification even if Article 6(2) does not apply, so no discrimination outcome is determined.

impact_families.title: Promotion within employment protection
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(1)(a)–(c), read with Article 2(2)(a).
impact_families.effect: An employer refuses an otherwise comparable employee promotion to a managerial position solely because of sexual orientation.
impact_families.rationale:
The Czech phrase names acquiring practical experience instead of promotion. However, the phrase introduces an example rather than an exhaustive category. Even accepting that substitution, promotion can remain access to employment or occupation at a higher professional level and an employment condition under Article 3(1)(c). Practical experience is already covered by Article 3(1)(b), so the substitution also establishes no clear expansion.
Counterreading: The Czech references to all professional levels and employment conditions support continued promotion coverage internally. The French and German express references to advancement reinforce that reading without giving English greater authority.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The textual difference is clear, but no promotion scenario has been established in which the substitution changes protection after the remaining operative wording is applied.
Unresolved: Is there a promotion decision covered only by the express example, outside both access at all professional levels and employment or working conditions? The available provisions establish none.

impact_families.title: Training action omitted; affirmative entitlement not established
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, recital 17; Article 2(2)(a), (2)(b)(i)–(ii); omitted operative training and accommodation provisions in Articles 3 and 5.
impact_families.effect: Test case: a disabled trainee cannot satisfy essential course requirements even with appropriate adjustments. The trainee argues that the recital's qualification limitation excludes only recruitment, promotion and continued employment, so cannot justify ending training.
impact_families.rationale:
The Polish list genuinely omits provision of training, although its preceding capability clause expressly includes continuing the relevant training. Giving the action-list omission substantive effect would remove an express recital argument; it would not itself supply an entitlement. Article 2(2)(a) still requires comparable circumstances and protected-ground less favourable treatment. Article 2(2)(b)(i) independently permits justified neutral requirements. For someone unable to meet essential course requirements after adjustments, these provisions may sustain exclusion regardless of the omission. The reviews' example therefore does not establish a changed result.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonization reads 'lub kontynuacji danego kształcenia' as evidence that the qualification principle concerns training too. Czech and German make both sides of that connection explicit. Even if this harmonization is rejected, the ordinary operative discrimination tests remain applicable and may produce the same outcome.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 3(1)(b) covers vocational training, and Article 5 requires appropriate employer accommodation absent disproportionate burden. Yet a trainee unable to meet essential course requirements even after adjustment may still be excluded under the operative discrimination and justification rules. The Polish recital's reference to continuing training also supports harmonization; omitting training from its action list has not shown a changed entitlement.

impact_families.title: Completed removal of discriminatory provisions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 16(b)'s abolition, invalidation and amendment alternatives, read with Article 2.
impact_families.effect: An undertaking retains a recruitment rule established to constitute prohibited discrimination, with no applicable exception. Courts can invalidate it, but no abolition, declaration of invalidity or corrective amendment has occurred, and it is not automatically void.
impact_families.rationale:
If completed correction is required, an effective invalidation procedure alone no longer satisfies Article 16(b). Abolition, invalidation or an amendment removing the discriminatory content would each satisfy the stronger reading. Article 16(a) does not independently remove the private rule. The change reaches all listed categories and concerns the legal compliance requirement itself.
Counterreading: All authentic versions have equal authority. Lithuanian's introductory duty to ensure correction could describe an effective framework operating when invoked. French, German and Dutch expressly preserve available invalidation; Polish, Croatian and Romanian use completed-result wording. A functional reading centered on effective corrective mechanisms offers a substantial reconciliation, so the stronger completed-result interpretation is not established as the ultimate meaning.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No actual discriminatory application, compensation entitlement or national compliance failure is established. Automatic legal invalidity would remove the difference, and the wording does not necessarily require separate proceedings or individual administrative action against every provision.
Unresolved: No additional dependency prevents the stated conditional compliance difference, provided the rule is within scope, established as discriminatory and remains legally intact despite an effective invalidation route.

impact_families.title: Reversed police authorisation condition
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(1), read with Articles 2, 4(1) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: Northern Ireland police recruitment gives a preference to an underrepresented major religious community, without express legislative authorisation. The literal Hungarian exception would give that treatment Article 15(1)'s non-discrimination protection; the authorisation-dependent reading would withhold it.
impact_families.rationale:
The phrase 'kivéve akkor, ha' introduces an exception where the other cited versions impose a prerequisite. Assuming that reversal prevails, access to Article 15(1)'s statutory protection changes for an identifiable recruitment category. Conversely, expressly authorised treatment loses this particular protection, but does not automatically become discriminatory.
Counterreading: Hungarian paragraph 2 makes express authorisation a positive condition. The corrective purpose and the express conditions in the equally authoritative French, German and English versions support the same structure in paragraph 1. That coherent reading is substantially stronger in multilingual context than an exemption triggered by the absence of authorisation.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The recruitment arrangement is hypothetical. Article 2's definition of direct discrimination still requires less favourable treatment on a protected ground in a comparable situation; loss of the Article 15(1) protection alone does not establish those elements or final liability. Qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently support a measure addressing underrepresentation. Article 4(1) would require distinct evidence of a genuine and determining occupational requirement; community balancing alone does not prove one.
Unresolved: Article 2(2)(b)(i) concerns objectively justified indirect discrimination and does not automatically resolve an expressly religion-based preference. Article 2(5) separately requires necessary statutory measures. Neither prevents the conditional change in Article 15(1) eligibility; ultimate legality under other provisions and national law remains undetermined.

impact_families.title: Care and maintenance responsibilities
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), including Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: An age-differentiated employment measure supports workers caring for financially independent relatives. A maintenance-only reading excludes these carers from the express example. Conversely, it includes financial providers who perform no personal care.
impact_families.rationale:
The Polish wording supports a maintenance-based category, but both versions expressly make the examples non-exhaustive. Inclusion in Article 6(1)(a) does not dispense with objective and reasonable justification, a legitimate aim, and appropriate and necessary means. Exclusion does not remove access to that same general test. The other examples likewise do not turn the beneficiary list into an exhaustive eligibility condition. Neither direction of the wording difference therefore establishes a concrete changed legal outcome.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats care and dependency as overlapping forms of responsibility warranting employment support. German care terminology and French dependency terminology illustrate this range without making English controlling.
