A narrower category could nevertheless survive within the example without narrowing Article 6(1) itself.
impact_families.uncertainty: Whether care and maintenance can be reconciled through a common broader reading is open. Even on a maintenance-only reading, Article 6(1)(a) is a non-exhaustive example governed by the same general legitimate-aim and necessity test. Exclusion from the example does not by itself change an exemption or entitlement, so the practical legal effect remains unresolved.

impact_families.title: Retirement ages and scheme admission
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 6(2), 6(1), including 6(1)(b), and 2(2)(a).
impact_families.effect: National law invokes Article 6(2) for an occupational pension scheme excluding employees under 25 from membership. Admission is distinct from retirement and acquisition of pension rights. The rule involves no actuarial calculation and neither originates in nor produces sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
If the Slovenian wording covers retirement and pension-rights ages but excludes distinct admission ages, the entry restriction loses Article 6(2) eligibility. Different ages for employee categories elaborate the covered thresholds, while the actuarial limb does not independently exempt membership exclusion. Article 6(1) may offer another justification without restoring the specific exemption. The scheme context does not establish a general exemption for compulsory dismissal.
Counterreading: Retirement terminology can describe pension-scheme conditions, and acquiring pension rights may encompass entry. German, French and Dutch expressly distinguish membership from entitlement, supporting an interpretation that includes admission while preserving the occupational-scheme limitation. Croatian's similar retirement wording reinforces the need for contextual reconciliation but does not itself establish a dismissal exemption.
impact_families.uncertainty: The admission scenario requires an actual scheme to separate membership from pension-rights acquisition; that distinction may disappear under real scheme terms. National law must exercise Article 6(2), and the rule must neither originate in nor produce sex discrimination. The multilingual reading may still include admission, and a separate Article 6(1) justification could remain available. No compulsory-retirement or overall discrimination outcome is determined.

impact_families.title: Employment-only contractual correction
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 2, 3(1)(b) and 16(b).
impact_families.effect: A private vocational-training admission agreement contains a term established to exclude applicants because of sexual orientation, with no applicable exception. It creates no employment relationship, and the term appears in no collective, undertaking or professional rule.
impact_families.rationale:
Article 3(1)(b) covers access to vocational training in the public and private sectors. If Czech Article 16(b)'s contractual limb reaches only employment and collective agreements, this separate admission agreement loses that Article's express voiding-or-amendment duty; the Directive's substantive protection and other remedies still apply.
Counterreading: All authentic versions have equal authority. German, Finnish and Italian also specify employment contracts, whereas French and Dutch use broader contractual language. Harmonization could either give the contractual category a broader occupational meaning or preserve an employment-specific limb alongside protection elsewhere. The Directive's general purpose alone does not resolve that choice.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The conditional effect depends on the agreement truly being outside employment and every other Article 16(b) category. The authentic versions may be reconciled by a broader reading of the contractual limb. No actual national failure or lawful discrimination follows.
Unresolved: The agreement’s precise classification and the reach of the contractual limb under a multilingual reading remain open; the conditional change to the express Article 16(b) duty is otherwise identifiable.

impact_families.title: Conciliation is included without an appropriateness condition
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(1), subject to Article 9(3).
impact_families.effect: A hypothetical Member State provides judicial enforcement for timely, covered workplace-discrimination complaints but makes no conciliation procedure available because it considers conciliation inappropriate.
impact_families.rationale:
The Estonian inclusion contains no equivalent to the express appropriateness qualification. If it requires conciliation availability unconditionally, providing judicial access alone would not satisfy that additional requirement. The administrative-or-judicial wording does not expressly make the included conciliation optional. A distinct procedural avenue therefore changes under the disputed construction, supporting moderate impact without assuming compulsory settlement or any different merits result.
Counterreading: Kaasa arvatud may include conciliation within the procedures whose accessibility must be ensured when available, without requiring its creation in every system. Reading that phrase with the other authentic qualifications preserves discretion.
impact_families.uncertainty: Estonian inclusion may describe conciliation where available rather than require every Member State to create it. Finnish, German and Slovenian expressly preserve a Member State appropriateness assessment, supporting harmonization. Moderate applies only if the Estonian wording nonetheless imposes an additional conciliation route; no actual breach or compulsory settlement is established.

impact_families.title: Implied police recruitment permission
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(1), read with Articles 2, 4(1) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: National legislation genuinely permits by implication a Northern Ireland police recruitment preference addressing a major religious community's underrepresentation, without expressly authorising that preference. If implied permission satisfies the Estonian condition, Article 15(1) protects the preference; an express-permission requirement does not.
impact_families.rationale:
Estonian requires permission by national legislation but contains no separate expressness requirement. Assuming that wording admits implied permission, the same recruitment measure gains a statutory declaration of non-discrimination. This is a moderate eligibility change for a defined recruitment group, without establishing the measure's final legality.
Counterreading: Permission 'by national legislation' can itself demand a sufficiently specific legislative basis. Finnish, French and English expressly require authorisation, supporting that narrower understanding when all versions are read together. Bulgarian also lacks a separate expressness term and refers to legislative regulation, illustrating why lexical omission alone does not establish permission by implication. The broader interpretation remains possible but is less persuasive in context.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No national provision establishing implied permission is identified. Mere silence, absence of prohibition or employer discretion does not necessarily amount to permission by legislation. Qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently support a measure addressing underrepresentation. Article 4(1) would require distinct evidence of a genuine and determining occupational requirement; community balancing alone does not prove one.
Unresolved: Article 2(2)(b)(i) addresses justified indirect discrimination and does not automatically protect a religion-based preference. Article 2(5) requires necessity beyond legislative permission. Other provisions may affect final liability, but do not prevent the conditional change in Article 15(1) eligibility.

impact_families.title: Pension entitlement and membership ages
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), including its employee-group and actuarial clauses; Articles 6(1), including (b), and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: A covered occupational pension scheme admits employees only from age 25. This membership condition is distinct from acquiring pension entitlement and from actuarial calculations. National law exercises the Article 6(2) option and no sex discrimination results.
impact_families.rationale:
Both Lithuanian alternatives concern a right to receive a pension being granted or acquired. If that entitlement-only reading prevails, the stipulated membership condition loses Article 6(2) eligibility. The phrase introduced by 'įskaitant' remains subordinate to the preceding pension-age rule; its references to employee ages, groups and categories do not clearly create a free-standing exemption for all classifications. The actuarial limb does not cover a standalone membership restriction. Article 6(1), including the example concerning employment-linked advantages, remains a separate route subject to its general conditions. Article 2(2)(b) and Article 2(5) offer no unconditional alternative exemption.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading understands acquisition of pension rights as including admission into the arrangement that creates those rights. German and French expressly distinguish membership or adhesion from benefit entitlement, supporting admission coverage. Estonian and Finnish benefit-focused formulations support the narrower textual possibility. Neither group of authentic versions can resolve the issue by numerical weight.
impact_families.uncertainty: Membership may confer pension rights in an actual scheme; the scenario assumes a separate entry condition. The multilingual interpretation of admission remains open. Scheme coverage, the rule’s real function and national adoption must be checked in any application. Article 6(1) may independently justify an age rule even if Article 6(2) does not exempt it; this assessment does not determine unlawful discrimination.

impact_families.title: Discriminatory origin versus consequences
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2)'s final condition, read with Articles 6(1) and 2.
impact_families.effect: A Member State has exercised the Article 6(2) option for an occupational pension-entitlement age. The age rule arose independently of sex discrimination but causes legally established indirect sex discrimination. Absence of discriminatory origin is assumed separately from absence of discriminatory intent.
impact_families.rationale:
If the Slovenian condition tests only origin, the stated rule passes that condition; an effects-based condition excludes it from Article 6(2). The different-employee-ages and actuarial limbs remain subject to the same final condition and do not bypass it. Another age justification under Article 6(1) would not erase this change in eligibility for the specific exemption. Passing the age exemption does not authorize sex discrimination.
Counterreading: The safeguard's protective function and the consequence-based wording in German, French and Croatian favour reading Slovenian as preventing discriminatory effects. The literal reversal of causal direction is real, but an origin-only condition is unlikely to prevail in a coherent multilingual interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty: The scenario assumes legally established indirect sex discrimination but an age rule with an origin independent of sex discrimination; absence of discriminatory intent alone would not suffice. Article 6(2) concerns only the age exemption. Actual discriminatory effects and the rule's origin would need proof under applicable sex-equality law, and this assessment does not determine overall lawfulness under that law.

impact_families.title: Willingness differs from availability; alternative grounds prevent a demonstrated outcome
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, recital 17; Article 2(2)(a), (2)(b)(i)–(ii) and (5); omitted scope and occupational-requirement provisions.
impact_families.effect: Test case: an otherwise qualified and willing applicant cannot attend a required weekly shift because of religious observance. The employer rejects the applicant under a neutral attendance requirement.
impact_families.rationale:
Greek 'πρόθυμο' expresses willingness or readiness and does not expressly reproduce temporal availability. But accepting that distinction leaves 'κατάλληλο' and 'ικανό', suitability and capability, operative within the same sentence. Inability to attend genuinely essential shifts may fall within those limbs. Article 2(2)(b)(i) also independently permits appropriate and necessary scheduling requirements serving a legitimate aim. Conversely, if the shift is unnecessary, the availability formulations tied to essential functions do not obviously create an unrestricted refusal defence. Neither branch establishes a different hiring outcome merely from the lexical difference.
Counterreading: Read willingness as readiness to perform the particular duties in their actual setting, while keeping suitability and capability as separate requirements. For disability-related restrictions, the express accommodation safeguard remains; the religious-observance example does not itself trigger that disability-specific safeguard. Article 2(5) requires qualifying measures laid down by national law and cannot simply be assumed to validate an employer's roster.
impact_families.uncertainty: Greek willingness may be reconciled with practical readiness through the separate suitability and capability terms. The hiring result depends on whether the shift is essential and whether a neutral attendance requirement is appropriate and necessary under Article 2(2)(b)(i). Article 4(1), if invoked, has its own genuine-and-determining occupational-requirement conditions. Willingness alone establishes no changed outcome.

impact_families.title: Accommodation wording diverges; changed operative outcome unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, recital 17; Article 2(1), (2)(a), (2)(b)(i)–(ii) and (5); expressly cross-referenced Article 5.
impact_families.effect: Test case: a disabled employee can perform essential functions with an appropriate adjustment but is dismissed following an assessment without that adjustment. The disputed reading treats present, unadjusted capability as sufficient for the recital's employment limitation.
impact_families.rationale:
The Slovak phrase 'bez ohľadu na' supports 'regardless of', creating genuine tension with formulations expressly preserving accommodation. Nevertheless, accepting that meaning does not establish permission to disregard a separate operative duty. The supplied Slovak Article 2(2)(b)(ii) expressly connects appropriate measures to Article 5. Article 2 also retains direct-discrimination comparability and indirect-discrimination justification requirements. The recital's statement that employment is not required is not itself an operative derogation. The proposed dismissal therefore remains legally unresolved even on the disputed reading.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonization treats qualification requirements and accommodation as coexisting: the Directive does not guarantee employment irrespective of essential-function capability, while capability must be assessed consistently with applicable accommodation obligations. German 'unbeschadet', French 'sans préjudice' and the Slovak Article 2 cross-reference support this construction through legal coherence, not language counting or English priority.
impact_families.uncertainty: Article 5 expressly requires employers to provide appropriate disability accommodation unless it imposes a disproportionate burden; Article 2(2)(b)(ii) refers to those measures. The Slovak recital can be read consistently with that duty. Its 'regardless of' wording alone has not been shown to permit an unadjusted capability assessment or change the proposed dismissal outcome.

impact_families.title: Benefit amount calculation exemption
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), read with Articles 6(1) and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: A covered occupational pension scheme uses a flat age-band multiplier to reduce benefit amounts, without actuarial calculation. National law exercises Article 6(2), admission and entitlement ages remain unchanged, and no sex discrimination results.
impact_families.rationale:
The Polish phrase expressly concerns calculating benefit amounts and contains no actuarial qualifier. If that reading prevails, the multiplier gains Article 6(2) exemption eligibility. The separate age-setting limb, including different ages for employee categories, does not independently cover an amount adjustment. Article 6(1) remains a conditional alternative rather than an equivalent categorical exemption. Article 2(2)(b) does not automatically justify an expressly age-based multiplier, and Article 2(5) requires additional national-measure and necessity conditions. The supported outcome is changed exemption eligibility, not a finding of unlawful discrimination.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing construction treats benefit calculation as actuarial benefit valuation in this insurance context. German insurance-mathematical, French actuarial and Lithuanian actuarial terms give concrete support for retaining a technical limitation. Latvian's benefit wording supports taking the Polish lexical difference seriously, but neither formulation alone determines the common legal meaning.
impact_families.uncertainty: The finding also suggests a converse question about actuarial contribution or funding calculations, which requires separate analysis. The rated scenario concerns only a genuinely non-actuarial benefit-amount rule. Actual methodology, coverage and national adoption need verification. Article 6(1) may independently justify the age distinction even if Article 6(2) does not exempt it; this assessment establishes no violation.

impact_families.title: Organisations’ procedural entitlement is framed as initiating proceedings
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(2), read with Article 9(1) and (3).
impact_families.effect: An organisation meeting national legitimate-interest criteria obtains consent to support an employee's pending, timely direct-discrimination case. Hypothetical national rules permit organisational initiation but exclude participation after the claimant has filed.
impact_families.rationale:
Aloittaa means to begin or initiate. If that limits the guaranteed organisational role to commencement, later participation falls outside the Article 9(2) minimum. Under a participation-inclusive construction, the same exclusion would conflict with the protected role. Article 9(1)'s individual-access guarantee does not supply that organisational entitlement. Moderate reflects a concrete procedural difference without assuming loss of the underlying claim.
Counterreading: Häntä tukeakseen can encompass continuing assistance, and starting an intervention may itself constitute initiating a procedure. This reading could preserve access to an existing case despite aloittaa. The rating assumes a narrower construction excluding that possibility.
impact_families.uncertainty: Finnish 'aloittaa' may include starting an intervention in a pending case, and its support language may allow an ongoing role. German and Swedish participation wording reinforces that harmonizing reading. The Moderate scenario assumes an initiation-only minimum, a qualified organisation, claimant consent and a timely claim; it establishes no actual national exclusion.

impact_families.title: Temporary-residence safeguards
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(2), read with Articles 3(1) and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: A temporary resident challenges an employment restriction attached to a residence permit that particularly disadvantages people of a particular religion.
impact_families.rationale:
Bulgarian expressly qualifies residence as permanent. Even if that qualification limits the residence-provisions safeguard, the same paragraph independently preserves treatment arising from legal status and provisions concerning entry. A temporary permit's employment restriction may remain protected on those grounds. Narrowing one safeguard consequently does not establish that this restriction becomes subject to the Directive.
Counterreading: The unrestricted residence wording in French and Czech, together with Bulgarian's own unqualified legal-status safeguard, supports coverage of temporary residence within the overall protection. Recital 12 also refers to residence without a permanent-residence limit.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The restriction's connection to legal status or entry must be resolved first. If an indirect-discrimination claim falls within scope, objective justification under Article 2(2)(b) and any applicable Article 2(5) measure would also require examination.
Unresolved: Can a temporary-residence provision affect a protected employment activity without also being preserved as an entry provision or treatment arising from legal status? The stated permit scenario does not establish that distinction.

impact_families.title: Individual contracts outside collective wording
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 16(a)–(b), read with Article 2.
impact_families.effect: An individually negotiated employment contract contains a term established to discriminate unlawfully because of sexual orientation. The term is unconnected with any collective agreement and appears in no undertaking, professional or organisational rule.
impact_families.rationale:
If the Maltese phrase covers only collective-agreement contracts, this term loses the express Article 16(b) requirement for invalidation, availability of invalidation or amendment. None of the other listed private instruments captures it as described, and Article 16(a) addresses public provisions. This is a concrete change in a specific corrective obligation even though substantive discrimination remains prohibited.
Counterreading: All authentic versions have equal authority. Greek, Dutch and Swedish expressly include individual contracts, and Czech and Finnish expressly include employment contracts. These formulations and the provision's corrective purpose strongly support reading Maltese as encompassing individual employment contracts. Bulgarian's collective-contract wording supports the narrower textual possibility, but does not establish the common interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The result does not establish that the term becomes enforceable, that other remedies disappear, or that any actual Member State has failed to comply. National law may already provide the same correction independently.
Unresolved: No unresolved dependency prevents the stated difference in the express Article 16(b) duty. Incorporation into another listed instrument would remove the example from the disputed boundary.

impact_families.title: Proof protection in representative proceedings
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 9(2) and 10(1)–(5).
impact_families.effect: An organisation pursues a worker's civil discrimination claim under Article 9(2). Reading Latvian paragraph 4 as confined to criminal proceedings removes the express extension to that civil action, but does not necessarily remove its burden shift.
impact_families.rationale:
Latvian expressly says criminal proceedings. Nevertheless, paragraph 1 generally protects wronged persons presenting indicative facts before a court or competent authority. Narrowing paragraph 4 therefore does not itself establish that a represented person loses protection. Paragraph 3 also remains applicable: paragraph 4 cannot be read as introducing the burden shift into criminal proceedings.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonising reading treats paragraph 4 as extending the proof provisions to proceedings generally under Article 9(2), while preserving the criminal exclusion. Independently, paragraph 1 may already cover a worker acting through an organisation even under a literal reading of paragraph 4.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The conditional loss of protection remains unresolved. Separately, a criminal-only interpretation is difficult to sustain alongside paragraph 1, paragraph 3 and the general extension expressed in the other authentic versions.
Unresolved: Article 9(2) permits qualifying associations, with the complainant’s approval, to act on behalf of or support the complainant in judicial or administrative enforcement. Article 10(1) may still shift proof in a represented claim. No proceeding has been identified where paragraph 4 alone supplies that protection; paragraphs 2 and 5 may also affect the result.

impact_families.title: Retirement ages and scheme admission
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), including its differentiated-age and actuarial clauses; Articles 6(1), including (b), and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: National law exercises Article 6(2) for a covered occupational pension scheme that bars membership before age 25. The entry restriction is separate from retirement eligibility, pension-entitlement ages and actuarial calculations, and produces no sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
The Slovak wording links both possibility and entitlement to retirement on an old-age or invalidity pension. If that retirement-linked reading prevails, the standalone membership cutoff loses Article 6(2) eligibility. The following 'vrátane' clause elaborates the preceding age-setting rule rather than independently exempting every age restriction in a scheme. The actuarial limb does not turn a standalone membership condition into a calculation. Article 6(1), including its employment-advantage example, remains available only under its general justification conditions. Article 2(2)(b) and the necessary-national-measures reservation in Article 2(5) do not automatically restore the specific exemption.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading interprets the retirement opportunity broadly enough to include access to the pension arrangement. German and Dutch expressly separate membership from benefit entitlement, supporting that result. Croatian and Slovenian also use retirement-focused formulations, supporting the reality of the narrower textual reading. The explicit retirement link makes harmonization an interpretive step rather than a literal synonym, and the supplied versions do not conclusively settle it.
impact_families.uncertainty: An actual membership rule may also control when pension rights arise; the scenario assumes these are separate. Whether the narrower reading would prevail across the authentic versions is open. The scheme’s functions, coverage and national adoption must be checked before applying this assessment to a real case. Even if the Article 6(2) exemption were unavailable, Article 6(1) might independently justify the age rule; no discrimination outcome is determined.

impact_families.title: Associations’ procedural entitlement may cover initiation only
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(2), read with Article 9(1) and (3).
impact_families.effect: A nationally eligible organisation, with the claimant's consent, seeks to support a pending, timely direct-discrimination employment case. Hypothetical national procedure allows organisations to initiate cases but excludes later participation.
impact_families.rationale:
Iniția expressly describes initiation. If it exhausts the guaranteed organisational role, later participation is outside the Article 9(2) minimum; a participation-inclusive reading would protect that role. Paragraph 1's individual-access obligation, including its reference to both procedural categories, does not independently confer organisational participation. This supports moderate procedural impact without establishing loss of the claimant's action or any merits outcome.
Counterreading: În sprijinul reclamantului can support an ongoing role, and initiating an intervention could satisfy iniția without initiating the principal case. A broader procedural meaning could therefore eliminate the proposed difference.
impact_families.uncertainty: Romanian 'iniția' may include initiating an intervention in an existing case, while its support wording and German and Croatian participation language favour that reading. Moderate assumes an initiation-only minimum despite those counterreadings, with national eligibility, consent and time limits satisfied. No actual Member State procedure or breach has been established.

impact_families.title: Proof rules where courts investigate facts
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 10(1)–(3) and (5), read with Recital 32.
impact_families.effect: A non-criminal judicial procedure assigns fact-finding to the court, while national law retains the burden shift described in paragraph 1. A prohibitory interpretation of Polish paragraph 5 prevents applying paragraph 1, but the same protection might survive through a national rule permitted by paragraph 2.
impact_families.rationale:
Polish 'nie mogą stosować' expresses prohibition rather than permission to dispense with the rule. However, paragraph 2 expressly accommodates more favourable evidentiary rules. Prohibiting application of paragraph 1 does not, without resolving that relationship, establish that an equivalent national protection must disappear.
Counterreading: Reading paragraph 5 as relieving states of an obligation preserves both national discretion and paragraph 2's permission. Even on a literal prohibitory reading, paragraph 2 could sustain an independent national burden shift because paragraph 5 names only paragraph 1. Recital 32 describes proceedings in which the court investigates the facts and the claimant need not prove them, supporting the optional-exception reading.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Even assuming the prohibitory wording prevails, the practical allocation of proof remains unresolved. Separately, the discretionary wording of other authentic versions and paragraph 2 strongly favour an optional exception in the multilingual context.
Unresolved: Does the prohibition reach equivalent national evidence rules, or only application of paragraph 1 as such? The answer is necessary before concluding that a claimant loses protection. Paragraph 3 independently excludes criminal proceedings.

impact_families.title: Available amendment versus completed amendment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 16(b)'s alternative corrective measures, read with Article 2.
impact_families.effect: National law provides an effective judicial power to amend an undertaking's recruitment rule established to be discriminatory, but no route to declare it void. No amendment has occurred, and the rule is not automatically invalid.
impact_families.rationale:
If Estonian permission extends to amendment, the effective amendment power could satisfy that alternative. A reading requiring completed amendment would not accept it while the rule remains unchanged. Available invalidation would independently satisfy Article 16(b), so its absence is essential. Article 16(a) does not correct the private rule, and Article 2's substantive prohibition remains.
Counterreading: The authentic versions have equal authority. Estonian's infinitive construction plausibly places amendment under permission, while Slovak and Slovenian also admit a possibility extending to amendment. French, German and Finnish distinguish possible invalidation from completed amendment. The requirement to take necessary measures supports an effective corrective mechanism rather than empty permission, but does not conclusively settle whether amendment must already have occurred.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The conclusion concerns this specific compliance duty, not the legality of applying the discriminatory rule or compliance with every other obligation. Ordinary freedom to negotiate an amendment may be insufficient; the scenario therefore uses an effective judicial corrective power.
Unresolved: No further dependency prevents the stated conditional Article 16(b) difference. An available invalidation route, automatic invalidity or completed corrective amendment would eliminate it.

impact_families.title: Professional codes outside organisational statutes
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 2, 3(1)(a) and 16(a)–(b).
impact_families.effect: A private professional code contains a religion-based entry condition established to be unlawful, with no applicable exception. It is neither an organisational statute nor a contractual term, undertaking rule, or legislative, regulatory or administrative provision.
impact_families.rationale:
A strict organisational-statutes reading could exclude the code from Article 16(b)'s correction duty. Article 16(a) and the remaining contractual and undertaking-rule categories do not capture the example as described. The additional Greek reference to profit-making and non-profit-making organisations does not necessarily capture a separate code or extend the Directive beyond its substantive scope.
Counterreading: The authentic versions have equal authority. French and Danish also use statutes terminology, which can describe substantive professional regulation rather than a document's formal title. Finnish and Italian refer more broadly to rules governing independent activity, while Swedish combines association rules with professional rules. Together, these support a functional reading that could encompass the code; the restrictive Greek reading is therefore not established as the ultimate interpretation.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Article 3(1)(a) covers access to occupations, including private-sector access. What remains unproven is whether a private code with real effect on entry can sit outside an organisational statute, contract, undertaking rule, public provision and every other Article 16 category. Its institutional source and legal force determine that boundary; other remedies may still apply.
Unresolved: Can an operative non-contractual private entry code actually remain outside all those Article 16 categories?

impact_families.title: Integration and protection purposes
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(1), particularly its opening justification rule and Article 6(1)(a), read with Article 2(2).
impact_families.effect: An age-based dismissal safeguard protects older workers without promoting their vocational integration. A cumulative Dutch reading removes it from the express example. The converse example is an integration-only training measure.
impact_families.rationale:
Dutch 'en' supports a conjunctive reading within the example. Nevertheless, 'onder meer' makes the examples non-exhaustive, and the opening rule permits a legitimate aim subject to objective and reasonable justification and appropriate and necessary means. A protection-only or integration-only measure can be assessed under that unchanged rule. Conversely, meeting both purposes does not dispense with its requirements. Even assuming the cumulative reading prevails, a changed exemption outcome is therefore unestablished.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats the conjunction as a collective description of policy purposes rather than two mandatory purposes for every measure. German and French expressly use alternatives, while Lithuanian also joins the purposes conjunctively. The multilingual evidence therefore supports a real interpretive question, but the shared non-exhaustive structure and general test constrain its legal consequence.
impact_families.uncertainty: Whether the Dutch conjunction would be read cumulatively across the authentic versions is open. More decisively, Article 6(1)(a) gives a non-exhaustive example within the general legitimate-aim and necessity test. Losing the express example does not establish that a measure fails that test or changes a legal outcome, so no impact level is assigned.

impact_families.title: School employment beyond recruitment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(2), read with Articles 2, 4(1)–(2) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: National legislation expressly authorises a religion-based teacher-promotion arrangement in Northern Ireland schools serving the stated employment-balance and reconciliation purpose. If the Danish school-wide reading prevails, Article 15(2) excludes those promotions from the religion-or-belief provisions; a recruitment-only reading does not.
impact_families.rationale:
The changed outcome is eligibility for statutory non-application, independently of whether a particular promotion decision is unlawful. Article 2's discrimination definitions do not restore provisions excluded by Article 15(2). This supports a moderate effect for an identifiable employment group under one exception; the text does not establish the wider practical reach needed for a higher assessment.
Counterreading: The Danish purpose remains teacher-specific, and paragraph 1 expressly addresses recruitment. French, German and English paragraph 2 expressly link the exception to recruiting teachers in schools. Reading these equally authoritative formulations together strongly favours treating the Danish reference to schools as confined to teacher recruitment. The broader reading is therefore less persuasive in multilingual context.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No actual national authorisation or promotion arrangement is established. The exclusion concerns religion or belief, and does not establish compliance with national law or remove protection concerning other grounds. A genuine and determining occupational requirement under Article 4, including an applicable religious-ethos rule under Article 4(2), or qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently affect lawfulness. Neither follows from Article 15 eligibility or legislative authorisation alone.
Unresolved: Article 2(5) could independently protect a necessary statutory measure, but authorisation alone does not establish necessity. The conditional Article 15(2) eligibility change does not depend on resolving the measure’s lawfulness under Articles 2, 4, 7 and national law.

impact_families.title: Post-relationship procedural guarantee specifies employment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 9(1), including its all-persons guarantee; Article 9(3); Article 2.
impact_families.effect: A former professional-association member brings a timely discrimination claim about treatment during membership. Continued access is contested because the ended relationship was not employment.
impact_families.rationale:
Työsuhde specifies employment, narrowing the express survival assurance. Nevertheless, the surrounding Finnish sentence guarantees procedures to all persons who consider themselves wronged, and the employment phrase is an inclusive parenthesis. Retaining its employment-specific meaning does not establish an exclusion from the general guarantee. A concrete changed access outcome therefore remains unresolved, and no impact tier is awarded.
Counterreading: Myös adds an express assurance for former employees rather than limiting other claimants. Other authentic versions reinforce continuity, while the Finnish general-access wording itself supports protection without expanding työsuhde beyond employment.
impact_families.uncertainty: The Finnish employment-specific parenthesis may give former employees an additional assurance without excluding others. Article 3(1)(d) covers membership of professional organisations, and Article 9(1) grants access to all persons who consider themselves wronged, subject to Article 9(3) deadlines. The hypothetical assumes a timely claim on a protected ground. No identified provision removes that general access solely because professional-organisation membership ended. A changed access outcome remains unestablished even if the disputed phrase is read narrowly.

impact_families.title: Cumulative discrimination threshold
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 10(1)–(5), read with Article 2(1)–(2) and Recitals 15 and 31.
impact_families.effect: A worker establishes facts suggesting dismissal expressly because of sexual orientation, without an apparently neutral provision or practice suggesting indirect discrimination. In ordinary civil proceedings, a cumulative reading would withhold the mandatory burden shift because the facts indicate only direct discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
Requiring both forms removes a central evidentiary protection from single-form claims, supporting a substantial conditional effect. Article 2 separately defines and prohibits each form, but does not independently allocate proof. The example excludes criminal proceedings and court-led fact-finding and assumes no national rule under paragraph 2 already preserves the shift.
Counterreading: Polish Article 2(1) expressly uses 'lub' between the forms, and Article 2(2) defines them separately. Reading 'i' as collectively identifying the two protected categories, rather than requiring their simultaneous presence, reconciles Article 10 with those definitions and the alternative wording in other equally authoritative versions. Recital 15 likewise refers to facts from which direct or indirect discrimination may be inferred, while Recital 31 requires a prima facie evidential case before the burden shifts.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The cumulative reading is strongly disfavoured by the surrounding text. Its conditional procedural effect is nevertheless clear; losing the mandatory shift does not establish that a claimant would lose the action.
Unresolved: No additional dependency prevents the stated conditional loss of mandatory protection. Actual consequences depend on whether independent national evidence rules preserve it and whether the facts support one or both forms. Article 2's justification and accommodation limbs remain relevant to indirect-discrimination claims.

impact_families.title: Actual benefit calculation exemption
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), read with Articles 6(1) and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: A covered occupational retirement scheme applies a fixed age-based reduction when calculating benefit amounts, without actuarial valuation. National law exercises Article 6(2), entitlement and admission ages remain unchanged, and the reduction produces no sex discrimination.
impact_families.rationale:
The Latvian words describe actually calculating benefits, rather than expressly requiring actuarial calculations. If that construction prevails, the specified reduction gains Article 6(2) eligibility. Changing amounts does not independently satisfy the admission or entitlement-age limb, including its employee-category elaboration. Article 6(1) supplies a separate justification route with additional conditions, not an automatic substitute. Article 2(2)(b)'s neutral-practice exception and Article 2(5)'s necessary-national-measure reservation do not automatically cover the stipulated direct age adjustment. The conditional outcome is the exemption boundary, not established discrimination liability.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats the Latvian phrase as referring to actuarial calculation of benefits within the occupational-insurance context. Lithuanian, German and French expressly technical wording supports that construction. Polish benefit-amount wording provides a genuine parallel to Latvian, so the difference cannot be dismissed merely because English uses a technical term.
impact_families.uncertainty: The relevant authentic versions do not settle the boundary between actuarial and other benefit calculations. The scenario assumes a genuinely non-actuarial adjustment in a covered scheme. A real scheme’s method, coverage and national adoption require verification. An Article 6(1) justification may remain possible even if the Article 6(2) exemption is unavailable; no violation is determined.

impact_families.title: Alleging facts to shift proof
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 10(1)–(5), read with Article 2(1)–(2) and Recitals 15 and 31.
impact_families.effect: In an ordinary civil dismissal claim, a worker alleges specific statements connecting dismissal to sexual orientation. The account satisfies the disputed lower threshold but has not established the statements under the competing threshold. If that lower reading prevails, the employer must prove absence of discrimination at this earlier stage.
impact_families.rationale:
The changed outcome is an earlier mandatory allocation of proof to the respondent. The example assumes no equivalent national rule under paragraph 2 and excludes criminal proceedings and proceedings subject to the paragraph 5 exception. Article 2 still determines what constitutes discrimination; shifting proof does not establish liability.
Counterreading: Spanish still requires facts permitting a presumption. French 'établit' and German 'glaubhaft machen', alongside presentation language in other equally authoritative versions, support a common preliminary assessment of a credible factual basis. This harmonising interpretation is stronger than an automatic shift on unsupported assertion. Recitals 15 and 31 assign factual appraisal to the competent body and require an evidential prima facie case before the shift; an unsupported allegation does not suffice even if the preliminary threshold is lower.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Whether 'alegue' actually lowers the threshold is separate from its conditional effect. The text does not establish that a bare accusation or facts incapable of supporting a presumption suffice.
Unresolved: No additional provision is needed to identify the conditional procedural change under the stated assumptions. National evidentiary standards and the particular factual account determine whether an actual claim falls between the two thresholds.

impact_families.title: Invoking facts to shift proof
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 10(1)–(5), read with Article 2(1)–(2) and Recitals 15 and 31.
impact_families.effect: A worker challenging dismissal invokes specific statements linking it to sexual orientation. Those statements have not been established under the competing evidentiary threshold, but the account meets the disputed invocation threshold and supports a presumption. On that reading, the employer's proof obligation arises sooner.
impact_families.rationale:
Hungarian describes the ability to invoke facts and then assigns proof to the respondent. If this entails a lower preliminary showing, the procedural consequence follows directly. The example excludes criminal proceedings and the paragraph 5 exception and assumes no equivalent national protection under paragraph 2. Article 2's substantive discrimination requirements remain applicable.
Counterreading: The facts must still permit a presumption. French establishment language, German credibility language and presentation language elsewhere support a common preliminary evidentiary assessment across equally authoritative versions. This makes a substantive divergence less persuasive than the isolated verb suggests. Recitals 15 and 31 assign factual appraisal to the competent body and require an evidential prima facie case before the shift; an unsupported allegation does not suffice even if the preliminary threshold is lower.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The wording may concern presentation of facts rather than a different evidentiary standard. Neither invocation alone nor the resulting burden shift establishes that discrimination occurred.
Unresolved: The conditional procedural effect requires no further legal premise beyond the stated lower-threshold reading and exclusions. Whether any particular account qualifies depends on its content and the applicable national evidentiary standard.

impact_families.title: Conditional exclusion of administrative complainants
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 11; Articles 1–10, 15 and 17; recital 30.
impact_families.effect: A qualified civilian employee brings a timely administrative claim about sexual-orientation discrimination, without an internal complaint or judicial proceedings. The employer dismisses them solely for initiating enforcement. Assume no independent protected-ground discrimination in the dismissal and no additional national protection.
impact_families.rationale:
The Estonian override confirms court-specific kohtumenetlusele. Employee status, employer action, causation and enforcement purpose are satisfied; dismissal independently satisfies the treatment limb. The internal-complaint alternative is absent. No Articles 2–7 or 15 exception applies. Articles 9 and 17 do not independently supply the missing retaliation trigger; Article 8 does not guarantee additional protection. Assuming the court-only reading survives harmonisation, the Directive's protection changes.
Counterreading: Article 9, English Article 10(4), broader German and Dutch wording, and effective enforcement support inclusive protection. Conversely, several authentic versions use judicial terminology, and English 'legal proceedings' can mean litigation. Recital 30 concerns judicial protection against retaliation, rather than expressly restricting its trigger.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The multilingual interpretation remains open; English is not controlling. This interpretive doubt does not undermine the stipulated conditional consequence.
Unresolved: Whether harmonisation includes administrative proceedings and whether national law independently protects the employee.

impact_families.title: Statistical calculation exemption
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 6(2), including its age-setting limb and sex-discrimination condition; Articles 6(1) and 2(2), (5).
impact_families.effect: In a covered occupational retirement scheme, national law exercises the Article 6(2) option. Benefits are reduced for an age group using descriptive workforce statistics without actuarial valuation. Admission and entitlement ages remain unchanged, and no sex discrimination results.
impact_families.rationale:
If statistical calculations include ordinary age statistics, the specified calculation gains Article 6(2) exemption eligibility that an actuarial-only construction would withhold. The admission, entitlement and differentiated-age clauses concern fixing ages, not a standalone adjustment of amounts. Article 6(1) can independently justify an arrangement, but requires its own justification and proportionality conditions; it does not erase the change in Article 6(2) eligibility. Article 2(2)(b)'s neutral-practice justification does not automatically shelter an expressly age-based adjustment, and Article 2(5) requires a qualifying necessary national measure. Neither provides an unconditional alternative here.
Counterreading: The occupational-insurance context strongly supports understanding statistical calculations as insurance statistics. German insurance-mathematical and French actuarial wording reinforce that technical construction. Polish and Latvian benefit-calculation formulations show that the multilingual wording is not uniform, but do not establish a general ordinary-statistics exemption. Harmonization could therefore remove the proposed extension.
impact_families.uncertainty: The boundary between descriptive statistics and actuarial valuation remains uncertain across the authentic versions. The scenario assumes a genuinely non-actuarial method. A real scheme’s calculation, coverage and national adoption need checking. Article 6(1) may independently justify the age distinction even if Article 6(2) does not exempt it; no discrimination outcome is determined.

impact_families.title: Occupational access beyond employment
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(1)(a), read with Article 3(1)(b)–(d) and Article 2(2)(a).
impact_families.effect: An authority refuses authorisation for an unpaid professional activity solely because of sexual orientation, before any employment or self-employment begins.
impact_families.rationale:
Polish lacks a separately named occupation category. However, authorisation preceding employment can itself be a condition of access to employment or self-employment; timing does not place it outside those categories. An unpaid role also cannot simply be assumed both to qualify as occupation and to fall outside every remaining limb. The Directive does not itself establish that classification.
Counterreading: The Polish reference to every field and professional level supports broad access protection. German likewise uses two broad activity categories, while Italian combines occupation and work with dependent and autonomous forms. These authentic formulations show why counting separately named categories does not establish narrower coverage.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The meanings of employment, self-employment and occupation, and their application to the proposed activity, remain unresolved even assuming the absence of a separate Polish category has substantive significance.
Unresolved: What concrete activity qualifies as occupation while escaping the remaining Polish categories and Article 3(1)(b)–(d)? An unpaid role or a preliminary licence, without further classification, does not establish such an activity.

impact_families.title: Conditional exclusion of administrative complainants
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 11; Articles 1–10, 15 and 17; recital 30.
impact_families.effect: A qualified civilian employee brings a timely administrative sexual-orientation discrimination claim, without an internal complaint or judicial proceedings. The employer dismisses them solely for initiating enforcement. Assume no independent protected-ground discrimination in that dismissal and no additional national protection.
impact_families.rationale:
The Czech override confirms judicial soudní řízení while Article 9 separately recognises administrative proceedings. Employee status, dismissal by the employer, responsive causation and equality-enforcement purpose are satisfied. Neither narrower trigger applies. No relevant Articles 2–7 or 15 exception intervenes; Articles 9 and 17 do not expressly replace the missing trigger, and Article 8 does not ensure additional protection. The conditional loss therefore survives the remaining-limb check.
Counterreading: Czech Article 10(4) covers all Article 9(2) proceedings; Article 9, effective enforcement and broader German and Dutch wording support inclusive Article 11 protection. Court-specific authentic versions and English's possible litigation meaning support the competing interpretation. Recital 30 does not expressly restrict protected initiating proceedings.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Whether the apparent linguistic difference survives harmonisation remains uncertain. The complete Czech and English context supplies no independent operative protection defeating this stipulated scenario.
Unresolved: Whether harmonised Article 11 includes administrative enforcement and whether national law independently protects the dismissal.

impact_families.title: Comparable non-state benefit schemes
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 3(3), read with Article 3(1)(c)–(d), Article 2 and Recital 13.
impact_families.effect: A non-state scheme resembling a state social-protection scheme refuses a payment because of the recipient's sexual orientation. The recipient seeks coverage as employment remuneration or an organisational benefit.
impact_families.rationale:
Slovenian expressly identifies state programmes without separately naming similar schemes. A state-only reading could therefore narrow the exclusion. That does not establish positive coverage: neither private administration nor an employment connection alone demonstrates that a payment is covered remuneration or an organisational benefit. Recital 13 explains that the Directive does not apply to social-security and social-protection schemes whose benefits are not treated as income under the then Article 141 concept. No concrete payment is established that both satisfies the positive scope requirements and falls within the disputed comparable-scheme exclusion after that recital is applied.
Counterreading: State programmes can operate through non-state administrators, and the Slovenian reference to social systems permits a functional reading. German and French expressly include equivalent or assimilated schemes, supporting a harmonized exclusion extending beyond direct state administration.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Whether the payment is employment remuneration or an organisational benefit, and whether it instead belongs to a social-security or social-protection scheme of the kind Recital 13 describes as outside the Directive, must be established. Private administration alone does not settle either question.
Unresolved: Which payment is both from a genuinely non-state scheme comparable to a state scheme and independently within Article 3(1) after Recital 13 is applied?

impact_families.title: Teacher exclusion under legislative silence
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 15(2), read with Articles 2, 4(1)–(2) and 7(1).
impact_families.effect: A Northern Ireland school recruits teachers through a religious-community balancing arrangement serving the stated purpose, while national legislation is silent on authorising the exclusion. A literal 'unless' reading leaves the religion-or-belief provisions inapplicable; an express-authorisation prerequisite leaves Article 15(2) unavailable.
impact_families.rationale:
The ordinary meaning of 'chyba że' reverses the conditional structure. Legislative silence provides a concrete comparison that does not require resolving what the pronoun 'to' refers to when permission is actually given. The resulting difference in statutory coverage supports moderate impact.
Counterreading: Polish paragraph 1 uses 'o ile' to make express legislative permission a prerequisite for the parallel police exception. That structure, the common purpose, and the conditions in equally authoritative French, German and English paragraph 2 strongly favour construing the teacher exception as requiring authorisation. The literal reversal is less persuasive in multilingual context.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No actual recruitment arrangement or legislative silence is established. The pronoun's referent complicates the express-permission branch. Reapplication of the Directive would require assessment under its substantive rules and would not automatically establish discrimination. A genuine and determining occupational requirement under Article 4, including an applicable religious-ethos rule under Article 4(2), or qualifying positive action under Article 7 may independently affect lawfulness. Neither follows from Article 15 eligibility or legislative authorisation alone.
Unresolved: Article 2(2)(b)(i) can justify certain indirect differences but does not determine Article 15(2) coverage. Article 2(5) requires necessary measures laid down by national law; legislative silence alone cannot establish that protection. No further dependency prevents the stated conditional coverage change.

impact_families.title: Setting out facts to shift proof
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Article 10(1)–(5), read with Article 2(1)–(2) and Recitals 15 and 31.
impact_families.effect: In a civil dismissal claim, a worker sets out specific statements connecting dismissal to sexual orientation. The account meets a less demanding presentation threshold and supports a presumption, but the statements have not been established under the competing threshold. The lower reading would require the employer to disprove discrimination at that stage.
impact_families.rationale:
If 'espongono' permits the lower showing, paragraph 1 changes when the respondent must carry the burden of proof. This is a concrete procedural outcome for an identifiable group. The example assumes ordinary non-criminal proceedings outside paragraph 5 and no equivalent national rule under paragraph 2; it does not establish liability under Article 2.
Counterreading: Italian retains the requirement that the facts support a presumption. Reading 'espongono' as presenting sufficiently substantiated facts harmonises it with French establishment language, German credibility language and other authentic versions using presentation language. The wording alone does not compel a lower standard. Recitals 15 and 31 assign factual appraisal to the competent body and require an evidential prima facie case before the shift; an unsupported allegation does not suffice even if the preliminary threshold is lower.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Setting out facts may already entail substantiation sufficient for the common preliminary standard. National procedure may therefore produce identical results under both formulations.
Unresolved: No additional legal dependency prevents the conditional change under the stated assumptions. Actual application requires a factual account satisfying the proposed lower threshold but failing the competing standard.

impact_families.title: Independent trades outside intellectual professions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2000/78/EC, Articles 2, 3(1)(a) and 16(a)–(b).
impact_families.effect: A private code contains a religion-based entry condition for an independent manual trade established to be unlawful, with no applicable exception. It is neither contractual nor an undertaking rule, public regulatory provision, or rule of a workers’ or employers’ organisation.
impact_families.rationale:
If the Hungarian professional category is restricted to intellectual liberal professions, the code could escape its express correction duty. The contractual and organisational limbs remain operative, and public trade-access rules remain covered by Article 16(a). The example therefore depends on a private code genuinely outside those categories.
Counterreading: The authentic versions have equal authority. Italian and Slovenian refer broadly to autonomous work or self-employment, and Finnish covers independent professional activity. German and French use liberal-profession terminology. A functional occupational interpretation could reconcile these formulations, although the Hungarian intellectual qualifier gives the restrictive reading a textual basis. Its ultimate acceptance remains uncertain.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Article 3(1)(a) covers access to independent occupations. What remains unproven is whether a private rule governing entry to a manual trade can operate outside contracts, organisational or undertaking rules, and public regulation. Its institutional source and legal force determine that boundary; other remedies may still apply.
Unresolved: Can an operative private trade-access code actually remain outside all those Article 16 categories?

legislation.title: DIRECTIVE 2009/24/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 23 April 2009 on the legal protection of computer programs (Codified version) (Text with EEA relevance)

unavailable_languages.name: Irish
unavailable_languages.reason: No official language expression exists for this exact version in Cellar metadata.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
DIRECTIVE 2009/24/EC OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 23 April 2009
on the legal protection of computer programs
(Codified version)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty establishing the European Community and in particular Article 95 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the procedure laid down in Article 251 of the Treaty ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | The content of Council Directive 91/250/EEC of 14 May 1991 on the legal protection of computer programs ( 3 ) has been amended ( 4 ) . In the interests of clarity and rationality the said Directive should be codified.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | The development of computer programs requires the investment of considerable human, technical and financial resources while computer programs can be copied at a fraction of the cost needed to develop them independently.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Computer programs are playing an increasingly important role in a broad range of industries and computer program technology can accordingly be considered as being of fundamental importance for the Community's industrial development.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Certain differences in the legal protection of computer programs offered by the laws of the Member States have direct and negative effects on the functioning of the internal market as regards computer programs.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Existing differences having such effects need to be removed and new ones prevented from arising, while differences not adversely affecting the functioning of the internal market to a substantial degree need not be removed or prevented from arising.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | The Community's legal framework on the protection of computer programs can accordingly in the first instance be limited to establishing that Member States should accord protection to computer programs under copyright law as literary works and, further, to establishing who and what should be protected, the exclusive rights on which protected persons should be able to rely in order to authorise or prohibit certain acts and for how long the protection should apply.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | For the purpose of this Directive, the term ‘computer program’ shall include programs in any form, including those which are incorporated into hardware. This term also includes preparatory design work leading to the development of a computer program provided that the nature of the preparatory work is such that a computer program can result from it at a later stage.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | In respect of the criteria to be applied in determining whether or not a computer program is an original work, no tests as to the qualitative or aesthetic merits of the program should be applied.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | The Community is fully committed to the promotion of international standardisation.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | The function of a computer program is to communicate and work together with other components of a computer system and with users and, for this purpose, a logical and, where appropriate, physical interconnection and interaction is required to permit all elements of software and hardware to work with other software and hardware and with users in all the ways in which they are intended to function. The parts of the program which provide for such interconnection and interaction between elements of software and hardware are generally known as ‘interfaces’. This functional interconnection and interaction is generally known as ‘interoperability’; such interoperability can be defined as the ability to exchange information and mutually to use the information which has been exchanged.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | For the avoidance of doubt, it has to be made clear that only the expression of a computer program is protected and that ideas and principles which underlie any element of a program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive. In accordance with this principle of copyright, to the extent that logic, algorithms and programming languages comprise ideas and principles, those ideas and principles are not protected under this Directive. In accordance with the legislation and case-law of the Member States and the international copyright conventions, the expression of those ideas and principles is to be protected by copyright.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘rental’ means the making available for use, for a limited period of time and for profit-making purposes, of a computer program or a copy thereof. This term does not include public lending, which, accordingly, remains outside the scope of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | The exclusive rights of the author to prevent the unauthorised reproduction of his work should be subject to a limited exception in the case of a computer program to allow the reproduction technically necessary for the use of that program by the lawful acquirer. This means that the acts of loading and running necessary for the use of a copy of a program which has been lawfully acquired, and the act of correction of its errors, may not be prohibited by contract. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, including when a copy of the program has been sold, any other act necessary for the use of the copy of a program may be performed in accordance with its intended purpose by a lawful acquirer of that copy.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | A person having a right to use a computer program should not be prevented from performing acts necessary to observe, study or test the functioning of the program, provided that those acts do not infringe the copyright in the program.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | The unauthorised reproduction, translation, adaptation or transformation of the form of the code in which a copy of a computer program has been made available constitutes an infringement of the exclusive rights of the author. Nevertheless, circumstances may exist when such a reproduction of the code and translation of its form are indispensable to obtain the necessary information to achieve the interoperability of an independently created program with other programs. It has therefore to be considered that, in these limited circumstances only, performance of the acts of reproduction and translation by or on behalf of a person having a right to use a copy of the program is legitimate and compatible with fair practice and must therefore be deemed not to require the authorisation of the rightholder. An objective of this exception is to make it possible to connect all components of a computer system, including those of different manufacturers, so that they can work together. Such an exception to the author's exclusive rights may not be used in a way which prejudices the legitimate interests of the rightholder or which conflicts with a normal exploitation of the program.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | Protection of computer programs under copyright laws should be without prejudice to the application, in appropriate cases, of other forms of protection. However, any contractual provisions contrary to the provisions of this Directive laid down in respect of decompilation or to the exceptions provided for by this Directive with regard to the making of a back-up copy or to observation, study or testing of the functioning of a program should be null and void.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | The provisions of this Directive are without prejudice to the application of the competition rules under Articles 81 and 82 of the Treaty if a dominant supplier refuses to make information available which is necessary for interoperability as defined in this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | The provisions of this Directive should be without prejudice to specific requirements of Community law already enacted in respect of the publication of interfaces in the telecommunications sector or Council Decisions relating to standardisation in the field of information technology and telecommunication.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | This Directive does not affect derogations provided for under national legislation in accordance with the Berne Convention on points not covered by this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | This Directive should be without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Object of protection
1. In accordance with the provisions of this Directive, Member States shall protect computer programs, by copyright, as literary works within the meaning of the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works. For the purposes of this Directive, the term ‘computer programs’ shall include their preparatory design material.
2. Protection in accordance with this Directive shall apply to the expression in any form of a computer program. Ideas and principles which underlie any element of a computer program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive.
3. A computer program shall be protected if it is original in the sense that it is the author's own intellectual creation. No other criteria shall be applied to determine its eligibility for protection.
4. The provisions of this Directive shall apply also to programs created before 1 January 1993, without prejudice to any acts concluded and rights acquired before that date.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Authorship of computer programs
1. The author of a computer program shall be the natural person or group of natural persons who has created the program or, where the legislation of the Member State permits, the legal person designated as the rightholder by that legislation.
Where collective works are recognised by the legislation of a Member State, the person considered by the legislation of the Member State to have created the work shall be deemed to be its author.
2. In respect of a computer program created by a group of natural persons jointly, the exclusive rights shall be owned jointly.
3. Where a computer program is created by an employee in the execution of his duties or following the instructions given by his employer, the employer exclusively shall be entitled to exercise all economic rights in the program so created, unless otherwise provided by contract.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
Beneficiaries of protection
Protection shall be granted to all natural or legal persons eligible under national copyright legislation as applied to literary works.

passages.label: Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Restricted acts
1. Subject to the provisions of Articles 5 and 6, the exclusive rights of the rightholder within the meaning of Article 2 shall include the right to do or to authorise:
(a) | the permanent or temporary reproduction of a computer program by any means and in any form, in part or in whole; in so far as loading, displaying, running, transmission or storage of the computer program necessitate such reproduction, such acts shall be subject to authorisation by the rightholder;
(b) | the translation, adaptation, arrangement and any other alteration of a computer program and the reproduction of the results thereof, without prejudice to the rights of the person who alters the program;
(c) | any form of distribution to the public, including the rental, of the original computer program or of copies thereof.
2. The first sale in the Community of a copy of a program by the rightholder or with his consent shall exhaust the distribution right within the Community of that copy, with the exception of the right to control further rental of the program or a copy thereof.

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Exceptions to the restricted acts
1. In the absence of specific contractual provisions, the acts referred to in points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) shall not require authorisation by the rightholder where they are necessary for the use of the computer program by the lawful acquirer in accordance with its intended purpose, including for error correction.
2. The making of a back-up copy by a person having a right to use the computer program may not be prevented by contract in so far as it is necessary for that use.
3. The person having a right to use a copy of a computer program shall be entitled, without the authorisation of the rightholder, to observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program if he does so while performing any of the acts of loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do.

passages.label: Article 6
passages.text:
Article 6
Decompilation
1. The authorisation of the rightholder shall not be required where reproduction of the code and translation of its form within the meaning of points (a) and (b) of Article 4(1) are indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, provided that the following conditions are met:
(a) | those acts are performed by the licensee or by another person having a right to use a copy of a program, or on their behalf by a person authorised to do so;
(b) | the information necessary to achieve interoperability has not previously been readily available to the persons referred to in point (a); and
(c) | those acts are confined to the parts of the original program which are necessary in order to achieve interoperability.
2. The provisions of paragraph 1 shall not permit the information obtained through its application:
(a) | to be used for goals other than to achieve the interoperability of the independently created computer program;
(b) | to be given to others, except when necessary for the interoperability of the independently created computer program; or
(c) | to be used for the development, production or marketing of a computer program substantially similar in its expression, or for any other act which infringes copyright.
3. In accordance with the provisions of the Berne Convention for the protection of Literary and Artistic Works, the provisions of this Article may not be interpreted in such a way as to allow its application to be used in a manner which unreasonably prejudices the rightholder's legitimate interests or conflicts with a normal exploitation of the computer program.

passages.label: Article 7
passages.text:
Article 7
Special measures of protection
1. Without prejudice to the provisions of Articles 4, 5 and 6, Member States shall provide, in accordance with their national legislation, appropriate remedies against a person committing any of the following acts:
(a) | any act of putting into circulation a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
