(b) | the possession, for commercial purposes, of a copy of a computer program knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is an infringing copy;
(c) | any act of putting into circulation, or the possession for commercial purposes of, any means the sole intended purpose of which is to facilitate the unauthorised removal or circumvention of any technical device which may have been applied to protect a computer program.
2. Any infringing copy of a computer program shall be liable to seizure in accordance with the legislation of the Member State concerned.
3. Member States may provide for the seizure of any means referred to in point (c) of paragraph 1.

passages.label: Article 8
passages.text:
Article 8
Continued application of other legal provisions
The provisions of this Directive shall be without prejudice to any other legal provisions such as those concerning patent rights, trade-marks, unfair competition, trade secrets, protection of semi-conductor products or the law of contract.
Any contractual provisions contrary to Article 6 or to the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) and (3) shall be null and void.

passages.label: Article 9
passages.text:
Article 9
Communication
Member States shall communicate to the Commission the provisions of national law adopted in the field governed by this Directive.

passages.label: Article 10
passages.text:
Article 10
Repeal
Directive 91/250/EEC, as amended by the Directive indicated in Annex I, Part A, is repealed, without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time-limits for transposition into national law of the Directives set out in Annex I, Part B.
References to the repealed Directive shall be construed as references to this Directive and shall be read in accordance with the correlation table in Annex II.

passages.label: Article 11
passages.text:
Article 11
Entry into force
This Directive shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Article 12
passages.text:
Article 12
Addressees
This Directive is addressed to the Member States.

impact_families.title: Article 5(3): possible contractual prerequisite for observation, study or testing
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 5(3), aligned across supplied versions by source_id art_5, read with Articles 1(2), 4(1)(a), 5(1), 6 and 8 and recitals 13–16.
impact_families.effect: Assume a person may lawfully use a copy and perform the relevant operations through statutory entitlement, without performing a contract. Studying the program during those operations satisfies the entitlement-based wording. A strict reading of Portuguese 'em execução do seu contrato' could exclude that person from Article 5(3). However, the reviewers’ example of already-authorised running and accompanying study does not establish an additional restricted act or enforceable restriction that would produce a different legal outcome.
impact_families.rationale:
The supplied Portuguese wording refers to contractual performance, whereas English, French and German refer to entitlement to perform the operations. This comparison uses art_5, not language-local paragraph identifiers. The textual distinction is supported; the accepted finding's assertion that Portuguese legally requires a contract is too categorical. Its own opening, 'Quem tiver direito a utilizar uma cópia', supports broader eligibility. Both reviewers correctly identify possible harmonisation and overlapping protections, but their scenarios demonstrate possible loss of express coverage rather than a net legal consequence: Article 5(1) may already authorise necessary reproduction, and studying unprotected ideas does not itself establish infringement. Moreover, absence of contractual provisions governing an operation does not establish absence of a contract under which it occurs. I therefore disagree with both reviewers’ medium confidence in the legal-effect mechanism. Moderate remains a conditional estimate if a substantive residual exclusion is established; the operative boundary remains unresolved.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonising interpretation treats 'em execução do seu contrato' as describing the ordinary setting of lawful operations rather than imposing an exhaustive source-of-entitlement requirement. Portuguese Article 5(3)'s broad opening, Article 5(1)'s recognition of necessary use without specific contractual provisions, the entitlement-based formulations in other authentic versions, and the supplied English recitals 14 and 16 and Article 8 support this construction. Their significance is contextual coherence, not the number of versions supporting it. The contractual phrase nevertheless creates textual tension that requires checking the Portuguese context. Article 6 provides a separate, conditional decompilation exception and cannot generally substitute for Article 5(3).
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, requiring needs_review. Contrary to review A's suggestion, Portuguese Article 5(1) is supplied and expressly addresses the absence of specific contractual provisions; it has been considered here. Portuguese surrounding articles and recitals are missing. Article 8's English nullity rule supports the mandatory character of Article 5(3), but does not alone determine its beneficiaries or eliminate a supposed contractual prerequisite. No independent retrieval of the EUR-Lex originals was available, so the supplied transcriptions, completeness claims and provenance have not been independently authenticated. These limitations and the unresolved alternative protection justify low confidence.
Unresolved: Does the original Portuguese surrounding text support the harmonising construction? Can a concrete case identify both a non-contractual entitlement to the relevant operations and a legal restriction that Article 5(3) defeats, but Articles 1(2), 5(1) and other applicable protections do not? Would contractual performance encompass operations whose authorisation also derives from statute?

impact_families.title: Latvian recital 12: public-use wording in the public-lending exclusion
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, recital 12 (source_id rct_12), read with Article 4(1)(c), Article 4(2), and Articles 5–6.
impact_families.effect: Following the first authorised Community sale of a physical program copy, a provider supplies that copy to members of the public for successive limited periods for profit, without independently restricted reproduction or alteration. If the Latvian sentence excluded that transaction from rental protection, it could undermine the rental control expressly retained by Article 4(2). Merely offering public access to software does not establish this scenario.
impact_families.rationale:
I aligned the supplied authentic passages by source_id rct_12, including Croatian p0013 alongside the other languages’ p0019. The Latvian second sentence describes allowing the general public to use a program and lacks an express lending limitation. English, French and the other supplied second sentences expressly identify public lending. This supports a textual discrepancy, but does not establish an operative exclusion. I therefore qualify the packet’s assertion that the wording ‘broadens’ the exclusion: it presents a possible literal argument whose legal effect remains unresolved. The earlier rationale that context cannot supply the omitted limitation understates the strongest harmonizing interpretation. I find no material disagreement with either reviewer’s needs_review assessment or conditional moderate impact. However, review B’s reference to public-facing access is broader than the demonstrated rental mechanism; the scenario must involve a qualifying rental. Neither reviewer’s agreement supplies evidence that the broader construction would survive interpretation.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation reads the Latvian second sentence as an imprecise description of public lending within a recital defining rental. Its first sentence expressly requires limited duration and profit-making purposes. Article 4(1)(c) expressly covers distribution to the public, including rental, and Article 4(2) preserves control over further rental after exhaustion. Construing the recital as excluding public rental generally would substantially defeat those provisions. A recital cannot independently create a derogation from an operative rule. Articles 5–6 supply no general public-use exception. Moreover, exclusion from the rental definition alone would not automatically eliminate protection under the broader distribution limb or separate reproduction rights.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review. I re-examined the legal text reproduced in the packet, but no source-retrieval capability or resources were available to independently verify the linked originals. The complete English context does not replace missing Latvian operative context. The supplied Polish first sentence also says ‘w celach niedochodowych’ (non-profit purposes), so unqualified agreement among authentic versions on the profit condition cannot be assumed; that separate discrepancy does not negate their shared reference to public lending in the second sentence. The principal uncertainty is whether any broader Latvian construction survives contextual interpretation and actually changes the retained rental entitlement. Confidence concerns that mechanism, not the visible wording difference.
Unresolved: Do the original Latvian Article 4 provisions preserve the same distribution and retained-rental boundaries? Does the original source confirm the quoted recital wording? After checking the missing authentic context, is there a concrete transaction for which the broader interpretation changes an operative entitlement despite the harmonizing reading and any independently applicable rights?

impact_families.title: Article 7(2): seizure availability versus compulsory execution
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 7(2), aligned by source_id art_7 across the supplied authentic versions, irrespective of language-local passage IDs; read with Article 7(1) and (3), Articles 4–6 and Article 12.
impact_families.effect: Assume an established infringing copy satisfies national seizure conditions, but national law permits the competent authority to decline seizure because another remedy is adequate. A compulsory-execution interpretation could require removal of that discretion; an availability interpretation would not itself prohibit it. Neither the existence of such national discretion nor the adequacy of the alternative remedy is established by the packet.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied legal text confirms a linguistic tension: Slovak ‘budú zabavené’ describes copies being seized, whereas English ‘shall be liable to seizure’, French ‘est susceptible de saisie’ and Swedish ‘ska kunna tas i beslag’ expressly describe susceptibility or availability. Danish and Slovenian also use result-oriented seizure formulations, so the issue is not uniquely Slovak. These comparisons inform interpretation rather than constitute a language vote. The finding’s categorical title, ‘Slovak provision requires seizure’, overstates what the wording establishes after contextual interpretation. Both reviewers correctly identify a possible discretion boundary and appropriately leave the assigned level unresolved. Their conditional moderate assessment is defensible for an identifiable group under this specific remedial rule, but their scenarios demonstrate only a hypothesis: satisfying national procedural conditions does not establish that the Directive removes substantive discretion. I disagree with their medium confidence because the operative effect of the national-law qualification and the strongest harmonizing reading remain unresolved. Review B’s exclusion of permanent forfeiture is appropriate as a limit on claimed consequences, not as a determination of what seizure means.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation treats Article 7(2) as requiring Member States to make infringing copies legally susceptible to seizure under national law. Slovak’s future passive can describe the operation of that required regime when its national conditions are met. Article 7(3) then distinguishes mandatory availability for infringing copies from optional availability for circumvention means, without distinguishing compulsory execution from discretionary execution. Article 7(1)’s framework of appropriate remedies and Article 12’s legislative addressees support this interpretation. The national-law qualification provides a textual basis for harmonization; it need not expressly rewrite the Slovak verb. This substantially weakens, but does not conclusively eliminate, the competing compulsory-execution reading.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review despite the complete supplied English context. The review is based on the original-language passages reproduced in the packet; the linked EUR-Lex pages were not independently retrieved. Complete corresponding non-English context is unavailable. The national-law reference may govern conditions, procedure and individual remedial discretion, rather than procedure alone. Neither reviewer establishes which interpretation prevails. Their statements that Article 7(2) lacks repeated knowledge and commercial-purpose conditions are textually accurate, but cannot establish unlimited reach. The text also does not settle whether seizure is temporary, final, or dependent on additional safeguards. These uncertainties justify low confidence in the legal-effect mechanism, while leaving the textual contrast clear.
Unresolved: Does complete authentic-language context sustain the harmonized availability interpretation? Which aspects of seizure are reserved to national law? Can a concrete case establish that an otherwise lawful decision to decline seizure would breach Article 7(2) under the competing reading?

impact_families.title: Recital 13: unresolved contractual effect of Spanish «desarrollo»
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, recital 13, read with Articles 4(1)(a)–(b), 5 and 8.
impact_families.effect: A lawful acquirer must adapt protected program code to use its copy for its intended purpose, but a specific contractual clause prohibits that adaptation. Assume the activity goes beyond loading, running and error correction and does not independently qualify under the observation or interoperability exceptions. A different outcome would arise only if «desarrollo» supported interpreting the operative provisions as protecting that adaptation against contractual prohibition.
impact_families.rationale:
I compared the supplied legal passages by source_id rct_13, including Croatian p0014 alongside the other language-local p0020 entries. Spanish «carga y de desarrollo» differs lexically from English “loading and running,” French «chargement et d'exécution» and German «Laden und Ablaufen». That comparison establishes a wording issue, not an operative development entitlement. I disagree with the packet's categorical title that Spanish protects necessary development and with treating its accepted or substantial designation as establishing legal effect. Both reviewers appropriately identify the missing operative boundary; their matching conclusions provide no additional evidence. Their conditional moderate assessment is defensible only as a hypothetical consequence. Article 5(1) already encompasses necessary acts under Article 4(1)(a) and (b), including adaptations, absent specific contractual provisions. The disputed incremental consequence therefore concerns protection against a contractual restriction, rather than whether adaptation can ever be permitted. Article 8's omission of Article 5(1) from its express nullity rule complicates the expansion argument, but does not by itself establish that every restriction on necessary use is valid. Any suggestion in the reviews that the harmonized reading conclusively validates the scenario's prohibition would go beyond this evidence.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation understands «desarrollo» here as the program's operation or execution. The sentence pairs it with loading; the recital begins with technically necessary reproduction for lawful use and ends by leaving other necessary acts subject to specific contractual provisions. Italian «svolgimento» further cautions against automatically reading the term as software creation. Articles 4 and 5 supply an operative framework for reproduction, alteration and intended use. Together these features strongly resist deriving a new mandatory development exception from the recital. Even if «desarrollo» denotes development linguistically, the recital cannot independently expand the operative exception. Nor does the wording establish that running loses protection.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review despite the complete supplied English context. Spanish operative provisions and equivalent context across authentic versions are missing. I rechecked the packet's legal text, but could not independently retrieve the cited EUR-Lex originals with the available tools; their transcription and completeness remain unverified. The reviewers' interpretation of «desarrollo» as execution is contextually strong but is not independently established as a linguistic fact. Conversely, translating it as development does not establish the proposed legal extension. No material difference between the two reviewers changes these unresolved points.
Unresolved: Do the original Spanish Articles 4, 5 and 8 and corresponding authentic provisions support any additional protection against contractual restrictions? How should recital 13's non-prohibition language be reconciled with Article 5(1)'s contractual qualification and Article 8's enumerated nullity rule? Does any adaptation outside the existing protected activities actually cross the proposed outcome boundary?

impact_families.title: Potential qualification of the normal-exploitation prohibition
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 6(3), read with Article 6(1)–(2), its Berne reference and recital 15.
impact_families.effect: Decompilation satisfies Article 6(1)–(2) but conflicts with normal exploitation. If that interference is considered justified and does not unreasonably prejudice legitimate interests, the Romanian shared qualifier could preserve the exception.
impact_families.rationale:
Romanian places both coordinated objects under 'aduce atingere în mod nejustificat', whereas English states a separate, unqualified exploitation limb. Both reviewers identify the same conditional expansion and no material disagreement. Ordinary competition or lost sales alone cannot establish the required conflict with legally defined normal exploitation.
Counterreading: The express Berne reference, separate safeguards in other authentic versions and English recital 15 favor preserving an autonomous exploitation prohibition. Context could treat conflict with normal exploitation as necessarily unjustified, eliminating the proposed difference.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Whether a legally recognized exploitation conflict could nevertheless be justified remains unresolved. Romanian recital 15 is not supplied, despite earlier packet commentary invoking it. Context_limited is true.
Unresolved: Does complete Romanian context preserve the independent prohibition, and can a concrete justified conflict survive both the legitimate-interests limb and every other Article 6 condition?

impact_families.title: Potential removal of the unreasonable-prejudice threshold
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 6(3), read with Article 6(1)–(2), Article 4(1) and recital 15.
impact_families.effect: Otherwise qualifying decompilation causes reasonable prejudice to a legally legitimate interest without conflicting with normal exploitation. Finnish's unqualified harm wording could exclude reliance on Article 6.
impact_families.rationale:
Finnish 'aiheuttaa haittaa' states harm without expressly requiring unreasonableness. Both reviewers correctly preserve the independent normal-exploitation prohibition: conduct already caught there cannot demonstrate this omission's effect. Their assessments contain no material disagreement.
Counterreading: The express Berne reference, qualified wording in other authentic versions and the exception's purpose support restoring the threshold through interpretation. 'Legitimate interests' itself limits cognizable harm. English recital 15 also uses unqualified prejudice, showing that abbreviated wording need not establish a different standard.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No concrete example establishes reasonable harm to a legitimate interest outside the normal-exploitation prohibition. Full Finnish context is absent, and context_limited is true.
Unresolved: Does complete Finnish context preserve the reasonableness threshold, and what qualifying harm survives the separate normal-exploitation test?

impact_families.title: Employer title versus exclusive exercise of economic rights
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 2(3), aligned by source_id art_2 across the supplied authentic versions, including Croatian p0023; read with Article 2(1)–(2), Articles 3–6 and 8.
impact_families.effect: An employee creates a protected program within Article 2(3), without a contrary agreement. The employer later transfers the economic rights without obtaining an employee assignment. A different outcome would arise only if employer title permits that transfer while exclusive exercise leaves employee title that independently prevents it. The supplied directive does not establish that latter premise.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied original-language texts confirms a wording distinction: Spanish allocates 'la titularidad de los derechos económicos'; English grants exclusive entitlement to exercise all economic rights. French, German and Italian also use exercise formulations. This is textual evidence, not a vote among versions. Article 2(2) expressly addresses joint rights, but does not establish that employee title survives paragraph 3. I disagree with treating the packet's accepted 'substantial' finding as an established outcome difference: translating titularidad as ownership does not itself prove different transfer powers. Review A tests an employer transfer; review B tests an employee transfer. These are complementary hypotheses, not contradictory findings, but both require unsupported consequences of residual title. In particular, an employee might transfer only title burdened by the employer's unchanged exclusive powers. That would not establish a change in exploitation authority. Both reviewers appropriately leave the assigned level unresolved. Conditional moderate impact is defensible only if a distinct title-dependent transfer outcome is subsequently demonstrated; neither broad coverage nor reviewer agreement establishes high impact.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation gives the employer the same comprehensive default economic entitlement under every version, while allowing national law to implement it through different ownership structures. Spanish titularidad can identify the holder of that entitlement without settling all incidents of underlying title. English 'all economic rights' need not exclude transfer powers. Finnish 'oikeus määrätä kaikista taloudellisista oikeuksista' also supports considering powers of disposition. Article 4's reference to the Article 2 rightholder reinforces equivalent authorization powers. Article 2(1) distinguishes authorship and rightholder status but does not reserve employee economic ownership. Articles 5–6 limit exploitation, and Article 8 preserves other law without resolving title or overriding Article 2(3). This interpretation substantially weakens the proposed divergence.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, requiring needs_review despite the complete supplied English context. I rechecked the original-language passages reproduced in the packet; independent retrieval from the linked pages was unavailable. Complete surrounding authentic-language context remains unchecked. Neither review establishes that English preserves employee ownership, that Spanish requires a particular national vesting mechanism, or that exclusive exercise excludes disposition. The packet's suggested enforcement consequences likewise remain unsubstantiated. Conditional moderate describes the specified hypothetical, not a confirmed divergence.
Unresolved: Does complete authentic-language context require a particular allocation of economic title, or only equivalent employer powers? Does any residual employee title constrain an employer transfer or support an independently consequential employee transfer? What source-supported rule establishes that consequence? An editor must supply and check the missing context before assigning an impact level.

impact_families.title: Article 7(2): required availability of seizure versus compulsory execution
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 7(2), aligned by source_id art_7; read with Article 7(1) and (3), Articles 1 and 4–6, and Article 12.
impact_families.effect: An identified infringing copy meets national conditions for seizure, but the authority would otherwise have lawful discretion to decline it. A compulsory-execution interpretation would require seizure; an availability interpretation could preserve that discretion. The packet does not establish that such residual discretion exists in a particular national system.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied original-language passages confirms a textual contrast: Slovenian ‘se zaseže’ uses a categorical seizure formulation, while English ‘shall be liable to seizure’, French ‘est susceptible de saisie’, and Swedish ‘ska kunna tas i beslag’ describe susceptibility or required capability. Danish ‘skal beslaglægges’ supplies another categorical formulation. These are aligned provisions under art_7, irrespective of language-local pNNNN identifiers; their number does not determine interpretation. The strongest contextual reading distinguishes a mandatory national framework for seizing infringing copies under paragraph 2 from optional provision for seizing circumvention tools under paragraph 3. That distinction accommodates the categorical formulations without necessarily requiring execution in each case. The accepted finding therefore supports an interpretive concern, but not an established substantial legal divergence. Both reviewers appropriately retain needs_review and identify a plausible moderate conditional consequence. I depart from their medium confidence because the decisive boundary—whether discretion remains after national conditions are met—is unresolved, as is the harmonizing counterreading. Review A’s reference to continued possession must also be qualified: declining seizure does not establish any right to retain or use an infringing copy. Conditional moderate impact remains reasonable for a changed seizure decision under one specific rule; neither broad wording alone nor the supplied evidence establishes permanent deprivation or another consequence warranting high impact.
Counterreading: All authentic formulations can plausibly express a common obligation to make every infringing copy legally susceptible to seizure under national law. Slovenian’s categorical present can describe the applicable legal regime rather than an unconditional command to seize each copy. Paragraph 3’s ‘may provide’ concerns legislative choice over tool seizure; it does not establish that paragraph 2 removes case-specific enforcement discretion. This harmonization is substantial and remains unrebutted by the supplied context.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, requiring needs_review. The supplied Article 7 units are marked complete, but complete non-English surrounding provisions are unavailable. This review rechecked packet transcriptions; the linked originals were not independently retrieved. Contrary to any implication that the national-law qualification merely supplies procedural conditions, it may also preserve substantive remedial discretion. Conversely, it cannot simply be assumed to permit Member States to make seizure unavailable altogether. Neither reviewer resolves this distinction. Seizure’s duration, practical effects, and relationship to confiscation or destruction are also unestablished.
Unresolved: Does complete authentic-language context distinguish legal susceptibility from compulsory execution? Does the national-law qualification preserve discretion once eligibility conditions are satisfied? What concrete national situation would produce different outcomes under the competing readings, and what would seizure entail there?

impact_families.title: Article 1(4): preservation of pre-1993 acts versus agreements
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 1(4), aligned by source_id art_1; Articles 4–8 and 10; Annex II.
impact_families.effect: Assume a noncontractual reproduction was completed before 1 January 1993, was lawful when performed, generated no acquired right, and would otherwise face adverse consequences from applying the Directive. A safeguard covering completed acts could preserve its treatment; an agreements-only safeguard might not. The packet does not establish that these conditions can all be satisfied. Neither reading automatically immunizes later exploitation of an older program.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied original-language passages by art_1 confirms the lexical difference: Hungarian 'kötött megállapodások' means concluded agreements. German likewise uses 'getroffener Vereinbarungen', and Romanian uses 'contractelor încheiate'. Danish, Spanish, Dutch and Swedish refer more broadly to completed or performed acts. English 'acts concluded' and French 'actes conclus' also admit a legal-transaction reading. This is a multilingual interpretive question, not an established Hungarian error. Croatian art_1 is correctly aligned despite its different local identifier p0022. The strongest harmonizing interpretation preserves settled historical legal situations while applying protection to older programs prospectively. Article 10 and Annex II reinforce continuity by mapping Article 1(4) to former Article 9(2); they do not establish retrospective liability. I therefore do not adopt the packet's accepted/substantial characterization as a demonstrated legal effect. Review A's references to rights and remedies establish possible consequences only after temporal applicability is shown. Review B's lawful-reproduction example makes the hypothesis clearer but does not establish that the narrower wording would expose that act to liability. The reviewers have no material disagreement on classification, but their agreement supplies no independent support for the outcome boundary. Moderate is defensible solely as the conditional consequence of losing a meaningful safeguard for the specified historical group.
Counterreading: All versions can plausibly preserve concluded legal arrangements and vested legal positions without reopening completed conduct. English 'acts concluded' need not encompass every factual act, while Hungarian 'agreements' need not imply that other historical conduct becomes newly actionable. Applying the Directive to programs created before 1993 concerns the age of the protected subject matter; it does not necessarily apply new restrictions to acts completed before that date. Under this reading, the lexical difference produces no changed outcome.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review notwithstanding the complete supplied English context. I rechecked the reproduced legal texts; the linked source pages were not independently retrieved. Both reviews leave the decisive causal step unresolved: omission of an express safeguard for noncontractual acts does not itself authorize adverse retrospective consequences. The acquired-rights limb may cover some unilateral transactions, but cannot simply be assumed to cover every completed act. Conversely, absence of an acquired right does not prove exposure. Articles 5–6 require their own factual conditions, and Article 8 does not itself resolve the temporal question. Neither review supplies a concrete example surviving all these qualifications.
Unresolved: Does the missing authentic-language context support an independent safeguard for completed factual conduct? What concrete noncontractual act would suffer a changed legal outcome under the narrower reading despite acquired rights, applicable exceptions and temporal protections? Does the proposed dispute concern completed historical conduct or subsequent exploitation? These questions require resolution before assigning impact.

impact_families.title: Prior provision potentially substitutes for ready availability
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 6(1)(b), subject to Article 6(1)'s opening necessity requirement and Article 6(2)–(3).
impact_families.effect: Information is nominally supplied through an inaccessible mechanism, never becomes readily available, and decompilation remains the only possible means of obtaining it. A difference arises only if Bulgarian nevertheless treats that nominal supply as prior provision.
impact_families.rationale:
Bulgarian lacks an express accessibility qualifier, but its opening paragraph requires decompilation to be the 'only possible way'. Actual usable receipt normally defeats necessity under either version. Reviewer B treats a surviving boundary as plausible enough for medium confidence; reviewer A identifies the unresolved compatibility of prior provision with that necessity requirement. The packet does not resolve this, supporting low confidence.
Counterreading: 'Предоставена' can mean effectively made available. Read with necessity and the interoperability purpose, it can exclude merely nominal delivery. Conversely, readily available but unsolicited information generally defeats indispensability, so non-delivery alone does not establish broader permission.
impact_families.uncertainty:
A burdensome supply process alone proves neither indispensability nor a changed outcome. The disagreement concerns this missing causal step, not the wording. Bulgarian context outside Article 6 is missing, and context_limited is true.
Unresolved: Can inaccessible delivery legally count as provision while decompilation remains the only possible means of obtaining the necessary information?

impact_families.title: Potential expansion of the similarity restriction
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 6(2)(c), read with Articles 1(2), 5(3), 6(1)–(3) and recitals 10–11 and 15.
impact_families.effect: A lawful licensee independently develops an internal scheduling program with substantially similar functionality to the licensed original but materially different protected expression. It must exchange scheduling information with existing licensed installations and mutually use that information. The protocol information has never been available; authorised observation and testing cannot reveal it. The licensee must reproduce and translate only the indispensable interface code, using the information exclusively for interoperability and disclosing it to nobody. These acts are unnecessary for the original program's intended use or error correction, are not backup creation, and exceed observation during authorised operations. The original is protected, the relevant rights belong to the claimant, and no separate authorisation covers the extraction. Existing licensed installations remain necessary; the internal implementation neither displaces licensing opportunities nor otherwise conflicts with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudices legitimate interests. No other infringement or independently applicable restriction is involved. The expression-limited reading permits this extraction-and-use workflow; the disputed functional-similarity reading prevents reliance on Article 6 for that workflow.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied original-language provisions confirms the missing Latvian qualifier. The conditional scenario satisfies Article 6(1): independent creation, indispensability, eligible actor, unavailable information and confinement to necessary parts. Both reproduction and translation occur, avoiding dependence on the conjunction differences between versions. Recital 10's interoperability definition and Article 6(2)(a)–(b) are satisfied; materially different expression and no separate infringement satisfy the expression-qualified Article 6(2)(c). Article 6(3) is addressed expressly. Article 5 supplies no alternative permission; distribution exhaustion does not authorise these reproductions or translations. Article 8 preserves other legal regimes but invalidates contractual provisions contrary to Article 6. I reach moderate independently of the reviewers' agreement. Their central mechanism is supported, with two qualifications: Article 6 does not create a general prohibition on functionally similar programs, and review B's 'without ... copying protected expression' must concern the resulting program, since the preliminary reproduction and translation are precisely the protected acts requiring an exception. The changed outcome is loss of permission for the specified extraction-and-use workflow, not automatic infringement by the resulting program or an established damages entitlement.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonising interpretation reads Latvian substantial similarity as similarity in protected expression. Latvian Article 1(2) excludes underlying ideas and principles, and recital 11 expressly distinguishes their expression. Recitals 10 and 15 support interoperability between independently created programs. Article 6(2)(c)'s concluding reference to 'any other act' infringing copyright further connects the restriction to copyright-protected subject matter. The explicit expression limitations in English, French and German reinforce that reading without deciding the issue by counting languages. Nevertheless, Article 6 independently limits uses of extracted information, so Article 1(2) alone does not logically preclude a broader condition on this exception. Assuming that broader condition survives harmonisation, the stated outcome changes.
impact_families.uncertainty:
There is substantial doubt that the broader reading would survive harmonised interpretation. Both reviewers recognise this, and it does not defeat the conditional tier. Their Article 6(3) conclusions are hypothetical conditions, not demonstrated facts about an actual implementation; continued licensing alone would not establish compliance with that safeguard. Likewise, independent authorship alone does not establish materially different expression. The scenario expressly requires both findings. The supplied complete English and Latvian acts provide the relevant context; omission of complete acts in other languages identifies no additional operative blocker here. Source text was rechecked within the packet, without independent live retrieval. National implementation, remedies and actual affected-product frequency remain unestablished.
Unresolved: No operative limb remains unresolved within the expressly conditioned scenario. An actual case would require proof of indispensability, substantial functional similarity, distinct expression and compliance with Article 6(3). Whether the broader interpretation ultimately prevails remains an interpretive question. Sale-versus-marketing wording and other Article 6 divergences are outside this finding.

impact_families.title: Hungarian Article 7(1)(c): missing unauthorised-purpose qualification
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 7(1)(c), its reservation for Articles 4–6, and Article 7(3); Articles 4–6 and 8 provide interpretive context.
impact_families.effect: An independent supplier commercially circulates a hardware service tool whose sole intended purpose is directly to disable an external technical device actually protecting an original computer program created after 1993. The program's eligible rightholder expressly authorizes both tool distribution and every intended removal operation. The tool contains no protected program expression, and its distribution and operation neither reproduce nor alter the protected program. Removal is elective retirement of protection, unnecessary for program use, error correction, backup, observation, testing or interoperability. No infringing program copy is circulated or commercially possessed. Under the authorization-qualified reading, Article 7(1)(c) does not require remedial coverage for this conduct. Assuming the unqualified Hungarian reading prevails, the supplier's circulation of this exclusively removal-purpose tool enters the category for which Member States must provide appropriate remedies.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied original-language passages and complete English and Hungarian acts confirms that Hungarian Article 7(1)(c) describes an exclusive intended purpose of removal or circumvention ('eltávolítása vagy megkerülése') without expressly qualifying it as unauthorized. English expressly says 'to facilitate the unauthorised removal or circumvention'; German, French and Swedish likewise express an authorization boundary. Their relevance is interpretive, not a vote among versions. The scenario satisfies protected subject matter, eligible rights ownership, actual program protection, circulation and exclusive intended purpose. Direct removal also satisfies the English facilitation formulation, so omission of 'facilitate' does not independently drive this outcome. Article 4 supplies no competing infringement ground because no protected-program act occurs. Article 4(2) exhaustion is therefore immaterial. Articles 5 and 6 do not independently protect the stipulated standalone tool circulation, and their necessary-use, backup, observation and interoperability predicates are absent. Article 7(1)(a)–(b) and 7(2) are inapplicable because there is no infringing copy. Article 8 preserves other law but supplies no separate exception for this tool. The conditional result is a substantive expansion of remedial coverage for an identifiable group, supporting moderate impact. There is no material disagreement with either reviewer's conditional tier or rejection of an independently established facilitation discrepancy. I use the narrower, no-program-act scenario to avoid review B's unnecessary reliance on authorization of possible reproduction or alteration. Neither reviewer establishes mandatory seizure, damages or an actual claim against this supplier, and none is inferred.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation reads Hungarian removal or circumvention as implicitly unauthorized. Article 7 provides special protection within a copyright scheme whose Article 4 rights include authorization, and its opening reservation preserves Articles 4–6. Recitals 13–16 reinforce protection of lawful uses and carefully bounded exceptions. Express authorization limitations in other authentic versions clarify the same boundary. That interpretation plausibly eliminates the discrepancy altogether. However, if the unqualified reading survives that interpretive exercise as stipulated, authorization of an independent hardware tool is not itself an express Article 4–6 exception to tool circulation.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The strongest uncertainty is whether the unqualified reading could survive harmonized interpretation: the protective purpose, express authorization language elsewhere, and Article 7's reservation for Articles 4–6 strongly favor reading an authorization limitation into Hungarian. This concerns interpretive success, not the conditional tier. Both reviewers appropriately distinguish those questions. Their statements that the reservation does not independently defeat the scenario are sustainable only for the carefully confined standalone-tool facts; they should not be generalized to removal necessary for protected uses under Articles 5 or 6. National law, consent, standing and remedial discretion could prevent a particular enforcement outcome. Accordingly, the supported consequence is expanded required coverage, not an automatic remedy against a consenting rightholder's supplier. Complete acts in languages other than English and Hungarian are omitted, but no specific unresolved contextual limb has been identified that defeats this confined coverage change once the disputed reading is assumed.
Unresolved: The ultimate harmonized interpretation and the form of national remedies remain open. Article 7(3) makes seizure provisions optional; broader classification would expand the referenced category without compelling seizure. No unresolved operative predicate prevents the stated conditional coverage change. The packet marks context_limited false and supplies complete English and Hungarian context, so its incomplete whole-act coverage across other languages does not alone require needs_review.

impact_families.title: Article 8: potentially narrower preservation of other legal provisions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2009/24/EC, Article 8, first paragraph, aligned across authentic versions by source_id art_8; read with Article 8, second paragraph, Articles 1 and 4–6, and recitals 6 and 16–19.
impact_families.effect: An otherwise applicable rule in an unlisted legal field requires an act restricted by the Directive. A changed outcome would arise only if an exhaustive reading of Article 8 left that rule displaced, while an illustrative reading preserved it, after checking substantive scope, exceptions and other safeguards. No rule meeting those conditions is established in the packet.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied legal text, English expressly introduces examples through ‘any other legal provisions such as’; Slovenian refers to other provisions ‘ki se nanašajo’ to the listed fields without an express illustrative marker. This supports a textual ambiguity, not an established exhaustive legal boundary. Alignment is by art_8, including Croatian p0029 alongside other versions’ p0036. French ‘notamment’, German ‘so für’ and Croatian ‘kao što su’ provide interpretive evidence of exemplification, without resolving the issue by counting versions. I disagree with the underlying finding insofar as its ‘substantial’ severity implies an established consequential narrowing. Both reviewers correctly distinguish omission from a safeguard from actual displacement. Their moderate conditional assessment is defensible only as a hypothesis about a specific changed legal outcome; neither establishes that outcome. Reviewer B’s inspection example adds specificity but no supporting legal rule. Reviewer A’s abstract scenario avoids that unsupported detail but still leaves the decisive conflict unidentified. The issue is confined to whether the first-paragraph list is exhaustive; terminology within listed fields and contractual invalidity are separate questions.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation reads Slovenian ‘drugih pravnih predpisov’ and its following list as identifying examples of other applicable laws. The absence of an explicit equivalent to ‘such as’ does not itself require exhaustiveness. Express exemplification in other authentic versions, the bounded copyright framework described in recital 6, and recital 16’s recognition of other forms of protection support this reading. Recitals 17–19 reinforce contextual compatibility with additional rules. Article 8’s second paragraph nevertheless expressly invalidates contracts contrary to Article 6 or Article 5(2)–(3); the preservation clause cannot erase those limits. This harmonizing interpretation could eliminate the alleged outcome difference entirely.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review. I rechecked the original wording reproduced in the packet; independent retrieval of the linked pages was unavailable. Complete Slovenian contextual provisions are not supplied. Reviewer B’s proposed disclosure duty does not necessarily engage a restricted act: disclosure alone is not automatically reproduction or distribution to the public under Article 4. Copying could engage Article 4, but the applicable duty, authorization, exceptions and conflict would still need identification. Both reviewers’ references to recitals 17–19 require qualification: those recitals provide contextual support for continued application of specified rules, not a general operative preservation clause covering every unlisted field. Neither the English word ‘any’ nor an illustrative list establishes unconditional priority over the Directive’s mandatory provisions.
Unresolved: Does complete Slovenian context reinforce exemplification? Which concrete unlisted rule requires preservation by Article 8? What restricted act and genuine legal conflict arise? After applying the Directive’s scope, exceptions and other safeguards, would exhaustiveness change the result or merely remove express reassurance?

legislation.title: DIRECTIVE 2011/7/EU OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 16 February 2011 on combating late payment in commercial transactions (recast) (Text with EEA relevance)

unavailable_languages.name: Irish
unavailable_languages.reason: No official language expression exists for this exact version in Cellar metadata.

passages.label: Title
passages.text:
DIRECTIVE 2011/7/EU OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL
of 16 February 2011
on combating late payment in commercial transactions
(recast)
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND THE COUNCIL OF THE EUROPEAN UNION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and in particular Article 114 thereof,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to the proposal from the European Commission,

passages.label: Citation 3
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | A number of substantive changes are to be made to Directive 2000/35/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 June 2000 on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( 3 ) . It is desirable, for reasons of clarity and rationalisation, that the provisions in question be recast.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | Most goods and services are supplied within the internal market by economic operators to other economic operators and to public authorities on a deferred payment basis whereby the supplier gives its client time to pay the invoice, as agreed between parties, as set out in the supplier’s invoice or as laid down by law.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Many payments in commercial transactions between economic operators or between economic operators and public authorities are made later than agreed in the contract or laid down in the general commercial conditions. Although the goods are delivered or the services performed, many corresponding invoices are paid well after the deadline. Such late payment negatively affects liquidity and complicates the financial management of undertakings. It also affects their competitiveness and profitability when the creditor needs to obtain external financing because of late payment. The risk of such negative effects strongly increases in periods of economic downturn when access to financing is more difficult.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Judicial claims related to late payment are already facilitated by Council Regulation (EC) No 44/2001 of 22 December 2000 on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters ( 4 ) , Regulation (EC) No 805/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 April 2004 creating a European Enforcement Order for uncontested claims ( 5 ) , Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 creating a European order for payment procedure ( 6 ) and Regulation (EC) No 861/2007 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 July 2007 establishing a European Small Claims Procedure ( 7 ) . However, in order to discourage late payment in commercial transactions, it is necessary to lay down complementary provisions.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Undertakings should be able to trade throughout the internal market under conditions which ensure that transborder operations do not entail greater risks than domestic sales. Distortions of competition would ensue if substantially different rules applied to domestic and transborder operations.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | In its Communication of 25 June 2008 entitled ‘ “Think Small First” — A “Small Business Act” for Europe’, the Commission emphasised that small and medium-sized enterprises’ (SMEs) access to finance should be facilitated and that a legal and business environment supportive of timely payments in commercial transactions should be developed. It should be noted that public authorities have a special responsibility in this regard. The criteria for the definition of SMEs are set out in Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC of 6 May 2003 concerning the definition of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises ( 8 ) .

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | One of the priority actions of the Commission Communication of 26 November 2008 entitled ‘European Economic Recovery Plan’ is the reduction of administrative burdens and the promotion of entrepreneurship by, inter alia, ensuring that, as a matter of principle, invoices, including to SMEs, for supplies and services are paid within 1 month to ease liquidity constraints.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | The scope of this Directive should be limited to payments made as remuneration for commercial transactions. This Directive should not regulate transactions with consumers, interest in connection with other payments, for instance payments under the laws on cheques and bills of exchange, or payments made as compensation for damages including payments from insurance companies. Furthermore, Member States should be able to exclude debts that are subject to insolvency proceedings, including proceedings aimed at debt restructuring.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | This Directive should regulate all commercial transactions irrespective of whether they are carried out between private or public undertakings or between undertakings and public authorities, given that public authorities handle a considerable volume of payments to undertakings. It should therefore also regulate all commercial transactions between main contractors and their suppliers and subcontractors.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | The fact that the liberal professions are covered by this Directive should not oblige Member States to treat them as undertakings or merchants for purposes outside the scope of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | The delivery of goods and the provision of services for remuneration to which this Directive applies should also include the design and execution of public works and building and civil engineering works.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | Late payment constitutes a breach of contract which has been made financially attractive to debtors in most Member States by low or no interest rates charged on late payments and/or slow procedures for redress. A decisive shift to a culture of prompt payment, including one in which the exclusion of the right to charge interest should always be considered to be a grossly unfair contractual term or practice, is necessary to reverse this trend and to discourage late payment. Such a shift should also include the introduction of specific provisions on payment periods and on the compensation of creditors for the costs incurred, and, inter alia, that the exclusion of the right to compensation for recovery costs should be presumed to be grossly unfair.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | Accordingly, provision should be made for business-to-business contractual payment periods to be limited, as a general rule, to 60 calendar days. However, there may be circumstances in which undertakings require more extensive payment periods, for example when undertakings wish to grant trade credit to their customers. It should therefore remain possible for the parties to expressly agree on payment periods longer than 60 calendar days, provided, however, that such extension is not grossly unfair to the creditor.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | In the interest of consistency of Union legislation, the definition of ‘contracting authorities’ in Directive 2004/17/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 March 2004 coordinating the procurement procedures of entities operating in the water, energy, transport and postal services sectors ( 9 ) and in Directive 2004/18/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 March 2004 on the coordination of procedures for the award of public works contracts, public supply contracts and public services contracts ( 10 ) should apply for the purposes of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | Statutory interest due for late payment should be calculated on a daily basis as simple interest, in accordance with Regulation (EEC, Euratom) No 1182/71 of the Council of 3 June 1971 determining the rules applicable to periods, dates and time limits ( 11 ) .

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | This Directive should not oblige a creditor to claim interest for late payment. In the event of late payment, this Directive should allow a creditor to resort to charging interest for late payment without giving any prior notice of non-performance or other similar notice reminding the debtor of his obligation to pay.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | A debtor’s payment should be regarded as late, for the purposes of entitlement to interest for late payment, where the creditor does not have the sum owed at his disposal on the due date provided that he has fulfilled his legal and contractual obligations.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | Invoices trigger requests for payment and are important documents in the chain of transactions for the supply of goods and services, inter alia, for determining payment deadlines. For the purposes of this Directive, Member States should promote systems that give legal certainty as regards the exact date of receipt of invoices by the debtors, including in the field of e-invoicing where the receipt of invoices could generate electronic evidence and which is partly governed by the provisions on invoicing contained in Council Directive 2006/112/EC of 28 November 2006 on the common system of value added tax ( 12 ) .

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | Fair compensation of creditors for the recovery costs incurred due to late payment is necessary to discourage late payment. Recovery costs should also include the recovery of administrative costs and compensation for internal costs incurred due to late payment for which this Directive should determine a fixed minimum sum which may be cumulated with interest for late payment. Compensation in the form of a fixed sum should aim at limiting the administrative and internal costs linked to the recovery. Compensation for the recovery costs should be determined without prejudice to national provisions according to which a national court may award compensation to the creditor for any additional damage regarding the debtor’s late payment.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | In addition to an entitlement to payment of a fixed sum to cover internal recovery costs, creditors should also be entitled to reimbursement of the other recovery costs they incur as a result of late payment by a debtor. Such costs should include, in particular, those incurred by creditors in instructing a lawyer or employing a debt collection agency.

passages.label: Recital 21
passages.text: (21) | This Directive should be without prejudice to the right of Member States to provide for fixed sums for compensation of recovery costs which are higher and therefore more favourable to the creditor, or to increase those sums, inter alia, in order to keep pace with inflation.

passages.label: Recital 22
passages.text: (22) | This Directive should not prevent payments by instalments or staggered payments. However, each instalment or payment should be paid on the agreed terms and should be subject to the rules for late payment set out in this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 23
passages.text: (23) | As a general rule, public authorities benefit from more secure, predictable and continuous revenue streams than undertakings. In addition, many public authorities can obtain financing at more attractive conditions than undertakings. At the same time, public authorities depend less than undertakings on building stable commercial relationships for the achievement of their aims. Long payment periods and late payment by public authorities for goods and services lead to unjustified costs for undertakings. It is therefore appropriate to introduce specific rules as regards commercial transactions for the supply of goods or services by undertakings to public authorities, which should provide in particular for payment periods normally not exceeding 30 calendar days, unless otherwise expressly agreed in the contract and provided it is objectively justified in the light of the particular nature or features of the contract, and in any event not exceeding 60 calendar days.

passages.label: Recital 24
passages.text: (24) | However, account should be taken of the specific situation of public authorities carrying out economic activities of an industrial or commercial nature by offering goods or services on the market as a public undertaking. For that purpose, Member States should be allowed, under certain conditions, to extend the statutory payment period up to a maximum of 60 calendar days.

passages.label: Recital 25
passages.text: (25) | A particular cause for concern in connection with late payment is the situation of health services in a large number of Member States. Healthcare systems, as a fundamental part of Europe’s social infrastructure, are often obliged to reconcile individual needs with the available finances, as the population of Europe ages, as expectations rise, and as medicine advances. All systems have to deal with the challenge of prioritising healthcare in a way that balances the needs of individual patients with the financial resources available. Member States should therefore be able to grant public entities providing healthcare a certain amount of flexibility in meeting their commitments. For that purpose, Member States should be allowed, under certain conditions, to extend the statutory payment period up to a maximum of 60 calendar days. Member States should, nonetheless, make every effort to ensure that payments in the healthcare sector are made within the statutory payment periods.

passages.label: Recital 26
passages.text: (26) | In order not to jeopardise the achievement of the objective of this Directive, Member States should ensure that in commercial transactions the maximum duration of a procedure of acceptance or verification does not exceed, as a general rule, 30 calendar days. Nevertheless, it should be possible for a verification procedure to exceed 30 calendar days, for example in the case of particularly complex contracts, when expressly agreed in the contract and in any tender documents and if it is not grossly unfair to the creditor.

passages.label: Recital 27
passages.text: (27) | The Union institutions are in a situation comparable to that of the public authorities of Member States with regard to their financing and commercial relationships. Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002 of 25 June 2002 on the Financial Regulation applicable to the general budget of the European Communities ( 13 ) specifies that the validation, authorisation and payment of expenditure by Union institutions must be completed within the time limits laid down in its implementing rules. Those implementing rules are currently set out in Commission Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 2342/2002 of 23 December 2002 laying down detailed rules for the implementation of Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1605/2002 on the Financial Regulation applicable to the general budget of the European Communities ( 14 ) , and specify the circumstances in which creditors which are paid late are entitled to receive default interest. In the context of the ongoing review of those Regulations, it should be ensured that the maximum time limits for payment by the Union institutions are aligned with statutory periods applicable to public authorities in accordance with this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 28
passages.text: (28) | This Directive should prohibit abuse of freedom of contract to the disadvantage of the creditor. As a result, where a term in a contract or a practice relating to the date or period for payment, the rate of interest for late payment or the compensation for recovery costs is not justified on the grounds of the terms granted to the debtor, or it mainly serves the purpose of procuring the debtor additional liquidity at the expense of the creditor, it may be regarded as constituting such an abuse. For that purpose, and in accordance with the academic ‘Draft Common Frame of Reference’, any contractual term or practice which grossly deviates from good commercial practice and is contrary to good faith and fair dealing should be regarded as unfair to the creditor. In particular, the outright exclusion of the right to charge interest should always be considered as grossly unfair, whereas the exclusion of the right to compensation for recovery costs should be presumed to be grossly unfair. This Directive should not affect national provisions relating to the way contracts are concluded or regulating the validity of contractual terms which are unfair to the debtor.

passages.label: Recital 29
passages.text: (29) | In the context of enhanced efforts to prevent the abuse of freedom of contract to the detriment of creditors, organisations officially recognised as representing undertakings and organisations with a legitimate interest in representing undertakings should be able to take action before national courts or administrative bodies in order to prevent the continued use of contract terms or practices which are grossly unfair to the creditor.

passages.label: Recital 30
passages.text: (30) | In order to contribute to the achievement of the objective of this Directive, Member States should foster the spread of good practices, including by encouraging the publication of a list of prompt payers.

passages.label: Recital 31
passages.text: (31) | It is desirable to ensure that creditors are in a position to exercise a retention of title clause on a non-discriminatory basis throughout the Union, if the retention of title clause is valid under the applicable national provisions designated by private international law.

passages.label: Recital 32
passages.text: (32) | This Directive only defines the term ‘enforceable title’ but should not regulate the various procedures for forced execution of such a title or the conditions under which forced execution of such a title can be stopped or suspended.

passages.label: Recital 33
passages.text: (33) | The consequences of late payment can be dissuasive only if they are accompanied by procedures for redress which are rapid and effective for the creditor. In accordance with the principle of non-discrimination set out in Article 18 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, those procedures should be available to all creditors who are established in the Union.

passages.label: Recital 34
passages.text: (34) | In order to facilitate compliance with the provisions of this Directive, Member States should encourage recourse to mediation or other means of alternative dispute resolution. Directive 2008/52/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 May 2008 on certain aspects of mediation in civil and commercial matters ( 15 ) already sets a framework for systems of mediation at Union level, especially for cross-border disputes, without preventing its application to internal mediation systems. Member States should also encourage interested parties to draw up voluntary codes of conduct aimed, in particular, at contributing to the implementation of this Directive.

passages.label: Recital 35
passages.text: (35) | It is necessary to ensure that the recovery procedures for unchallenged claims related to late payment in commercial transactions be completed within a short period of time, including through an expedited procedure and irrespective of the amount of the debt.

passages.label: Recital 36
passages.text: (36) | Since the objective of this Directive, namely combating late payment in the internal market, cannot be sufficiently achieved by the Member States and can, therefore, by reason of its scale and effect, be better achieved at the Union level, the Union may adopt measures, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity as set out in Article 5 of the Treaty on European Union. In accordance with the principle of proportionality, as set out in that Article, this Directive does not go beyond what is necessary in order to achieve that objective.

passages.label: Recital 37
passages.text: (37) | The obligation to transpose this Directive into national law should be confined to those provisions which represent a substantive change as compared with Directive 2000/35/EC. The obligation to transpose the provisions which are unchanged arises under that Directive.

passages.label: Recital 38
passages.text: (38) | This Directive should be without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time limits for transposition into national law and application of Directive 2000/35/EC.

passages.label: Recital 39
passages.text: (39) | In accordance with point 34 of the Interinstitutional Agreement on better law-making ( 16 ) , Member States are encouraged to draw up, for themselves and in the interest of the Union, their own tables which will, as far as possible, illustrate the correlation between this Directive and their transposition measures, and to make those tables public,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAVE ADOPTED THIS DIRECTIVE:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Subject matter and scope
1. The aim of this Directive is to combat late payment in commercial transactions, in order to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market, thereby fostering the competitiveness of undertakings and in particular of SMEs.
2. This Directive shall apply to all payments made as remuneration for commercial transactions.
3. Member States may exclude debts that are subject to insolvency proceedings instituted against the debtor, including proceedings aimed at debt restructuring.

passages.label: Article 2
Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
Transactions between undertakings
1. Member States shall ensure that, in commercial transactions between undertakings, the creditor is entitled to interest for late payment without the necessity of a reminder, where the following conditions are satisfied:
(a) | the creditor has fulfilled its contractual and legal obligations; and
(b) | the creditor has not received the amount due on time, unless the debtor is not responsible for the delay.
2. Member States shall ensure that the applicable reference rate:
(a) | for the first semester of the year concerned shall be the rate in force on 1 January of that year;
(b) | for the second semester of the year concerned shall be the rate in force on 1 July of that year.
3. Where the conditions set out in paragraph 1 are satisfied, Member States shall ensure the following:
(a) | that the creditor is entitled to interest for late payment from the day following the date or the end of the period for payment fixed in the contract;
(b) | where the date or period for payment is not fixed in the contract, that the creditor is entitled to interest for late payment upon the expiry of any of the following time limits: (i) 30 calendar days following the date of receipt by the debtor of the invoice or an equivalent request for payment; (ii) where the date of the receipt of the invoice or the equivalent request for payment is uncertain, 30 calendar days after the date of receipt of the goods or services; (iii) where the debtor receives the invoice or the equivalent request for payment earlier than the goods or the services, 30 calendar days after the date of the receipt of the goods or services; (iv) where a procedure of acceptance or verification, by which the conformity of the goods or services with the contract is to be ascertained, is provided for by statute or in the contract and if the debtor receives the invoice or the equivalent request for payment earlier or on the date on which such acceptance or verification takes place, 30 calendar days after that date.
4. Where a procedure of acceptance or verification, by which the conformity of the goods or services with the contract is to be ascertained, is provided for, Member States shall ensure that the maximum duration of that procedure does not exceed 30 calendar days from the date of receipt of the goods or services, unless otherwise expressly agreed in the contract and provided it is not grossly unfair to the creditor within the meaning of Article 7.
5. Member States shall ensure that the period for payment fixed in the contract does not exceed 60 calendar days, unless otherwise expressly agreed in the contract and provided it is not grossly unfair to the creditor within the meaning of Article 7.

passages.label: Article 4
passages.text:
Article 4
Transactions between undertakings and public authorities
1. Member States shall ensure that, in commercial transactions where the debtor is a public authority, the creditor is entitled upon expiry of the period defined in paragraphs 3, 4 or 6 to statutory interest for late payment, without the necessity of a reminder, where the following conditions are satisfied:
(a) | the creditor has fulfilled its contractual and legal obligations; and
(b) | the creditor has not received the amount due on time, unless the debtor is not responsible for the delay.
2. Member States shall ensure that the applicable reference rate:
(a) | for the first semester of the year concerned shall be the rate in force on 1 January of that year;
(b) | for the second semester of the year concerned shall be the rate in force on 1 July of that year.
3. Member States shall ensure that in commercial transactions where the debtor is a public authority:
(a) | the period for payment does not exceed any of the following time limits: (i) 30 calendar days following the date of receipt by the debtor of the invoice or an equivalent request for payment; (ii) where the date of receipt of the invoice or the equivalent request for payment is uncertain, 30 calendar days after the date of the receipt of the goods or services; (iii) where the debtor receives the invoice or the equivalent request for payment earlier than the goods or the services, 30 calendar days after the date of the receipt of the goods or services; (iv) where a procedure of acceptance or verification, by which the conformity of the goods or services with the contract is to be ascertained, is provided for by statute or in the contract and if the debtor receives the invoice or the equivalent request for payment earlier or on the date on which such acceptance or verification takes place, 30 calendar days after that date;
(b) | the date of receipt of the invoice is not subject to a contractual agreement between debtor and creditor.
4. Member States may extend the time limits referred to in point (a) of paragraph 3 up to a maximum of 60 calendar days for:
(a) | any public authority which carries out economic activities of an industrial or commercial nature by offering goods or services on the market and which is subject, as a public undertaking, to the transparency requirements laid down in Commission Directive 2006/111/EC of 16 November 2006 on the transparency of financial relations between Member States and public undertakings as well as on financial transparency within certain undertakings ( 17 ) ;
(b) | public entities providing healthcare which are duly recognised for that purpose.
If a Member State decides to extend the time limits in accordance with this paragraph, it shall send a report on such extension to the Commission by 16 March 2018.
On that basis, the Commission shall submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council indicating which Member States have extended the time limits in accordance with this paragraph and taking into account the impact on the functioning of the internal market, in particular on SMEs. That report shall be accompanied by any appropriate proposals.
5. Member States shall ensure that the maximum duration of a procedure of acceptance or verification referred to in point (iv) of point (a) of paragraph 3 does not exceed 30 calendar days from the date of receipt of the goods or services, unless otherwise expressly agreed in the contract and any tender documents and provided it is not grossly unfair to the creditor within the meaning of Article 7.
6. Member States shall ensure that the period for payment fixed in the contract does not exceed the time limits provided for in paragraph 3, unless otherwise expressly agreed in the contract and provided it is objectively justified in the light of the particular nature or features of the contract, and that it in any event does not exceed 60 calendar days.

passages.label: Article 5
passages.text:
Article 5
Payment schedules
This Directive shall be without prejudice to the ability of parties to agree, subject to the relevant provisions of applicable national law, on payment schedules providing for instalments. In such cases, where any of the instalments is not paid by the agreed date, interest and compensation provided for in this Directive shall be calculated solely on the basis of overdue amounts.

passages.label: Article 6
passages.text:
Article 6
Compensation for recovery costs
1. Member States shall ensure that, where interest for late payment becomes payable in commercial transactions in accordance with Article 3 or 4, the creditor is entitled to obtain from the debtor, as a minimum, a fixed sum of EUR 40.
2. Member States shall ensure that the fixed sum referred to in paragraph 1 is payable without the necessity of a reminder and as compensation for the creditor’s own recovery costs.
3.
