The creditor shall, in addition to the fixed sum referred to in paragraph 1, be entitled to obtain reasonable compensation from the debtor for any recovery costs exceeding that fixed sum and incurred due to the debtor’s late payment. This could include expenses incurred, inter alia, in instructing a lawyer or employing a debt collection agency.

passages.label: Article 7
passages.text:
Article 7
Unfair contractual terms and practices
1. Member States shall provide that a contractual term or a practice relating to the date or period for payment, the rate of interest for late payment or the compensation for recovery costs is either unenforceable or gives rise to a claim for damages if it is grossly unfair to the creditor.
In determining whether a contractual term or a practice is grossly unfair to the creditor, within the meaning of the first subparagraph, all circumstances of the case shall be considered, including:
(a) | any gross deviation from good commercial practice, contrary to good faith and fair dealing;
(b) | the nature of the product or the service; and
(c) | whether the debtor has any objective reason to deviate from the statutory rate of interest for late payment, from the payment period as referred to in Article 3(5), point (a) of Article 4(3), Article 4(4) and Article 4(6) or from the fixed sum as referred to in Article 6(1).
2. For the purpose of paragraph 1, a contractual term or a practice which excludes interest for late payment shall be considered as grossly unfair.
3. For the purpose of paragraph 1, a contractual term or a practice which excludes compensation for recovery costs as referred to in Article 6 shall be presumed to be grossly unfair.
4. Member States shall ensure that, in the interests of creditors and competitors, adequate and effective means exist to prevent the continued use of contractual terms and practices which are grossly unfair within the meaning of paragraph 1.
5. The means referred to in paragraph 4 shall include provisions whereby organisations officially recognised as representing undertakings, or organisations with a legitimate interest in representing undertakings may take action according to the applicable national law before the courts or before competent administrative bodies on the grounds that contractual terms or practices are grossly unfair within the meaning of paragraph 1, so that they can apply appropriate and effective means to prevent their continued use.

passages.label: Article 8
passages.text:
Article 8
Transparency and awareness raising
1. Member States shall ensure transparency regarding the rights and obligations stemming from this Directive, including by making publicly available the applicable rate of statutory interest for late payment.
2. The Commission shall make publicly available on the Internet details of the current statutory rates of interest which apply in all the Member States in the event of late payment in commercial transactions.
3. Member States shall, where appropriate, use professional publications, promotion campaigns or any other functional means to increase awareness of the remedies for late payment among undertakings.
4. Member States may encourage the establishment of prompt payment codes which set out clearly defined payment time limits and a proper process for dealing with any payments that are in dispute, or any other initiatives that tackle the crucial issue of late payment and contribute to developing a culture of prompt payment which supports the objective of this Directive.

passages.label: Article 9
passages.text:
Article 9
Retention of title
1. Member States shall provide in conformity with the applicable national provisions designated by private international law that the seller retains title to goods until they are fully paid for if a retention of title clause has been expressly agreed between the buyer and the seller before the delivery of the goods.
2. Member States may adopt or retain provisions dealing with down payments already made by the debtor.

passages.label: Article 10
passages.text:
Article 10
Recovery procedures for unchallenged claims
1. Member States shall ensure that an enforceable title can be obtained, including through an expedited procedure and irrespective of the amount of the debt, normally within 90 calendar days of the lodging of the creditor’s action or application at the court or other competent authority, provided that the debt or aspects of the procedure are not disputed. Member States shall carry out this duty in accordance with their respective national laws, regulations and administrative provisions.
2. National laws, regulations and administrative provisions shall apply the same conditions for all creditors who are established in the Union.
3. When calculating the period referred to in paragraph 1, the following shall not be taken into account:
(a) | periods for service of documents;
(b) | any delays caused by the creditor, such as periods devoted to correcting applications.
4. This Article shall be without prejudice to the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1896/2006.

passages.label: Article 11
passages.text:
Article 11
Report
By 16 March 2016, the Commission shall submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council on the implementation of this Directive. The report shall be accompanied by any appropriate proposals.

passages.label: Article 12
passages.text:
Article 12
Transposition
1. Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with Articles 1 to 8 and 10 by 16 March 2013. They shall forthwith communicate to the Commission the text of those provisions.
When Member States adopt those measures, they shall contain a reference to this Directive or shall be accompanied by such reference on the occasion of their official publication. They shall also include a statement that references in existing laws, regulations and administrative provisions to the repealed Directive shall be construed as references to this Directive. The methods of making such reference and the formulation of such statement shall be laid down by Member States.
2. Member States shall communicate to the Commission the text of the main provisions of national law which they adopt in the field covered by this Directive.
3. Member States may maintain or bring into force provisions which are more favourable to the creditor than the provisions necessary to comply with this Directive.
4. In transposing the Directive, Member States shall decide whether to exclude contracts concluded before 16 March 2013.

passages.label: Article 13
passages.text:
Article 13
Repeal
Directive 2000/35/EC is repealed with effect from 16 March 2013, without prejudice to the obligations of the Member States relating to the time limit for its transposition into national law and its application. However, it shall remain applicable to contracts concluded before that date to which this Directive does not apply pursuant to Article 12(4).
References to the repealed Directive shall be construed as references to this Directive and be read in accordance with the correlation table set out in the Annex.

passages.label: Article 14
passages.text:
Article 14
Entry into force
This Directive shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Article 15
passages.text:
Article 15
Addressees
This Directive is addressed to the Member States.

impact_families.title: Recital 33: Danish low-cost wording; operative effect unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Directive 2011/7/EU, recital 33 (source_id rct_33), read with Articles 1, 2(1), 6, 10 and 12(3)–(4), and recitals 19–20, 32 and 35.
impact_families.effect: An EU-established supplier seeks an enforceable title for an unchallenged commercial debt. The national procedure meets Article 10’s timing and equal-treatment requirements and remains practically effective, but entails creditor costs arguably exceeding 'small costs'. A changed outcome would require the Danish wording to support an additional affordability constraint that demands adjustment despite that effectiveness. Neither reviewer establishes that this boundary exists.
impact_families.rationale:
Rechecking the supplied legal text by source_id rct_33 confirms that Danish expressly adds 'der kun medfører små omkostninger for kreditor'—procedures entailing only small costs for the creditor. English and the other supplied recital versions lack that express qualification. Croatian p0034 belongs to this same source_id; language-local paragraph numbers do not control alignment. The textual difference is supported, but the finding’s 'substantial' severity is not established as legal impact. Both reviewers appropriately leave assignment unresolved. Their scenarios nevertheless require different qualifications: reviewer A’s substantial unreimbursed costs might already undermine creditor effectiveness under the harmonized reading; reviewer B’s substantial upfront but recoverable fees might ultimately entail only small creditor costs, or might already obstruct effective access. Neither scenario alone isolates a changed outcome attributable to the Danish addition. Conditional moderate impact remains plausible only if that addition changes the treatment of an otherwise effective procedure for an identifiable group. The evidence supports neither an autonomous fee ceiling nor a specific entitlement to fee relief.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing interpretation treats low creditor costs as an explanation of creditor-effective redress. Article 6 supplies a minimum EUR 40 and reasonable compensation for additional recovery costs incurred because of late payment; recitals 19–20 connect cost compensation with deterrence. Article 10 requires normally obtaining an enforceable title within 90 calendar days under its stated conditions and requires equal conditions for Union-established creditors, while leaving implementation to national law. It states no cost ceiling. Recital 33 can guide interpretation of these obligations without creating a separate low-fee requirement. Article 12(3) permits more creditor-favourable national provisions but does not make them mandatory. Recital 32 also cautions against extending this mechanism to regulation of forced execution.
impact_families.uncertainty:
context_limited is true, so assigned_level must remain needs_review despite the complete English context. I checked the original-language quotations and English provisions supplied in the packet; independent retrieval from the source URLs was unavailable. Complete Danish and other authentic-language operative context remains unchecked. Both reviewers identify the central uncertainty, but their common conditional rating does not resolve it. The text does not establish whether 'small costs' refers to upfront expenditure, ultimate net expense, or expense relative to claim value. Article 6 provides compensation against the debtor, not necessarily immediate funding, complete reimbursement of every procedural charge, or successful collection. Conversely, substantial unreimbursed costs do not themselves prove a distinct Danish obligation. The transition from recital objective to an operative procedural requirement remains unsupported.
Unresolved: Do the complete authentic versions of Article 6, Article 10 and surrounding recitals support a distinct cost standard? Which procedural expenses are compensable, when, and with what effect on access? Can an otherwise effective, nondiscriminatory procedure breach an existing Directive obligation solely because creditor costs exceed 'small costs'? What remedy would follow without deriving a new obligation solely from a recital?

COMMISSION REGULATION (EU) No 432/2012
of 16 May 2012
establishing a list of permitted health claims made on foods, other than those referring to the reduction of disease risk and to children’s development and health
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
Permitted health claims
1. The list of health claims which may be made on foods, as referred to in Article 13(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, is set out in the Annex to this Regulation.
2. Health claims referred to in paragraph 1 may be made on foods in compliance with the conditions set out in the Annex.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
Entry into force and application
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .
It shall apply from 14 December 2012.

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.

Fat content and composition The energy derived from fat shall not exceed 30 % of total available energy content of the product. The linoleic acid (in the form of glycerides) shall not be less than 1 g. 3. Protein content and composition The protein contained in the food shall provide not less than 25 % and not more than 50 % of the total energy content of the product. The chemical index of protein shall be equal to that set by the World Health Organization in ‘Energy and protein requirements’. Report of a Joint WHO/FAO/UNU Meeting. If the chemical index is lower than 100 % of the reference protein, the minimum protein levels shall be correspondingly increased. In any case the chemical index of the protein shall at least be equal to 80 % of that of the reference protein. findings.english_quote: with instructions to the target population to consume with each lactose containing meal.
findings.title: French lactase instructions refer to each lactose-containing product
findings.explanation: French ties the required lactase advice to every lactose-containing product, potentially including consumption outside meals. English ties it to each lactose-containing meal. This could change the required consumption instructions, although neither wording clearly requires separate doses for products eaten together.

findings.english_quote: in amounts such that consumption of such foods or drinks does not lower plaque pH below 5.7 during and up to 30 minutes after consumption
findings.title: French sugar-replacer conditions omit the pH requirement during consumption
findings.explanation: English requires the 5.7 pH threshold during consumption and for the following 30 minutes. French expressly covers only the following 30 minutes, potentially allowing the dental claim for a product that causes a temporary drop during consumption.

variants.quote: dans une proportion telle que la consommation des denrées alimentaires ou boissons n’abaisse pas le pH de la plaque dentaire sous 5,7 dans les 30 minutes après la consommation de celles-ci.
variants.translation: in a proportion such that consumption of the foods or drinks does not lower dental plaque pH below 5.7 within the 30 minutes after their consumption.
variants.explanation: English requires the 5.7 pH threshold during consumption and for the following 30 minutes. French expressly covers only the following 30 minutes, potentially allowing the dental claim for a product that causes a temporary drop during consumption.

review.method: Two independent Sol analyses; Astra evidence review

findings.english_quote: Warning of choking to be given for people with swallowing difficulties or when ingesting with inadequate fluid intake — advice on taking with plenty of water to ensure substance reaches stomach.
findings.title: French choking warnings describe unsuitable fluid rather than insufficient intake
findings.explanation: For both glucomannan claims, guar gum, both HPMC claims and both pectin claims, English expressly requires warning about inadequate fluid intake. French instead describes an unsuitable fluid. Labels could therefore communicate different choking risks, despite both versions advising plenty of water.

variants.translation: Warning about the risk of choking in cases of swallowing difficulties or ingestion with an unsuitable fluid — consumption with plenty of water is advised to ensure that the substance reaches the stomach.
variants.explanation: For both glucomannan claims, guar gum, both HPMC claims and both pectin claims, English expressly requires warning about inadequate fluid intake. passages.label: Title
passages.text:
COMMISSION REGULATION (EU) 2019/343
of 28 February 2019
providing derogations from Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council on nutrition and health claims made on food for the use of certain generic descriptors
(Text with EEA relevance)

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: THE EUROPEAN COMMISSION,

passages.label: Citation 1
passages.text: Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union,

passages.label: Citation 2
passages.text: Having regard to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 December 2006 on nutrition and health claims made on foods ( 1 ) , and in particular Article 1(4) thereof,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | Pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, any claim made on food which states, suggests or implies that a relationship exists between a food category, a food or one of its constituents and health is to be considered as a health claim and therefore must comply with that Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 provides for a possible derogation from the rules applicable pursuant to Article 1(3) of that Regulation for generic descriptors (denominations) which have traditionally been used to indicate a particularity of a class of foods or beverages which could imply an effect on human health.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Applications for a term to be used as generic descriptor may be submitted by food business operators to the national competent authority of a recipient Member State.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Pursuant to Commission Regulation (EU) No 907/2013 ( 2 ) setting the rules for applications concerning the use of generic descriptors (denominations), a valid application should be transmitted to the Commission and to all Member States; Member States concerned by the application shall provide the Commission with their opinions thereon.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | Following receipt of a valid application and the opinions of Member States concerned the Commission may initiate the procedure of approval of the generic descriptor pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | On 13 April 2015, the Austrian competent authority provided the Commission with an application from the Austrian Food Industries' Association, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the terms ‘Hustenbonbon’ and ‘Hustenstopper’ to be used as generic descriptors in Austria.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | On 13 April 2015, the Austrian competent authority provided the Commission with an application from Drapal GmbH, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘Hustenzuckerl’ to be used as generic descriptor in Austria.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | On 19 May 2015, the German competent authority provided the Commission with an application from the Association of the German Confectionary Industry, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘Brust-Caramellen’ to be used as generic descriptors in Germany and in Austria.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | On 29 May 2015, the German competent authority provided the Commission with an application from SOLDAN Holding + Bonbonspezialitäten GmbH and from the Association of the German Confectionery Industry, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘Hustenmischung’ to be used as generic descriptor in Germany.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | On 8 June 2015, the German competent authority provided the Commission with an application from SOLDAN Holding + Bonbonspezialitäten GmbH, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘Hustenperle’ to be used as generic descriptor in Germany.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | On 18 June 2015, the German competent authority provided the Commission with two applications from SOLDAN Holding + Bonbonspezialitäten GmbH and the Association of the German Confectionery Industry, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the terms ‘Halsbonbon’ and ‘keelpastille’ to be used as generic descriptors in Germany (‘Halsbonbon’) and in the Netherlands (‘keelpastille’).

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | On 18 November 2015, the German competent authority provided the Commission with three applications from SOLDAN Holding + Bonbonspezialitäten GmbH, Josef Mack GmbH & Co. KG and the Association of the German Confectionery Industry, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the terms ‘Hustenbonbon’, ‘hoestbonbon’, ‘rebucados para a tosse’, and ‘cough drops’, to be used as generic descriptors in Germany and in Austria (‘Hustenbonbon’), in the Netherlands (‘hoestbonbon’), in Portugal (‘rebucados para a tosse’) and in the United Kingdom (‘cough drops’).

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | The Austrian and German competent authorities provided all other Member States with the applications. The competent authorities of Member States concerned provided the Commission with their opinions on the applications.

passages.label: Recital 14
passages.text: (14) | The terms ‘Hustenbonbon’, ‘Hustenstopper’, ‘Hustenzuckerl’, ‘Brust-Caramellen’, ‘Hustenmischung’, ‘Hustenperle’‘Halsbonbon’, ‘keelpastille’, ‘hoestbonbon’, ‘rebuçados para a tosse’, and ‘cough drops’ fall into the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, because they can imply a relationship between the foods bearing these terms and health.

passages.label: Recital 15
passages.text: (15) | However, evidence has been provided that these terms have been traditionally used in Germany and in Austria (‘Hustenbonbon’, ‘Brust-Caramellen’), in Germany (‘Halsbonbon’, ‘Hustenmischung’ and ‘Hustenperle’), in Austria (‘Hustenstopper’ and ‘Hustenzuckerl’), in the Netherlands (‘keelpastille’, and ‘hoestbonbon’), in Portugal (‘rebuçados para a tosse’) and in the United Kingdom (‘cough drops’) in the meaning of Article 1(4) of this Regulation, as generic descriptors to describe a class of sweets based on sugars as well as sugar-free and calorie-reduced variants based on sweeteners (polyols and/or intense sweeteners) containing extracts of herbs, fruit or other plant substances, such as menthol, honey or malt.

passages.label: Recital 16
passages.text: (16) | In particular, the terms ‘Hustenbonbon’, ‘Brust-Caramellen’, ‘Halsbonbon’, ‘Hustenmischung’, ‘Hustenperle’, ‘Hustenstopper’, ‘Hustenzuckerl’, ‘keelpastille’, ‘hoestbonbon’, ‘rebuçados para a tosse’ and ‘cough drops’ have neither been used in Germany, in Austria, in the Netherlands, in Portugal and in the United Kingdom respectively, with the aim to indicate a health effect of this class of food nor are understood by an average consumer as claiming a health effect of this class of food.

passages.label: Recital 17
passages.text: (17) | Derogation from Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 should therefore be granted for the use of the generic descriptors ‘Hustenbonbon’ and ‘Brust-Caramellen’ in Germany and in Austria, ‘Halsbonbon’, ‘Hustenmischung’ and ‘Hustenperle’ in Germany, ‘Hustenstopper’ and ‘Hustenzuckerl’ in Austria, ‘keelpastille’ and ‘hoestbonbon’ in the Netherlands, ‘rebuçados para a tosse’ in Portugal and ‘cough drops’ in the United Kingdom when used in the respective Member State on sweets based on sugars as well as sugar-free and calorie-reduced variants based on sweeteners (polyols and/or intense sweeteners) containing extracts of herbs, fruit or other plant substances, honey or malt.

passages.label: Recital 18
passages.text: (18) | On 12 January 2017, the Finnish competent authority provided the Commission with an application from the Finnish Food Industries' Association, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘kurkkupastilli/halspastill’ to be used as generic descriptor in Finland.

passages.label: Recital 19
passages.text: (19) | The Finnish competent authority provided all other Member States with the application; it also provided the Commission with its opinion on the application.

passages.label: Recital 20
passages.text: (20) | The term ‘kurkkupastilli/halspastill’ falls into the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, because it can imply a relationship between foods bearing this term and health. However, evidence has been provided that this term has been used traditionally in Finland, in the meaning of Article 1(4) of this Regulation, as generic descriptor to describe a class of sweets based on sugars as well as sugar-free and calorie-reduced variants based on sweeteners (polyols and/or intense sweeteners).

passages.label: Recital 21
passages.text: (21) | In particular, the term ‘kurkkupastilli/halspastill’ has neither been used in Finland with the aim to indicate a health effect of this class of food nor is understood by an average consumer as claiming a health effect of this class of food.

passages.label: Recital 22
passages.text: (22) | Derogation from Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 should therefore be granted for the use of the generic descriptor ‘kurkkupastilli/halspastill’ when used in Finland on hard sweets based on sugars as well as sugar-free and calorie-reduced variants based on sweeteners (polyols and/or intense sweeteners).

passages.label: Recital 23
passages.text: (23) | On 13 April 2015, the Austrian competent authority provided the Commission with an application from Drapal GmbH, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘Hustensirup’ to be used as generic descriptor in Austria.

passages.label: Recital 24
passages.text: (24) | The Austrian competent authority provided all other Member States with the application; it also provided the Commission with its opinion on the application.

passages.label: Recital 25
passages.text: (25) | The term ‘Hustensirup’ falls into the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, because it can imply a relationship between foods bearing this term and health. However, evidence has been provided that this term has been used traditionally in Austria, in the meaning of Article 1(4) of this Regulation, as generic descriptor to describe a class of confectionery products made of solutions of sugar, starch syrup, inverted sugar and/or honey with the addition of herbal ingredients, ‘Hustensirup’ referring to a class of products in the form of a syrup.

passages.label: Recital 26
passages.text: (26) | In particular, the term ‘Hustensirup’ has neither been used with the aim to indicate a health effect of this class of food nor is understood by an average consumer as claiming a health effect of this class of food in Austria.

passages.label: Recital 27
passages.text: (27) | Derogation from Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 should therefore be granted for the use of the generic descriptor ‘Hustensirup’ when used in Austria on confectionery products made of solutions of sugar, starch syrup, inverted sugar and/or honey with the addition of herbal ingredients in the form of syrup.

passages.label: Recital 28
passages.text: (28) | Definitions for sugars intended for human consumption have been laid down in point A of the Annex to Council Directive 2001/111/EC ( 3 ) . In order to ensure legal certainty, those definitions should also apply for the purpose of this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 29
passages.text: (29) | On 2 April 2015, the UK competent authority provided the Commission with an application from the British Soft Drinks Association, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘tonic’ (in English) used as part of the descriptive name of a beverage in the form of ‘tonic water’, ‘Indian tonic water’ or ‘quinine tonic water’ and substituted in the same descriptive names with ‘tonique’ (in French), ‘tónico’ or ‘tonica’ (in Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese), ‘τονωτικό’ or ‘tonotiko’ (in Greek), ‘tonik’ (in Croatian, Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian), ‘тоник’ (in Bulgarian), to be used as generic descriptor in all Member States except in Romania.

passages.label: Recital 30
passages.text: (30) | On 30 September 2015, the Romanian competent authority provided the Commission with an application from the Romanian Soft Drinks Association, submitted pursuant Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘tonic’ (in English) used as part of the descriptive name of a beverage in the form of ‘tonic water’, ‘Indian tonic water’ or ‘quinine tonic water’ and substituted in the same descriptive names with ‘tónico’, ‘tonică’ or ‘tonica’ (in Romanian), to be used as generic descriptor in Romania.

passages.label: Recital 31
passages.text: (31) | The UK competent authority and the Romanian competent authority provided all other Member States with the applications; Member States have provided the Commission with their opinions on these applications.

passages.label: Recital 32
passages.text: (32) | The Greek competent authority considers that the term ‘τονωτικό’ and ‘tonotiko’ (‘τονωτικό’ with Latin characters) are considered as health claims within the meaning of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006. The Greek competent authority further considers that for non-alcoholic beverages containing quinine, the term ‘tonic’ used as part of the customary name of the food is traditionally widely used in Greece.

passages.label: Recital 33
passages.text: (33) | The German competent authority and the Austrian competent authority consider that the term ‘tonic’ used as part of ‘tonic water’, ‘Indian tonic water’ or ‘quinine tonic water’ is part of a customary name of the beverage and as such out of the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.

passages.label: Recital 34
passages.text: (34) | The French competent authority considers that the term ‘tonique’ is not used to describe a non-alcoholic carbonated beverage containing the bittering agent quinine.

passages.label: Recital 35
passages.text: (35) | Certain competent authorities consider that when the term ‘tonic’ (in English) is substituted by ‘tonik’ in Croatian, Hungarian, Polish and Slovenian, it is not considered as a health claim in those respective Member States within the meaning of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006; therefore in their views these terms are out of the scope of the Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 36
passages.text: (36) | The term ‘tonic’ and the equivalent linguistic forms, namely, ‘tonik’, ‘tónico’, ‘tónica’ and ‘tonică’, when they are used as part of the descriptive name of a beverage, fall into the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, because they can imply a relationship between a food bearing this term and health. However, evidence has been provided that these terms have been used traditionally, in the meaning of Article 1(4) of this Regulation, as generic descriptors to describe a class of beverages, namely, a non-alcoholic carbonated beverage containing the bittering agent quinine in the form of the flavourings FL 14.011, FL 14.152 or FL 14.155 as referred to in the Union list of flavourings laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 4 ) on flavourings and certain food ingredients with flavouring properties for use in and on foods.

passages.label: Recital 37
passages.text: (37) | In particular, the terms ‘tonic’ and the equivalent linguistic forms, namely, ‘tonik’, ‘tónico’, ‘tónica’ and ‘tonică’, when they are used as part of the descriptive name of a beverage, have neither been used with the aim to indicate a health effect of this class of beverages nor are understood by an average consumer as claiming a health effect of this class of beverages.

passages.label: Recital 38
passages.text: (38) | Derogation from Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 should therefore be granted for the use of the generic descriptor ‘tonic’ (in English), when used as part of the descriptive name of a non-alcoholic carbonated beverage containing the bittering agent quinine in the form of the flavourings FL 14.011, FL 14.152 or FL 14.155 as referred to in the Union list of flavourings as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008. The term ‘tonic’ (in English) may be substituted in the descriptive name by ‘тоник’ (in Bulgarian), ‘tonik’ (in Czech and in Slovak), ‘tónica’ (in Spanish and in Portuguese) ‘tonica’ (in Italian), or ‘tonică’ (in Romanian).

passages.label: Recital 39
passages.text: (39) | On 23 April 2015, the Italian competent authority provided the Commission with an application from Monviso SpA, submitted pursuant to Article 1(4) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, for the term ‘biscotto salute’ to be used as generic descriptor in Italy and in Malta.

passages.label: Recital 40
passages.text: (40) | The Italian competent authority provided all other Member States with the application; the Member States concerned have provided the Commission with their opinions on the application.

passages.label: Recital 41
passages.text: (41) | The term ‘biscotto salute’ falls into the scope of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, because it can imply a relationship between a food bearing this term and health. However, evidence has been provided that this term has been used traditionally in Italy, in the meaning of Article 1(4) of this Regulation, as a generic descriptor to describe a class of rusk-type bakery products.

passages.label: Recital 42
passages.text: (42) | In particular, the term ‘biscotto salute’ has neither been used with the aim to indicate a health effect of this class of foods nor is understood by an average consumer as claiming the health effect of this class of food in Italy.

passages.label: Recital 43
passages.text: (43) | Malta indicated that the term ‘biscotto salute’ was not used to describe rusk-type bakery products on the Maltese market.

passages.label: Recital 44
passages.text: (44) | Derogation from Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 should therefore be granted for the use of the generic descriptor ‘biscotto salute’ when used in Italy on rusk-type bakery products.

passages.label: Recital 45
passages.text: (45) | The measures provided for in this Regulation are in accordance with the opinion of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: HAS ADOPTED THIS REGULATION:

passages.label: Article 1
passages.text:
Article 1
The generic descriptors listed in the Annex to this Regulation are exempted from the application of Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006 under the conditions laid down in that Annex.

passages.label: Article 2
passages.text:
Article 2
For the purposes of this Regulation, the definitions for sugars intended for human consumption laid down in point A of the Annex to Council Directive 2001/111/EC shall apply.

passages.label: Article 3
passages.text:
Article 3
This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .

passages.label: Document context
passages.text:
This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.
Done at Brussels, 28 February 2019.
For the Commission
The President
Jean-Claude JUNCKER

( 4 ) Regulation (EC) No 1334/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 December 2008 on flavourings and certain food ingredients with flavouring properties for use in and on foods and amending Council Regulation (EEC) No 1601/91, Regulations (EC) No 2232/96 and (EC) No 110/2008 and Directive 2000/13/EC ( OJ L 354, 31.12.2008, p. 34 ).

impact_families.title: Provisional conditional narrowing of descriptor-exemption eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–7; Article 2 governs qualifying sugars.
impact_families.effect: A hard sweet based on qualifying sugars is marketed in Germany as Hustenbonbon. Its only potentially qualifying additional ingredient is ground, unextracted malt; it contains no honey or botanical extract, including any extract produced during manufacture. If the ingredient list excludes malt as an independent alternative, the product loses eligibility for this descriptor exemption.
impact_families.rationale:
The Danish wording lists extracts of botanical materials and honey without a separate malt alternative. Malt's botanical origin does not itself make unextracted malt an extract. Article 1 makes the Annex conditions operative, so the isolated ingredient difference can change exemption eligibility. Sugar-based status satisfies the base-product condition but does not independently dispense with the ingredient condition. Finland's ingredient-independent row concerns different descriptors and territory and cannot preserve this German Hustenbonbon exemption. This is a substantive eligibility change under a specific rule, supporting moderate rather than limited impact; the packet establishes neither broad market reach nor serious downstream consequences supporting high.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading understands the Danish omission in light of equally authoritative versions expressly including malt, such as English, German and French. Malt extract can also satisfy the Danish botanical-extract limb without harmonization. Those readings defeat a malt-extract example, but they do not defeat the stipulated unextracted-malt example if the restrictive ingredient reading prevails.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Actual manufacture could introduce a qualifying extract and eliminate the difference. Loss of this exemption does not establish unlawful labelling or a sanction: the substantive requirements of the referenced Regulation 1924/2006 are outside the supplied evidence.
Unresolved: No independent outcome dependency remains for the specified unextracted-malt scenario. Article 2 compliance is held constant rather than inferred from an external definition. comparator_omissions is empty and context_limited is false. Omitted provisions limit conclusions about downstream labelling obligations, but do not prevent the conditional Annex-eligibility comparison.

impact_families.title: Provisional conditional expansion of descriptor-exemption eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row 11: Biscotto salute, Italy.
impact_families.effect: A crisp baked biscuit outside the rusk-type category is marketed in Italy using Biscotto salute. If the Maltese food category independently encompasses crisp bakery products generally, the product satisfies the category condition and gains eligibility for the listed descriptor exemption.
impact_families.rationale:
The supplied Maltese wording describes a crisp type, while the English wording specifies a rusk type. Article 1 makes the listed food category a condition of the exemption. Assuming the broader category reading prevails, the complete row supplies no additional rusk requirement that defeats the scenario. Article 2's sugar definitions provide no independent restriction on this bakery category. Although confined to one descriptor and territory, the difference changes substantive eligibility for an identifiable product group, supporting moderate impact rather than an ancillary, limited effect.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats crispness as describing the same rusk-like category identified by the named Italian descriptor and by the Italian, French and German formulations. All versions have equal authority. That context may defeat the broad interpretation, but it is not a separate supplied eligibility condition that remains unsatisfied once the broad category reading is assumed to prevail.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The culinary scope of qarmeċ and the rusk-type classification of any actual product remain interpretive or factual questions. The assessment establishes no actual affected product, permission for additional claims, or general right to market a product under this name.
Unresolved: No independent dependency preventing the conditional exemption change is established in the supplied rules. comparator_omissions is empty and context_limited is false. Omitted recitals could inform interpretation of the category, but the packet identifies no omitted rule independently limiting eligibility to rusks after the broader interpretation is assumed. External marketing and claims consequences remain outside the assessment.

impact_families.title: Provisional conditional expansion of descriptor-exemption eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–7; Article 2 governs qualifying sugars.
impact_families.effect: A soft sweet based on qualifying sugars is marketed in Austria as Hustenzuckerl. It contains chopped, unextracted herbs but no botanical extracts, honey or malt. If the Slovak phrase makes herbs an independent ingredient alternative, the product becomes eligible for the descriptor exemption despite failing an extraction requirement.
impact_families.rationale:
The supplied Slovak text places alebo, meaning or, between extracts and herbs. On the disputed reading, that creates an independent herb alternative. The specified product therefore meets the broader ingredient condition and fails the extract-based condition. The sugar-based limb does not itself waive the ingredient requirement, and the ingredient-independent Finnish row does not cover Hustenzuckerl in Austria. The change concerns substantive exemption eligibility for an identifiable group under one rule, supporting moderate impact. No assessment of extracts from unspecified sources is needed to establish this narrower, concrete mechanism.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats the Slovak sequence as an awkward enumeration of the botanical sources of extracts. Czech, French and English expressly connect extraction to the botanical list, supporting that contextual reading without giving any version superior authority. If that interpretation prevails, the proposed expansion disappears; if the independent-herb reading prevails, the scenario survives the other supplied conditions.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The multilingual interpretation remains open. Actual processing must leave the herbs unextracted and introduce no other qualifying ingredient. Neither actual product prevalence nor downstream illegality is established.
Unresolved: No independent outcome dependency remains for the specified unextracted-herb scenario with qualifying sugar held constant. The separate possibility of unrestricted extract sources remains unassessed. comparator_omissions is empty and context_limited is false. The omitted substantive sugar definitions and external claims rules do not defeat this ingredient-only comparison, but cannot support further legal consequences.

impact_families.title: Dutch wording includes soft sweets
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation (EU) 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row for Kurkkupastilli/Halspastill in Finland
impact_families.effect: Consider an otherwise qualifying ordinary sugar-based soft sweet using Kurkkupastilli/Halspastill in Finland. The Dutch wording includes soft sweets; if that broader reading prevailed, the product could qualify for this Article 1 exemption. Under the hard-sweets reading it would not qualify through this Annex row.
impact_families.rationale: The Dutch Annex cell expressly includes soft sweets, while the English cell specifies hard sweets. Article 1 makes the Annex conditions determine eligibility for an exemption from Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006. A change in that eligibility is a legal outcome for an identifiable class, supporting Moderate conditional impact. This does not claim that any real product violates the underlying rule. Recital 22 and many other authentic versions point toward a hard-sweets reading; that bears on which interpretation ultimately prevails, not on the size of the outcome if the broader reading does prevail.
impact_families.uncertainty: All authentic versions have equal authority. Recital 22 and the wider multilingual context strongly support harmonizing the category as hard sweets, so the broader reading may not prevail. Specific duties under Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, any separate permission, and actual market use were not established in this trial. The hypothetical assumes the product meets other Annex conditions and the incorporated sugar definition; this rating concerns this Regulation’s exemption eligibility only.

impact_families.title: Calorie-condition narrowing unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–8; Article 2 incorporates sugar definitions, not an express calorie threshold.
impact_families.effect: A polyol-based Hustenperle in Germany contains herbal extract and has reduced but still high calories. Test both a sugar-free formulation and one containing incidental sugar that is not sugar-based.
impact_families.rationale:
Mazkaloriju supports an ordinary low-calorie reading distinct from relative calorie reduction. Nevertheless, the sugar-free example changes outcome only under cumulative variant conditions. Under separate classes it remains exempt. The incidental-sugar example requires separate calorie-reduced eligibility and exclusion from the sugar-based limb. A narrower calorie meaning alone therefore does not establish a changed outcome for either formulation. The moderate field indicates prospective scale only.
Counterreading: Mazkaloriju could denote relatively reduced-calorie variants in context. Alternatively, sugar-free status could independently preserve eligibility even if mazkaloriju retains an absolute low-calorie meaning.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The packet supplies no numerical calorie standard. No comparator omissions are recorded. Lithuanian separates sugar-free sweets from reduced-calorie sweets, while Bulgarian uses an express alternative; these authentic texts strengthen the independent-route counterreading without resolving the common interpretation by a vote.
Unresolved: Does the variant phrase impose cumulative conditions or identify separate classes? Which concrete formulation satisfies the initial route without another route preserving eligibility, and what calorie standard applies?

impact_families.title: Calorie-condition narrowing unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–8; Article 2 incorporates sugar definitions but supplies no calorie standard.
impact_families.effect: Test two polyol-based Keelpastille formulations in the Netherlands, both containing herbal extract and having reduced but still high calories: one is sugar-free; the other contains incidental sugar and is stipulated not to be sugar-based.
impact_families.rationale:
The sugar-free formulation loses eligibility only if sugar-free and calorie-qualified are cumulative requirements. If the phrase lists separate variant classes, it remains eligible. The incidental-sugar formulation avoids that rescue only if calorie-reduced variants are independently eligible in the first place and the sugar-based limb does not cover it. Thus assuming caloriearme imposes a narrower calorie condition still leaves the changed outcome dependent on another unresolved issue. Moderate describes prospective scale, not an assigned tier.
Counterreading: Caloriearme may mean relatively lower-calorie variants in context. Even retaining its narrower meaning, independently sufficient sugar-free eligibility may harmonize the practical outcome for Review A's example.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No numerical threshold or incorporation of nutrition-claim thresholds is established. No comparator omissions are recorded. The separate-class wording in Lithuanian and alternatives in Hungarian materially support an independent sugar-free route. Dutch row 8 also includes soft sweets, but that separate discrepancy does not resolve the selected Keelpastille scenario.
Unresolved: Are the variant conditions cumulative or alternative, and can an identified formulation escape both the sugar-free and sugar-based routes while qualifying under the calorie-reduced route? What calorie standard governs?

impact_families.title: Provisional expansion to non-herbal plant additions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row 9, Hustensirup in Austria; Article 2 incorporates sugar definitions.
impact_families.effect: A confectionery syrup marketed as Hustensirup in Austria uses a honey-and-water base with added pear purée, remains in syrup form, and contains no herbal ingredients.
impact_families.rationale:
Pear purée meets the plant-origin addition condition but fails a condition restricted to herbal ingredients. The expressly permitted honey base satisfies the separate base requirement without depending on starch-syrup classification. The other base alternatives do not waive the addition requirement. This supports a concrete conditional change in descriptor-exemption eligibility under one specific rule.
Counterreading: Read augucilmes in this context as confined to herbal additions, consistent with Polish ziołowych. Conversely, Swedish växtbaserade supports a broad botanical reading, and English herbal might receive that broader contextual meaning. Each is an equal-authority harmonizing possibility.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The ultimate botanical-versus-herbal interpretation remains open. No comparator omissions are recorded. Missing sugar definitions do not prevent the selected honey-base scenario.
Unresolved: No additional unresolved dependency defeats the stated outcome once the disputed plant-origin boundary is assumed.

impact_families.title: Estonian wording includes soft sweets
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation (EU) 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row for Kurkkupastilli/Halspastill in Finland
impact_families.effect: Consider an otherwise qualifying ordinary sugar-based soft sweet using Kurkkupastilli/Halspastill in Finland. The Estonian wording includes soft sweets; if that broader reading prevailed, the product could qualify for this Article 1 exemption. Under the hard-sweets reading it would not qualify through this Annex row.

Article 1 makes the Annex conditions determine eligibility for an exemption from Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006. A change in that eligibility is a legal outcome for an identifiable class, supporting Moderate conditional impact. This does not claim that any real product violates the underlying rule. Recital 22 and many other authentic versions point toward a hard-sweets reading; that bears on which interpretation ultimately prevails, not on the size of the outcome if the broader reading does prevail.
impact_families.uncertainty: All authentic versions have equal authority. Recital 22 and the wider multilingual context strongly support harmonizing the category as hard sweets, so the broader reading may not prevail. Specific duties under Article 1(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, any separate permission, and actual market use were not established in this trial. The hypothetical assumes the product meets other Annex conditions and the incorporated sugar definition; this rating concerns this Regulation’s exemption eligibility only.

impact_families.title: Provisional conditional narrowing of descriptor-exemption eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–7; Article 2 governs qualifying sugars.
impact_families.effect: A hard sweet based on qualifying sugars is marketed in the Netherlands as Hoestbonbon. It contains ground, unextracted malt but no malt extract, other botanical extract or honey, including any qualifying extract generated during manufacture. If malt must be present as malt extract, the product loses eligibility for this descriptor exemption.
impact_families.rationale:
The Estonian text expressly identifies linnaseekstrakti, malt extract, where the English and several other supplied versions identify malt. Unextracted malt does not satisfy an extraction requirement merely because it comes from plants. The general botanical-extract limb therefore does not rescue the specified scenario; neither does honey, which is absent. The parenthetical menthol example remains within the extract wording and supplies no independent whole-malt alternative. Sugar-based status does not waive the ingredient condition, and Finland's ingredient-independent row cannot supply an exemption for Hoestbonbon in the Netherlands. A conditional change in substantive exemption eligibility supports moderate impact.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading understands the Estonian malt-extract expression within the broader malt category expressly supplied by equally authoritative English, German, Dutch and Finnish versions. Separately, malt extract may already qualify under the general plant-extract limb. That overlap eliminates a changed outcome for extracted-malt products but does not cover whole, unextracted malt if the restrictive reading prevails.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The actual product and manufacturing process must establish the absence of qualifying extracts. Ultimate multilingual interpretation remains open. The packet supports an eligibility comparison, not an automatic prohibition, penalty or demonstrated enforcement consequence.
Unresolved: No independent outcome dependency remains for the stipulated unextracted-malt scenario, with qualifying sugar held constant. comparator_omissions is empty and context_limited is false. Omitted external definitions and claims rules limit downstream conclusions but do not prevent this isolated ingredient comparison.

impact_families.title: Sweetener-category expansion unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–8; Article 2 incorporates sugar definitions whose text is outside the packet.
impact_families.effect: A hard Hustenbonbon in Germany contains herbal extract and meets the applicable variant conditions, using a sweetener outside both the polyol and intense-sweetener classes. Eligibility would change only if it also falls outside the ordinary sugar-based route.
impact_families.rationale:
The German parenthesis literally extends beyond intense sweeteners. However, accepting that broader meaning does not establish a concrete additional qualifying formulation. The packet identifies no ingredient demonstrably outside the two named classes that satisfies the variant conditions without independently qualifying through the sugar-based limb. The exemption mechanism is clear, but the boundary group remains unsubstantiated. The moderate conditional-impact field describes the prospective scale only; no impact tier is assigned.
Counterreading: Both parentheses could illustrate the intended sweetener classes, or 'andere Süßungsmittel' could mean other sweeteners within the intense-sweetener class in context. The French 'édulcorants intenses' supports that harmonization without having superior authority.
impact_families.uncertainty:
Whether either parenthesis is exhaustive is an interpretive uncertainty. Separately, ingredient classification and alternative eligibility remain unresolved. No comparator omissions are recorded, but the incorporated sugar definitions are not supplied.
Unresolved: Which identifiable sweetener and formulation would meet the remaining conditions while falling outside both specified classes and the sugar-based alternative?

impact_families.title: Unresolved conditional change in descriptor-exemption eligibility
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–8; Article 2 incorporates definitions of sugars from Directive 2001/111/EC, whose substantive definitions are not supplied.
impact_families.effect: A polyol-based hard sweet marketed in Finland as Halspastill contains some sugar and has reduced calories relative to an ordinary counterpart, while allegedly falling outside an absolute low-calorie category. Exclusion under the Bulgarian calorie wording would change exemption eligibility only if neither the sugar-free alternative nor the ordinary sugar-based sweets limb covers it.
impact_families.rationale:
The Bulgarian text expresses low caloric content, whereas the English text expresses reduction. These concepts can differ, but that linguistic distinction alone does not establish a surviving eligibility change. Review A stipulates that its sugar-containing product is neither sugar-free nor sugar-based; the packet does not establish the legal boundary needed to support the latter classification. It also supplies no operative calorie criteria. Article 2 identifies an incorporated source but does not provide its definitions. Accordingly, even assuming an absolute-low-calorie interpretation prevails, the proposed product's exclusion remains unresolved. Moderate describes the potential effect if those dependencies are resolved; no impact tier is assigned.
Counterreading: The strongest harmonizing reading treats low-calorie and calorie-reduced formulations as descriptions of the same intended sweetener-based variants. Italian and Dutch supply low-calorie formulations, while French and other supplied versions express reduction; Hungarian expressly separates sugar-free and reduced-energy alternatives. These equally authoritative texts support contextual interpretation rather than treating English as controlling. Independently, the sugar-free or sugar-based limb could preserve eligibility.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No numerical calorie threshold or external nutrition-claim criterion is imported. The coordination of sugar-free and calorie-reduced variants also requires contextual interpretation: the authentic versions include both conjunctive and alternative formulations. No actual affected product or market reach is established.
Unresolved: What criteria establish that a sugar-containing, sweetener-based variant falls outside the sugar-based limb? What criteria separate low caloric content from calorie reduction here, and are the variant categories independent alternatives? comparator_omissions is empty and context_limited is false, but the omitted incorporated definitions and unresolved category boundaries still prevent a concrete conditional outcome.

impact_families.title: Provisional expansion to non-extracted unmalted barley
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–7; Article 2 governs the separate sugar-base condition.
impact_families.effect: A hard Hustenbonbon marketed in Germany has an otherwise qualifying sucrose base and contains milled unmalted barley, but no plant extracts, honey or malt.
impact_families.rationale:
If xgħir includes unmalted barley, the scenario satisfies the ingredient condition and gains the Article 1 derogation. Milled grain avoids the shared plant-extract alternative. The sugar-based limb supplies the base requirement; it does not dispense with the additional ingredient condition. This is an identifiable formulation group under a specific exemption, supporting moderate impact without evidence of wider consequences.
Counterreading: Read xgħir contextually as malted barley or malt, consistent with Maltese food terminology in this setting and comparator wording such as Italian malto. Alternatively, a barley extract already qualifies through the botanical-extract limb and would show no changed outcome. The scenario therefore uses unmalted meal.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The ultimate contextual meaning of xgħir remains open. No comparator omissions are recorded. The supplied concordance is not uniform: the Danish ingredient list omits malt, but still supplies no independent route for the stipulated non-extracted barley formulation.
Unresolved: No additional packet dependency defeats the specified conditional ingredient-boundary outcome. It establishes exemption eligibility only, not general permission to market the product.

impact_families.title: Calorie-condition narrowing unresolved
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex rows 2–8; Article 2 incorporates sugar definitions without establishing a calorie threshold.
impact_families.effect: A polyol-based Hustenzuckerl in Austria contains herbal extract and has reduced but still high calories. Compare a sugar-free formulation with one containing incidental sugar and falling outside the sugar-based category.
impact_families.rationale:
A basso contenuto calorico can impose a narrower condition than relative calorie reduction. However, a sugar-free formulation loses the exemption only if both variant conditions are cumulative. If they identify independent classes, it remains eligible. The incidental-sugar formulation avoids that rescue only if the calorie-reduced class is independent and the ordinary sugar-based route is unavailable. The conditional outcome therefore remains unresolved even accepting the narrower calorie meaning. Moderate indicates prospective scale, not an assigned tier.
Counterreading: The Italian expression may refer contextually to reduced-calorie variants. Alternatively, the coordinated phrase may list sugar-free and low-calorie classes independently, preserving exemption eligibility for sugar-free products despite a narrower calorie condition.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The packet establishes no numerical calorie cutoff or express incorporation of nutrition-claim thresholds. No comparator omissions are recorded. Lithuanian's separately described sweets and Hungarian's express alternative materially support separate categories; they cannot simply be displaced by the Italian conjunction.
Unresolved: Are the conditions cumulative or alternative? Can an identified formulation establish initial calorie-reduced eligibility while excluding both other routes, and what standard governs calorie qualification?

impact_families.title: Provisional expansion to non-herbal plant additions
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row 9, Hustensirup in Austria; Article 2 concerns sugar definitions.
impact_families.effect: A confectionery product marketed as Hustensirup in Austria remains in syrup form, uses a honey-and-water base, and contains added apple purée but no herbal ingredients.
impact_families.rationale:
Under a plant-based addition condition, apple purée qualifies; under a condition restricted to herbal additions, the stipulated formulation fails. Honey is an expressly listed base, avoiding the disputed starch-syrup classification. The base alternatives do not displace the separate added-ingredient requirement, and the sweets rows do not provide another route for this syrup descriptor. The resulting change concerns eligibility for the Article 1 derogation.
Counterreading: Swedish växtbaserade could be restricted contextually to herbal ingredients, supported by Finnish yrttiainesosia. Conversely, German pflanzlichen Bestandteilen supports broader plant additions. English herbal could itself receive a broad contextual meaning. These equal-authority readings might harmonize the texts; they concern whether the disputed boundary ultimately survives.
impact_families.uncertainty:
The eventual multilingual meaning of herbal and plant-based remains open. No comparator omissions are recorded. The omitted sugar definitions do not determine the selected honey-base route.
Unresolved: No additional unresolved condition defeats the stated scenario once the broader plant-versus-herbal boundary is assumed.

impact_families.title: Syrup-base substitution has unresolved alternative coverage
impact_families.legal_anchor: Regulation 2019/343, Article 1 and Annex row 9; Article 2 expressly incorporates Directive 2001/111/EC, Annex A, whose definitions are not supplied.
impact_families.effect: An Austrian Hustensirup confectionery syrup contains herbal ingredients and uses liquid starch-derived glucose syrup as its sole sweetening base, without crystalline glucose, separately added sucrose, invert sugar or honey.
impact_families.rationale:
Kristalglucose does not express the same ingredient description as starch syrup. Yet absence of crystalline glucose cannot establish exclusion if the formulation already qualifies through 'oplossingen van suiker'. Article 2 makes the omitted definitions directly relevant to that overlap. Conversely, dissolved crystalline glucose cannot be assumed to create an expansion: it too may already fall within sugar solutions or the starch-syrup category. Neither direction yields a concrete changed outcome on this packet. Moderate represents prospective scale only.
Counterreading: Read kristalglucose contextually as referring to the glucose-syrup base expressed in Italian sciroppo di glucosio, or retain its literal meaning while recognizing overlapping coverage through the separate sugar-solutions limb.
impact_families.uncertainty:
No comparator omissions are recorded, but the incorporated definitions are a decisive omitted dependency. The packet establishes their incorporation, not their contents or their application to a particular syrup.
Unresolved: Does the selected starch-derived syrup qualify through the incorporated sugar definitions and the sugar-solutions limb? Can any identified formulation establish either exclusion or expansion after that overlap is checked?

passages.label: Citation 4
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the European Economic and Social Committee ( 1 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 5
passages.text: Having regard to the opinion of the Committee of the Regions ( 2 ) ,

passages.label: Citation 6
passages.text: Acting in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure ( 3 ) ,

passages.label: Document context
passages.text: Whereas:

passages.label: Recital 1
passages.text: (1) | Information society services and especially intermediary services have become an important part of the Union’s economy and the daily life of Union citizens. Twenty years after the adoption of the existing legal framework applicable to such services laid down in Directive 2000/31/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 4 ) , new and innovative business models and services, such as online social networks and online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders, have allowed business users and consumers to impart and access information and engage in transactions in novel ways. A majority of Union citizens now uses those services on a daily basis. However, the digital transformation and increased use of those services has also resulted in new risks and challenges for individual recipients of the relevant service, companies and society as a whole.

passages.label: Recital 2
passages.text: (2) | Member States are increasingly introducing, or are considering introducing, national laws on the matters covered by this Regulation, imposing, in particular, diligence requirements for providers of intermediary services as regards the way they should tackle illegal content, online disinformation or other societal risks. Those diverging national laws negatively affect the internal market, which, pursuant to Article 26 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), comprises an area without internal frontiers in which the free movement of goods and services and freedom of establishment are ensured, taking into account the inherently cross-border nature of the internet, which is generally used to provide those services. The conditions for the provision of intermediary services across the internal market should be harmonised, so as to provide businesses with access to new markets and opportunities to exploit the benefits of the internal market, while allowing consumers and other recipients of the services to have increased choice. Business users, consumers and other users are considered to be ‘recipients of the service’ for the purpose of this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 3
passages.text: (3) | Responsible and diligent behaviour by providers of intermediary services is essential for a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment and for allowing Union citizens and other persons to exercise their fundamental rights guaranteed in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (the ‘Charter’), in particular the freedom of expression and of information, the freedom to conduct a business, the right to non-discrimination and the attainment of a high level of consumer protection.

passages.label: Recital 4
passages.text: (4) | Therefore, in order to safeguard and improve the functioning of the internal market, a targeted set of uniform, effective and proportionate mandatory rules should be established at Union level. This Regulation provides the conditions for innovative digital services to emerge and to scale up in the internal market. The approximation of national regulatory measures at Union level concerning the requirements for providers of intermediary services is necessary to avoid and put an end to fragmentation of the internal market and to ensure legal certainty, thus reducing uncertainty for developers and fostering interoperability. By using requirements that are technology neutral, innovation should not be hampered but instead be stimulated.

passages.label: Recital 5
passages.text: (5) | This Regulation should apply to providers of certain information society services as defined in Directive (EU) 2015/1535 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 5 ) , that is, any service normally provided for remuneration, at a distance, by electronic means and at the individual request of a recipient. Specifically, this Regulation should apply to providers of intermediary services, and in particular intermediary services consisting of services known as ‘mere conduit’, ‘caching’ and ‘hosting’ services, given that the exponential growth of the use made of those services, mainly for legitimate and socially beneficial purposes of all kinds, has also increased their role in the intermediation and spread of unlawful or otherwise harmful information and activities.

passages.label: Recital 6
passages.text: (6) | In practice, certain providers of intermediary services intermediate in relation to services that may or may not be provided by electronic means, such as remote information technology services, transport, accommodation or delivery services. This Regulation should apply only to intermediary services and not affect requirements set out in Union or national law relating to products or services intermediated through intermediary services, including in situations where the intermediary service constitutes an integral part of another service which is not an intermediary service as recognised in the case-law of the Court of Justice of the European Union.

passages.label: Recital 7
passages.text: (7) | In order to ensure the effectiveness of the rules laid down in this Regulation and a level playing field within the internal market, those rules should apply to providers of intermediary services irrespective of their place of establishment or their location, in so far as they offer services in the Union, as evidenced by a substantial connection to the Union.

passages.label: Recital 8
passages.text: (8) | Such a substantial connection to the Union should be considered to exist where the service provider has an establishment in the Union or, in the absence of such an establishment, where the number of recipients of the service in one or more Member States is significant in relation to the population thereof, or on the basis of the targeting of activities towards one or more Member States. The targeting of activities towards one or more Member States can be determined on the basis of all relevant circumstances, including factors such as the use of a language or a currency generally used in that Member State, or the possibility of ordering products or services, or the use of a relevant top-level domain. The targeting of activities towards a Member State could also be derived from the availability of an application in the relevant national application store, from the provision of local advertising or advertising in a language used in that Member State, or from the handling of customer relations such as by providing customer service in a language generally used in that Member State. A substantial connection should also be assumed where a service provider directs its activities to one or more Member States within the meaning of Article 17(1), point (c), of Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 6 ) . In contrast, mere technical accessibility of a website from the Union cannot, on that ground alone, be considered as establishing a substantial connection to the Union.

passages.label: Recital 9
passages.text: (9) | This Regulation fully harmonises the rules applicable to intermediary services in the internal market with the objective of ensuring a safe, predictable and trusted online environment, addressing the dissemination of illegal content online and the societal risks that the dissemination of disinformation or other content may generate, and within which fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter are effectively protected and innovation is facilitated. Accordingly, Member States should not adopt or maintain additional national requirements relating to the matters falling within the scope of this Regulation, unless explicitly provided for in this Regulation, since this would affect the direct and uniform application of the fully harmonised rules applicable to providers of intermediary services in accordance with the objectives of this Regulation. This should not preclude the possibility of applying other national legislation applicable to providers of intermediary services, in compliance with Union law, including Directive 2000/31/EC, in particular its Article 3, where the provisions of national law pursue other legitimate public interest objectives than those pursued by this Regulation.

passages.label: Recital 10
passages.text: (10) | This Regulation should be without prejudice to other acts of Union law regulating the provision of information society services in general, regulating other aspects of the provision of intermediary services in the internal market or specifying and complementing the harmonised rules set out in this Regulation, such as Directive 2010/13/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 7 ) including the provisions thereof regarding video-sharing platforms, Regulations (EU) 2019/1148 ( 8 ) , (EU) 2019/1150 ( 9 ) , (EU) 2021/784 ( 10 ) and (EU) 2021/1232 ( 11 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council and Directive 2002/58/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 12 ) , and provisions of Union law set out in a Regulation on European Production and Preservation Orders for electronic evidence in criminal matters and in a Directive laying down harmonised rules on the appointment of legal representatives for the purpose of gathering evidence in criminal proceedings. Similarly, for reasons of clarity, this Regulation should be without prejudice to Union law on consumer protection, in particular Regulations (EU) 2017/2394 ( 13 ) and (EU) 2019/1020 ( 14 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council, Directives 2001/95/EC ( 15 ) , 2005/29/EC ( 16 ) , 2011/83/EU ( 17 ) and 2013/11/EU ( 18 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council, and Council Directive 93/13/EEC ( 19 ) , and on the protection of personal data, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council ( 20 ) . This Regulation should also be without prejudice to Union rules on private international law, in particular rules regarding jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters, as Regulation (EU) No 1215/2012, and rules on the law applicable to contractual and non-contractual obligations. The protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data is governed solely by the rules of Union law on that subject, in particular Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Directive 2002/58/EC. This Regulation should also be without prejudice to Union law on working conditions and Union law in the field of judicial cooperation in civil and criminal matters. However, to the extent that those Union legal acts pursue the same objectives as those laid down in this Regulation, the rules of this Regulation should apply in respect of issues that are not addressed or not fully addressed by those other legal acts as well as issues on which those other legal acts leave Member States the possibility of adopting certain measures at national level.

passages.label: Recital 11
passages.text: (11) | It should be clarified that this Regulation is without prejudice to Union law on copyright and related rights, including Directives 2001/29/EC ( 21 ) , 2004/48/EC ( 22 ) and (EU) 2019/790 ( 23 ) of the European Parliament and of the Council, which establish specific rules and procedures that should remain unaffected.

passages.label: Recital 12
passages.text: (12) | In order to achieve the objective of ensuring a safe, predictable and trustworthy online environment, for the purpose of this Regulation the concept of ‘illegal content’ should broadly reflect the existing rules in the offline environment. In particular, the concept of ‘illegal content’ should be defined broadly to cover information relating to illegal content, products, services and activities. In particular, that concept should be understood to refer to information, irrespective of its form, that under the applicable law is either itself illegal, such as illegal hate speech or terrorist content and unlawful discriminatory content, or that the applicable rules render illegal in view of the fact that it relates to illegal activities. Illustrative examples include the sharing of images depicting child sexual abuse, the unlawful non-consensual sharing of private images, online stalking, the sale of non-compliant or counterfeit products, the sale of products or the provision of services in infringement of consumer protection law, the non-authorised use of copyright protected material, the illegal offer of accommodation services or the illegal sale of live animals. In contrast, an eyewitness video of a potential crime should not be considered to constitute illegal content, merely because it depicts an illegal act, where recording or disseminating such a video to the public is not illegal under national or Union law. In this regard, it is immaterial whether the illegality of the information or activity results from Union law or from national law that is in compliance with Union law and what the precise nature or subject matter is of the law in question.

passages.label: Recital 13
passages.text: (13) | Considering the particular characteristics of the services concerned and the corresponding need to make the providers thereof subject to certain specific obligations, it is necessary to distinguish, within the broader category of providers of hosting services as defined in this Regulation, the subcategory of online platforms.
